sections.title: Two Kinds of Charge and the Conservation Principle

board_events.text: Two Kinds of Charge
Rub a plastic comb on dry hair and it suddenly picks up tiny bits of paper. Rub a glass rod with silk, and a second rod treated the same way pushes the first one away.
Like charges repel. Unlike charges attract.

board_events.caption: Repulsion between like charges, attraction between unlike charges

board_events.text: Benjamin Franklin named them positive and negative -- arbitrarily, long before anyone knew electrons existed.
Charging = transferring electrons. Remove electrons: positive. Add electrons: negative.
No new charge is ever created -- it is only moved around.
Analogy: a kirana shop's total money (till + pockets) is fixed all day; money moves, the grand total never changes.
Charge behaves the same way: rubbing transfers electrons, so one body gains exactly what the other loses. The universe's books always balance.

segments.text: Let's start with the two most basic facts in all of electrostatics.
Think about rubbing a plastic comb on dry hair -- suddenly it can lift tiny bits of paper. Or rub a glass rod with silk, and if a second rod is treated the same way, it pushes the first one away.
That tells us something deep. There are exactly two kinds of electric charge, and like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
Same-sign charges shove each other apart. Opposite-sign charges pull together. That is the whole rulebook, in one picture.
Benjamin Franklin picked the names positive and negative, and he picked them arbitrarily -- centuries before anyone even knew electrons existed.

Today we know what is really going on. Every atom has a positive nucleus with negative electrons around it, so charging an object simply means shifting electrons. Take electrons away, and the object turns positive. Add electrons, and it turns negative.
<curious> Here is the crucial part: no new charge ever gets created. Charge only ever moves from one place to another.
Picture a busy kirana shop. The total money -- the till plus every customer's pocket -- stays fixed all day. Money moves around constantly, but nobody prints fresh notes mid transaction.
Charge behaves exactly the same way. Rubbing transfers electrons from one body to the other, so whatever one gains, the other loses. The universe's books always balance.
चलिए शुरू करते हैं electrostatics के सबसे basic दो facts से।

सोचो एक plastic comb को dry hair पर rub करो -- तुरंत वो tiny paper के bits उठा लेता है। या एक glass rod को silk से rub करो, और अगर दूसरा rod भी वैसे ही treat किया जाए, तो वो पहले वाले को push away कर देता है।
यह हमें कुछ deep बताता है। Electric charge के exactly दो types होते हैं, और like charges repel करते हैं जबकि unlike charges attract करते हैं।
Same-sign charges एक दूसरे को push करते हैं। Opposite-sign charges एक दूसरे को pull करते हैं। यही पूरा rulebook है, एक ही picture में।
Benjamin Franklin ने positive और negative नाम दिए, और वो नाम arbitrarily चुने गए थे -- electrons discover होने से भी काफी पहले।

आज हम जानते हैं असल में क्या हो रहा है। हर atom में positive nucleus होता है और उसके around negative electrons होते हैं, तो charging का मतलब simply electrons का shift होना है। Electrons हटाओ, object positive हो जाता है। Electrons add करो, object negative हो जाता है।
<curious> यहाँ एक crucial बात है: कोई भी नया charge कभी create नहीं होता। Charge सिर्फ एक जगह से दूसरी जगह move करता है।

सोचो एक busy किराना shop के बारे में। Total पैसा -- till plus हर customer की pocket -- पूरे दिन fixed रहता है। पैसा इधर-उधर move होता रहता है, लेकिन कोई भी mid-transaction fresh notes print नहीं करता।
Charge भी exactly वैसे ही behave करता है। Rubbing से electrons एक body से दूसरी body में transfer होते हैं, तो जो एक gain करता है वही दूसरा lose करता है। Universe की books हमेशा balance रहती हैं।

sections.title: Conductors, Insulators, and Earthing

board_events.text: Conductors vs Insulators
Materials split into two camps based on how freely charge moves through them.

board_events.caption: Free electrons in a conductor vs bound electrons in an insulator

board_events.text: Conductors -- metals, the human body, the earth, ionic solutions -- have loosely held electrons that roam freely, so charge spreads across the whole object almost instantly.
Insulators -- rubber, glass, dry wood, plastic -- have tightly bound electrons, so charge stays stuck exactly where you put it.
This is why a plastic comb holds its rubbed charge, but a metal rod held bare-handed does not -- the charge leaks away through you to the ground.
That leaking-away process is called earthing or grounding.
The divide is idealised -- real materials like semiconductors, and even the slightly-conducting human body, sit somewhere on a spectrum.

segments.text: Now, why does the plastic comb keep its charge while a metal rod refuses to?
It comes down to how freely charge can move through a material -- and materials split cleanly into two camps.

In a conductor, some electrons are only loosely held, so they roam freely through the material -- and because they all carry the same sign, they push each other apart until they are as spread out as they can get. In an insulator, electrons are tightly bound to their own atoms and simply cannot make that journey.
Conductors include metals, the human body, the earth itself, and ionic solutions. Because their electrons roam freely, charge placed anywhere spreads across the whole object almost instantly.
Insulators include rubber, glass, dry wood, and plastic. Their electrons are tightly bound, so charge stays stuck exactly where you put it.

That single difference explains everything. You can charge a plastic comb by rubbing, because the charge stays put. But hold a metal rod in your bare hand, and it will not hold charge at all -- it drains away through your body to the ground.
That draining-away process has a name: earthing, or grounding.
One honest caveat: this conductor-insulator split is idealised. Real materials, like semiconductors, and even the slightly-conducting human body, sit somewhere on a spectrum between the two.
अब, यह समझो कि plastic comb अपना charge क्यों रख लेता है, जबकि metal rod नहीं।
यह depend करता है कि charge कितनी freely material के through move कर सकता है -- और materials cleanly दो camps में बँट जाते हैं।

Conductor में कुछ electrons loosely held होते हैं, तो वो material के through freely roam करते हैं -- और क्योंकि सब same sign carry करते हैं, वो एक दूसरे को push करते रहते हैं जब तक जितना spread out हो सकते हैं हो नहीं जाते। Insulator में electrons अपने ही atoms से tightly bound होते हैं और वो journey कर ही नहीं सकते।
Conductors में metals, human body, earth खुद, और ionic solutions आते हैं। क्योंकि उनके electrons freely roam करते हैं, कहीं भी रखा गया charge पूरे object में almost instantly spread हो जाता है।
Insulators में rubber, glass, dry wood, और plastic आते हैं। उनके electrons tightly bound होते हैं, तो charge exactly वहीं stuck रह जाता है जहाँ उसे रखा गया।

यही single difference सब कुछ explain करता है। तुम plastic comb को rubbing से charge कर सकते हो, क्योंकि charge वहीं रुक जाता है। लेकिन metal rod को bare hand में पकड़ो, तो वो charge बिलकुल नहीं रखेगा -- वो तुम्हारे through ground में drain हो जाता है।
उस drain होने वाले process का नाम है earthing, या grounding।
एक honest caveat: यह conductor-insulator का divide idealised है। Real materials, जैसे semiconductors, और खुद slightly-conducting human body, इन दोनों के बीच एक spectrum पर कहीं बैठे होते हैं।

sections.title: Quantisation: Charge Comes in Packets

board_events.text: Charge Is Not Infinitely Divisible
A subtler, beautiful fact: you cannot have any arbitrary amount of charge.
Charge comes only in whole-number multiples of a fundamental quantum -- the charge on a single electron.

board_events.text: Like eggs sold only by the dozen, never by the half-egg -- charge comes in indivisible packets.
The elementary charge is tiny: about one point six times ten to the power negative nineteen coulomb.
At everyday, macroscopic scales this quantum is so absurdly tiny that charge appears continuous -- just as a sand dune looks smooth though it is built of discrete grains.
This quantisation is exact at every scale; it is only our inability to notice single electrons that makes charge feel smooth.

segments.text: There is one more foundational fact about charge, and it is a genuinely beautiful one.
You cannot have just any amount of charge you like -- charge is not infinitely divisible.
<excited> Charge comes only in whole-number multiples of a fundamental quantum -- the charge carried by a single electron.
Picture it as a number line where charge can only ever land on evenly spaced dots, never in the gaps between them.
Think of eggs sold only by the dozen, never by the half-egg. Charge comes in indivisible packets exactly like that.
That packet, the elementary charge, is tiny -- about one point six times ten to the power negative nineteen coulomb.

Because that quantum is so absurdly small compared to everyday charges, charge looks perfectly smooth and continuous at ordinary scales -- just like a sand dune looks smooth even though it is really built from countless discrete grains.
The quantisation itself is exact at every scale. It is only our inability to notice a single missing or extra electron that makes charge feel continuous.
Charge के बारे में एक और foundational fact है, और यह genuinely beautiful है।
तुम charge की कोई भी arbitrary amount नहीं रख सकते -- charge infinitely divisible नहीं है।
<excited> Charge सिर्फ एक fundamental quantum के whole-number multiples में आता है -- यह quantum है एक single electron का charge।
इसको एक number line की तरह सोचो जहाँ charge सिर्फ evenly spaced dots पर ही land कर सकता है, उनके बीच के gaps में कभी नहीं।
Eggs को सोचो जो सिर्फ dozen में बिकते हैं, half-egg में कभी नहीं। Charge exactly वैसे ही indivisible packets में आता है।
वो packet, elementary charge, बहुत tiny है -- roughly one point six times ten to the power negative nineteen coulomb।

क्योंकि वो quantum everyday charges के comparison में बहुत ही छोटा है, ordinary scales पर charge perfectly smooth और continuous लगता है -- बिलकुल एक sand dune की तरह जो smooth लगता है जबकि वो countless discrete grains से बना होता है।
Quantisation खुद हर scale पर exact होता है। सिर्फ हमारी यह inability है कि हम एक single missing या extra electron को notice नहीं कर सकते, इसलिए charge continuous feel होता है।

<text x="350" y="330" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" font-style="italic" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Friction: opposite signs. Conduction: same sign, and the source is drained.</text>

board_events.caption: Charging by rubbing two insulators, versus charging by direct contact

board_events.text: Procedure A -- friction. Rubbing two different insulators transfers electrons from the material that holds them less tightly to the one that holds them more tightly.
Glass rubbed with silk: the glass loses electrons and turns positive; the silk gains them and turns negative -- equal and opposite, consistent with conservation.
Procedure B -- conduction. Touch a charged body to a neutral conductor, and charge flows across until they share it.
The signature of conduction: the neutral body ends up with the same sign as the charging body, and the charging body loses some of its charge.
Keep that contrast sharp -- friction acts on two insulators and leaves them oppositely charged; conduction acts on a conductor and leaves both bodies the same sign.

segments.text: Now that we know the ground rules, let's look at how charging actually happens in practice.
There is no formal derivation for this part -- just two clean procedures worth mastering.

These two panels show the simplest ways to charge something, and I want you to watch the electron arrows in each. On the left, electrons move from glass into silk. On the right, electrons move from the neutral sphere into the positively charged one. In both cases it is electrons doing the travelling -- positive charge never moves.

Procedure A is friction. When you rub two different insulators together, electrons transfer from whichever material holds them less tightly to the one that holds them more tightly. Notice why the materials must be different -- if both gripped their electrons equally hard, there would be no reason for electrons to prefer one direction over the other, and nothing would happen.
Classic example: rub glass with silk. The glass loses electrons and turns positive. The silk gains those electrons and turns negative. Equal and opposite -- exactly what conservation demands.
Procedure B is conduction, meaning charging by contact. Touch a charged body to a neutral conductor, and charge flows across between them until they share it.
<whisper> Here is the tell-tale signature of conduction: the once-neutral body ends up with the same sign as the charging body, and the charging body itself loses some of its charge.
Keep that contrast sharp in your mind. Friction acts on two insulators and leaves them oppositely charged. Conduction acts on a conductor and leaves both bodies with the same sign.
अब जब हम ground rules जान गए हैं, देखते हैं charging practically कैसे होती है।
इस part के लिए कोई formal derivation नहीं है -- सिर्फ दो clean procedures हैं जो master करने लायक हैं।

यह दोनों panels सबसे simple तरीके दिखाते हैं किसी चीज़ को charge करने के, और मैं चाहता हूँ तुम हर एक में electron arrows देखो। बाईं तरफ, electrons glass से silk में move करते हैं। दाईं तरफ, electrons neutral sphere से positively charged sphere में move करते हैं। दोनों cases में electrons ही travel करते हैं -- positive charge कभी move नहीं करता।

Procedure A है friction। जब तुम दो different insulators को rub करते हो, electrons उस material से transfer होते हैं जो उन्हें less tightly hold करता है, उस material में जो उन्हें more tightly hold करता है। Notice करो materials different क्यों होने चाहिए -- अगर दोनों अपने electrons को equally hard पकड़ते, तो electrons के पास एक direction prefer करने की कोई वजह ही नहीं होती, और कुछ होता ही नहीं।
Classic example: glass को silk से rub करो। Glass electrons lose करके positive हो जाता है। Silk वो electrons gain करके negative हो जाता है। Equal और opposite -- exactly जो conservation demand करता है।
Procedure B है conduction, मतलब contact से charging। एक charged body को neutral conductor से touch करो, और charge उनके बीच flow करता है जब तक वो share नहीं कर लेते।
<whisper> यहाँ conduction का tell-tale signature है: पहले-neutral body अब charging body जैसा ही sign ले लेती है, और charging body खुद अपना कुछ charge lose कर देती है।
यह contrast अपने mind में sharp रखो। Friction दो insulators पर act करता है और उन्हें oppositely charged छोड़ देता है। Conduction एक conductor पर act करता है और दोनों bodies को same sign दे देता है।

board_events.caption: The four steps of charging by induction

board_events.text: Step one: bring the charged rod near, without touching, a neutral conductor. Free electrons rearrange -- the near side develops a charge opposite to the rod, the far side the same sign as the rod.
Step two: earth the conductor -- connect it to the ground -- while the rod stays exactly where it is. The like-sign charge on the far side is repelled and flows away to earth.
Step three: remove the earthing first, while the rod is still near. The conductor is now left with only the unlike charge, trapped there by the rod's attraction.
Step four: remove the rod. The induced charge spreads out over the whole conductor.
Key reasoning: because there is no contact, the rod never loses any charge -- and the conductor ends up opposite in sign to the rod.

segments.text: Here comes the procedure examiners love most -- charging by induction.
This is the single most-tested charging method, and the key feature is that it involves no contact at all.
Follow these four panels carefully -- this sequence shows up again and again in board and NEET questions.

Step one: bring the charged rod close to a neutral conductor, without touching it. The conductor's free electrons rearrange themselves -- the near side picks up a charge opposite to the rod, and the far side picks up the same sign as the rod.

Step two: earth the conductor, meaning connect it to the ground, while the rod stays exactly where it is. The like-sign charge sitting on the far side gets repelled and simply flows away into the earth.

Step three, and this order matters: remove the earthing connection first, while the rod is still sitting nearby. What is left on the conductor is only the unlike charge, trapped in place by the rod's attraction.
Step four: now remove the rod. That trapped, induced charge spreads itself out evenly over the whole conductor.

<whisper> Here is the reasoning to hold onto: because the rod never actually touches anything, it never loses any of its own charge -- yet the conductor ends up with a charge exactly opposite in sign to the rod.
यहाँ आता है वो procedure जो examiners सबसे ज्यादा पसंद करते हैं -- induction से charging।
यह सबसे ज्यादा tested charging method है, और इसकी key feature यह है कि इसमें कोई contact होता ही नहीं।
यह चार panels carefully follow करो -- यह sequence board और NEET questions में बार-बार आता है।

Step one: charged rod को neutral conductor के पास लाओ, touch किए बिना। Conductor के free electrons rearrange हो जाते हैं -- near side एक opposite charge ले लेता है rod से, और far side rod जैसा ही sign ले लेता है।
Step two: conductor को earth करो, मतलब उसे ground से connect करो, जबकि rod exactly वहीं रहा हो। Far side पर बैठा like-sign charge repel होकर simply earth में flow हो जाता है।
Step three, और यह order matter करता है: पहले earthing connection हटाओ, जबकि rod अभी भी पास है। Conductor पर सिर्फ unlike charge रह जाता है, जो rod के attraction से trapped है।
Step four: अब rod को हटाओ। वो trapped, induced charge पूरे conductor में evenly spread हो जाता है।
<whisper> यहाँ यह reasoning पकड़ के रखो: क्योंकि rod कभी actually touch नहीं करता, वो अपना कोई charge कभी lose नहीं करता -- लेकिन conductor rod से exactly opposite sign ले लेता है।

board_events.text: Touch a charged body to the metal disc on top. Charge spreads down the rod to both gold leaves.
Both leaves acquire the same sign, so they repel each other and diverge apart.
The angle of divergence shows roughly how much charge is present -- this is how the electroscope detects and measures charge.
One last subtlety: why do we never notice quantisation in daily life? Because e is so small that even a modest charge of one microcoulomb needs about six trillion electrons.
Adding or removing a single electron changes that count by roughly one part in a trillion -- utterly undetectable, so charge seems to vary smoothly even though it never really does.

segments.text: We have talked about charge as an idea -- now, how do we actually see it?
There is a wonderfully simple instrument for this job: the gold-leaf electroscope.

It is just a metal disc on top, connected by a rod down to two thin gold leaves hanging inside a glass case. Compare the two states here: on the left, uncharged, the leaves hang limply side by side. On the right, charged, they have swung apart.
Touch any charged object to the disc at the top, and charge travels down the rod to reach both gold leaves at the bottom.
Because both leaves end up with the same sign of charge, they repel each other and swing apart.

The bigger the angle they diverge to, the more charge is present -- that swing is literally how this instrument detects and roughly measures charge. And note what makes it trustworthy: the leaves are repelling, not attracting. Repulsion only ever happens between genuinely charged objects, so a diverging electroscope is proof of charge, not just a hint.

One last subtlety before we move on: why does nobody ever notice that charge is quantised? Because the elementary charge is so small that even a modest one microcoulomb charge represents roughly six trillion electrons.

Add or remove a single electron from that count, and the change is about one part in a trillion -- completely undetectable. That is exactly why charge feels perfectly smooth in everyday life, even though at heart it never is.
हमने charge को एक idea की तरह discuss किया -- अब, हम उसे actually देखते कैसे हैं?
इसके लिए एक wonderfully simple instrument है: gold-leaf electroscope।

यह सिर्फ एक metal disc है ऊपर, जो एक rod से नीचे दो thin gold leaves तक connected है, जो glass case के अंदर लटकी होती हैं। यहाँ दोनों states compare करो: बाईं तरफ, uncharged, leaves limply साथ-साथ लटकी हैं। दाईं तरफ, charged, वो apart swing कर गई हैं।
किसी भी charged object को ऊपर वाले disc से touch करो, और charge rod के through नीचे दोनों gold leaves तक पहुँच जाता है।
क्योंकि दोनों leaves same sign का charge ले लेती हैं, वो एक दूसरे को repel करके apart swing कर जाती हैं।

जितना बड़ा angle वो diverge करती हैं, उतना ज्यादा charge present है -- यह swing ही literally बताता है कि यह instrument charge कैसे detect और roughly measure करता है। और notice करो इसे trustworthy क्या बनाता है: leaves repel कर रही हैं, attract नहीं। Repulsion सिर्फ genuinely charged objects के बीच ही होता है, तो diverging electroscope charge का proof है, सिर्फ hint नहीं।

आगे बढ़ने से पहले एक last subtlety: कोई कभी यह notice क्यों नहीं करता कि charge quantised है? क्योंकि elementary charge इतना छोटा है कि एक modest one microcoulomb charge भी roughly six trillion electrons के बराबर होता है।

उस count से एक single electron add या remove करो, और change होता है roughly one part in a trillion -- बिलकुल undetectable। यही वजह है कि everyday life में charge perfectly smooth feel होता है, जबकि heart में वो कभी smooth नहीं होता।

sections.title: Formulas: Quantisation, Additivity, Conservation, and Sharing

board_events.text: Key Formulas and Definitions
Here e is the elementary charge, about $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C. An electron carries $-e$, a proton $+e$.
This is additivity: the total charge of a system is simply the algebraic sum of every individual charge, signs included.
When two identical conducting spheres carrying $q_1$ and $q_2$ touch and separate, this is exactly how the charge redistributes -- equally, using the algebraic sum.
One coulomb is enormous -- everyday charges are measured in microcoulombs or nanocoulombs. Electron mass is $9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, relevant whenever charge transfer implies mass transfer.

segments.text: Let's pin down the exact formulas behind everything we just built intuition for.
This is quantisation, written precisely: charge always equals an integer n times the elementary charge e -- n can be any positive or negative whole number, or zero.
That elementary charge is about one point six times ten to the power negative nineteen coulomb. An electron carries exactly negative e, a proton exactly positive e.
Next comes additivity, and it looks almost too simple to write down.
The total charge of any system is just the algebraic sum of every individual charge in it -- and algebraic means you keep the signs. Positive and negative charges genuinely cancel in this sum.
<curious> Now here is a formula worth memorizing cold: when two identical conducting spheres touch and separate, each one ends up with the average of the original two charges.
Notice it is the algebraic sum divided by two -- not the sum of magnitudes. Get the signs right here, or the whole answer flips.

Two quick number-sense notes. One coulomb is a genuinely enormous charge, so real-world charges live in microcoulombs or nanocoulombs. And the electron's mass, about nine point one times ten to the power negative thirty one kilogram, matters whenever a charge transfer also means a tiny mass transfer.
चलिए अब exact formulas pin down करते हैं जिनके लिए हमने अभी intuition बनाई।
यह है quantisation, precisely लिखा गया: charge हमेशा एक integer n times elementary charge e के बराबर होता है -- n कोई भी positive या negative whole number हो सकता है, या zero।
वो elementary charge roughly one point six times ten to the power negative nineteen coulomb होता है। Electron exactly negative e carry करता है, proton exactly positive e।
आगे आता है additivity, और यह लिखने में almost too simple लगता है।
किसी भी system का total charge सिर्फ हर individual charge का algebraic sum होता है -- और algebraic का मतलब है signs को रखना। Positive और negative charges genuinely इस sum में cancel हो जाते हैं।
<curious> अब यहाँ एक formula है जो cold memorize करने लायक है: जब दो identical conducting spheres touch करके separate होते हैं, हर एक original दोनों charges का average ले लेता है।
Notice करो यह algebraic sum divided by two है -- magnitudes का sum नहीं। यहाँ signs सही रखो, वरना पूरा answer flip हो जाएगा।

दो quick number-sense notes। एक coulomb genuinely एक enormous charge है, इसलिए real-world charges microcoulomb या nanocoulomb में होते हैं। और electron का mass, roughly nine point one times ten to the power negative thirty one kilogram, matter करता है जब भी charge transfer के साथ tiny mass transfer भी होता है।

sections.title: Worked Examples: Counting Electrons and a Speed-Trap Sharing Problem

board_events.text: Example 1 -- CBSE Board Level
A body carries a charge of magnitude one microcoulomb. How many excess electrons does it contain?
That works out to about $6.25 \times 10^{12}$ excess electrons. Negative charge always means excess electrons.
Example 2 -- NEET Speed Trap
Two identical conducting spheres carry $+q$ and $-3q$. They touch and separate. What is the final charge on each?

board_events.text: The trap: forgetting that sharing uses the algebraic sum, signs included -- plugging in magnitudes loses the answer.
Each sphere ends with $-q$. Sanity check: total charge before was $-2q$; total after is $-q + (-q) = -2q$. Conserved.

segments.text: Let's put quantisation and charge sharing to work with two quick board and NEET style problems.
First one: a body carries a charge of magnitude one microcoulomb. How many excess electrons does it hold?
Straight from quantisation, n equals q over e -- one microcoulomb divided by the elementary charge.
Carry out that division and you get roughly six point two five times ten to the power twelve excess electrons. Remember: a negative charge always means excess electrons sitting on the body.
Now the NEET speed trap -- this one is designed to catch you if you rush.
Two identical conducting spheres carry plus q and minus three q. They are brought into contact, then separated. What charge does each end up with?
Picture it exactly like this: before contact the spheres are wildly unequal; after contact and separation they share out evenly.
<whisper> Here is the trap students fall into -- forgetting that sharing uses the algebraic sum with signs included. Plug in bare magnitudes and you lose the correct answer entirely.
Done correctly: add plus q and minus three q, that gives minus two q, then divide by two -- each sphere ends with minus q.
Sanity check, always worth doing: total charge before contact was minus two q. Total after is minus q plus minus q, which is again minus two q. Charge is conserved, so the answer holds.
चलिए quantisation और charge sharing को use करते हैं दो quick board और NEET style problems में।
पहला: एक body का charge magnitude one microcoulomb है। उसमें कितने excess electrons हैं?
सीधा quantisation से, n equals q over e -- one microcoulomb divided by elementary charge।
यह division करो तो roughly six point two five times ten to the power twelve excess electrons मिलते हैं। याद रखो: negative charge का मतलब हमेशा excess electrons होते हैं body पर।
अब आता है NEET speed trap -- यह specially बनाया गया है उन लोगों को पकड़ने के लिए जो rush करते हैं।
दो identical conducting spheres plus q और minus three q carry करते हैं। उन्हें contact में लाया जाता है, फिर separate किया जाता है। हर एक का final charge क्या होगा?
इसको exactly ऐसे सोचो: contact से पहले spheres wildly unequal हैं; contact और separation के बाद वो evenly share हो जाते हैं।
<whisper> यहाँ students जो trap में फँसते हैं: यह भूल जाना कि sharing algebraic sum use करती है, signs के साथ। Bare magnitudes डालो तो correct answer पूरी तरह lose हो जाता है।
Correctly करके: plus q और minus three q add करो, मिलता है minus two q, फिर divide by two -- हर sphere minus q के साथ रह जाता है।
Sanity check, जो हमेशा करना चाहिए: contact से पहले total charge minus two q था। बाद में total है minus q plus minus q, जो फिर से minus two q है। Charge conserved है, तो answer सही है।

board_events.text: Example 3 -- JEE Main Level
A metal sphere has about $1.25 \times 10^{13}$ electrons removed from it. Find its charge, then find the force between two such identical spheres placed thirty centimetres apart in vacuum.
Removing electrons leaves the sphere positive: $q = 2.0\ \mu\text{C}$.

segments.text: This problem is a favourite because it chains two ideas together -- quantisation feeding straight into Coulomb's law.
A metal sphere has about twelve point five trillion electrons removed from it. Find its charge, and then find the force between two such identical spheres placed thirty centimetres apart in vacuum.
Start with quantisation: charge equals n times e, so multiply the number of electrons removed by the elementary charge.
Since we removed electrons, the sphere is left positively charged -- and the number works out to two point zero microcoulomb.
Now picture both spheres, each carrying that same positive charge, sitting thirty centimetres apart. Same sign, so we already know the force will push them apart.
Plug straight into Coulomb's law: nine times ten to the power nine, times the square of two point zero microcoulomb, divided by the square of thirty centimetres, in metres.
Because both spheres carry the identical positive charge, this one substitution hands us the force directly -- no extra bookkeeping needed.
<excited> Work through the arithmetic and you land on roughly zero point four newton, and it is repulsive, exactly as the matching signs predicted.
यह problem favourite है क्योंकि यह दो ideas को chain करता है -- quantisation सीधा Coulomb's law में feed होती है।
एक metal sphere से roughly twelve point five trillion electrons हटाए गए हैं। उसका charge निकालो, फिर दो ऐसे identical spheres, जो thirty centimetres apart रखे हैं vacuum में, उनके बीच force निकालो।
Quantisation से start करो: charge equals n times e, तो हटाए गए electrons की number को elementary charge से multiply करो।
क्योंकि हमने electrons हटाए हैं, sphere positively charged रह जाता है -- और number आता है two point zero microcoulomb।
अब सोचो दोनों spheres, हर एक same positive charge carry कर रहा है, thirty centimetres apart बैठे हैं। Same sign, तो हम already जानते हैं force उन्हें apart push करेगा।
सीधा Coulomb's law में डालो: nine times ten to the power nine, times two point zero microcoulomb का square, divided by thirty centimetres का square, metres में।
क्योंकि दोनों spheres identical positive charge carry करते हैं, यह एक substitution ही सीधा force दे देता है -- कोई extra bookkeeping नहीं चाहिए।
<excited> Arithmetic करके देखो तो roughly zero point four newton आता है, और यह repulsive है, exactly जैसा matching signs ने predict किया था।

board_events.text: After the first touch, the original and the first neutral sphere share equally: original keeps $Q/2$, sphere one gets $Q/2$.
After the second touch, the original's $Q/2$ is shared again with the next neutral sphere: original keeps $Q/4$, sphere two gets $Q/4$.
After the third touch, the original's $Q/4$ is shared once more: original keeps $Q/8$, sphere three gets $Q/8$.
Conservation check: $Q/8 + 7Q/8 = Q$. After $n$ touches the original retains $Q/2^n$ -- a geometric decay.

segments.text: This is the JEE Advanced favourite twist on charge sharing -- repeated contact, not just one touch.
A conducting sphere carries charge Q. One after another, it touches three identical neutral spheres, being separated each time before the next touch. What does the original sphere end up keeping?
Watch the pattern unfold across these three touches -- the original sphere hands away half of whatever it is currently holding, every single time.
After the first touch, the original and the first neutral sphere split equally. The original keeps Q over two, and sphere one also gets Q over two.
After the second touch, that remaining Q over two on the original gets shared again with the next neutral sphere. The original now keeps Q over four, and sphere two also gets Q over four.
After the third touch, the same thing happens to the Q over four. The original keeps Q over eight, and sphere three gets Q over eight.
Add up what the three outside spheres are carrying: Q over two, plus Q over four, plus Q over eight, comes out to seven Q over eight.

Always finish with a conservation check: Q over eight plus seven Q over eight gives back the full Q. And notice the deeper pattern -- after n such touches, the original retains Q divided by two to the power n, a beautiful geometric decay.
यह JEE Advanced का favourite twist है charge sharing पर -- repeated contact, सिर्फ एक touch नहीं।
एक conducting sphere charge Q carry करता है। एक के बाद एक, यह तीन identical neutral spheres को touch करता है, हर बार next touch से पहले separate होता है। Original sphere final में क्या keep करता है?
देखो pattern कैसे unfold होता है इन तीन touches में -- original sphere हर बार अपने current holding का आधा ही दे देता है।
First touch के बाद, original और first neutral sphere equally split करते हैं। Original Q over two keep करता है, और sphere one भी Q over two पाता है।
Second touch के बाद, original का बाकी Q over two next neutral sphere के साथ फिर share होता है। Original अब Q over four keep करता है, और sphere two भी Q over four पाता है।
Third touch के बाद, वही चीज़ Q over four के साथ होती है। Original Q over eight keep करता है, और sphere three Q over eight पाता है।
तीन outside spheres का total add करो: Q over two, plus Q over four, plus Q over eight, आता है seven Q over eight।

हमेशा conservation check के साथ finish करो: Q over eight plus seven Q over eight, full Q वापस दे देता है। और deeper pattern notice करो -- n touches के बाद, original Q divided by two to the power n retain करता है, एक beautiful geometric decay।

sections.title: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Charge Fundamentals

board_events.text: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Charge Fundamentals

Pitfall: confusing induction with conduction. Conduction needs contact, gives the same sign, and the rod loses charge. Induction needs no contact, gives the opposite sign, and the rod keeps its charge.
Pitfall: treating attraction as proof of charge. A charged object also attracts neutral conductors by induction -- only repulsion proves a body is truly charged.
Pitfall: forgetting signs in additivity or sharing. The share-equally rule uses the algebraic sum divided by two -- plugging in magnitudes loses the answer.
Pitfall: sloppy quantisation checks. A valid charge must give a whole number when divided by e -- always do that division to test 'is this possible' questions.
Pro-tip: for identical conductors touching, jump straight to the average. For N identical spheres touching all at once, each ends with the total divided by N. Always finish with a conservation check.
With these fundamentals locked in, we are ready to put real numbers on the push and pull between charges -- that is exactly where Coulomb's Law comes in next.

segments.text: Before we move to Coulomb's Law, let's lock in the mistakes that cost the most marks in this subtopic.

First pitfall: confusing induction with conduction. Conduction needs actual contact, gives both bodies the same sign, and the rod loses some charge. Induction needs no contact, gives the opposite sign, and the rod keeps every bit of its charge.

Second pitfall: treating attraction as proof that something is charged. A charged object attracts neutral conductors too, purely by induction. Only repulsion is a sure test that a body actually carries charge.

Third pitfall: forgetting signs when adding or sharing charge. The share-equally rule always uses the algebraic sum divided by two -- drop the signs and plug in bare magnitudes, and the answer falls apart.
Fourth pitfall: sloppy quantisation checks. Any valid charge must give a whole number when divided by e. Whenever a question asks whether some value is a possible charge, do that division and check.

<curious> Here is a pro-tip that collapses most charge-sharing questions into one line: for identical conductors touching, jump straight to the average of the two charges. For N identical spheres touching all at once, each one ends with the total charge divided by N. And always, always finish with a conservation check -- total before must equal total after.
With these fundamentals locked in, we are ready to put real numbers on the push and pull between charges -- and that is exactly where Coulomb's Law takes over next.
Coulomb's Law पर जाने से पहले, चलिए वो mistakes lock in करते हैं जो इस subtopic में सबसे ज्यादा marks काटती हैं।

पहला pitfall: induction को conduction से confuse करना। Conduction में actual contact चाहिए, दोनों bodies same sign लेती हैं, और rod कुछ charge lose करता है। Induction में contact की ज़रूरत नहीं, opposite sign मिलता है, और rod अपना पूरा charge रखता है।
दूसरा pitfall: attraction को charge का proof समझना। एक charged object neutral conductors को भी attract करता है, purely induction से। सिर्फ repulsion ही sure test है कि body actually charged है।
तीसरा pitfall: charge add या share करते वक्त signs भूल जाना। Share-equally rule हमेशा algebraic sum divided by two use करता है -- signs drop करो और bare magnitudes डालो, तो answer बिखर जाता है।

चौथा pitfall: sloppy quantisation checks। कोई भी valid charge, e से divide करने पर whole number देना चाहिए। जब भी कोई question पूछे कि कोई value possible charge है या नहीं, यह division करके check करो।

<curious> यहाँ एक pro-tip है जो ज़्यादातर charge-sharing questions को एक line में collapse कर देता है: identical conductors के touch करने पर, सीधा दोनों charges का average ले लो। N identical spheres के एक साथ touch करने पर, हर एक total charge divided by N लेता है। और हमेशा, हमेशा conservation check के साथ finish करो -- total पहले, total बाद में बराबर होना चाहिए।
यह fundamentals lock in होने के बाद, हम ready हैं charges के बीच push और pull पर real numbers रखने के लिए -- और वही exactly है जहाँ Coulomb's Law आगे लेते है।

sections.title: Force Across Empty Space and Coulomb's Torsion Balance

board_events.text: Force Across Empty Space
A charge sitting quietly in one corner of a room can shove or tug another charge across the room -- with no string, no rod, no contact of any kind.
The whole job of Coulomb's Law is to put a precise number on that invisible push-or-pull.

board_events.text: Charles Augustin de Coulomb worked this out in 1784 using a torsion balance -- a tiny see-saw hanging from a thin fibre that twists when a force acts on it.
The twist angle is the measurement: a bigger twist means a bigger force.
His clever trick: he varied charge without ever measuring it. Touch a charged sphere to an identical uncharged one and, by symmetry, the charge splits exactly in half. Touch again for a quarter.
By comparing twists for different charge pairs at different separations, he pinned down two clean dependencies -- and those two are the whole law.

segments.text: <curious> Let's start with something that should genuinely bother you.

A charge sitting quietly in one corner of a room can shove or tug another charge clear across that room. No string between them, no rod, no contact of any kind. They simply feel each other through empty space.
The entire job of Coulomb's Law is to put a precise number on that invisible push-or-pull -- to say exactly how strong it is.
And here is the apparatus that first measured it. A light horizontal beam hangs from a very thin fibre. Put charges on the balls at the ends, and the force between them twists the whole beam around.
Charles Augustin de Coulomb built this in seventeen eighty four. It is called a torsion balance -- essentially a tiny see-saw hanging from a fibre that twists when a force acts on it.
The twist angle is the measurement. A bigger twist means a bigger force, and the fibre is delicate enough to register forces far too small to feel.

<excited> Now here is his genuinely clever trick. He needed to vary the charge, but he had no way to measure charge -- that is what he was trying to discover. So he used symmetry instead. Touch a charged metal sphere to an identical uncharged one, and the charge must split exactly in half, because there is no reason for either sphere to get more. Touch again, and you have a quarter.
By comparing the twist for different charge pairs at different separations, he pinned down two clean dependencies. Those two dependencies are the entire law, and we will take them one at a time.
<curious> चलिए कुछ ऐसे से शुरू करते हैं जो तुम्हें genuinely परेशान करना चाहिए।

एक charge जो room के एक corner में चुपचाप बैठा है, वो पूरे room के पार दूसरे charge को push या pull कर सकता है। उनके बीच कोई string नहीं, कोई rod नहीं, किसी भी तरह का contact नहीं। वो simply empty space के through एक दूसरे को feel करते हैं।
Coulomb's Law का पूरा काम है उस invisible push-या-pull पर एक precise number रखना -- यह बताना कि वो exactly कितना strong है।
और यह रहा वो apparatus जिसने इसे पहली बार measure किया। एक light horizontal beam एक बहुत thin fibre से लटका है। सिरों की balls पर charges रखो, और उनके बीच का force पूरे beam को twist कर देता है।
Charles Augustin de Coulomb ने यह seventeen eighty four में बनाया था। इसे torsion balance कहते हैं -- essentially एक tiny see-saw जो एक fibre से लटका है जो force act करने पर twist हो जाता है।
Twist angle ही measurement है। बड़ा twist मतलब बड़ा force, और fibre इतना delicate है कि वो ऐसे forces register कर लेता है जो feel करने के लिए बहुत छोटे हैं।

<excited> अब यह उनका genuinely clever trick है। उन्हें charge vary करना था, लेकिन उनके पास charge measure करने का कोई तरीका नहीं था -- वही तो वो discover करने की कोशिश कर रहे थे। तो उन्होंने symmetry use की। एक charged metal sphere को identical uncharged sphere से touch करो, और charge exactly आधा-आधा बँट जाएगा, क्योंकि किसी एक sphere को ज्यादा मिलने की कोई वजह ही नहीं है। फिर touch करो, और एक quarter मिल जाता है।
अलग-अलग charge pairs के लिए, अलग-अलग separations पर twist compare करके, उन्होंने दो clean dependencies pin down कीं। वही दो dependencies पूरा law हैं, और हम उन्हें एक-एक करके लेंगे।

sections.title: The Two Dependencies: Product of Charges and Inverse Square

board_events.text: The Two Dependencies
First dependency: the force grows with the product of the two charges. Double either charge and the force doubles.
Second dependency: the force falls off as the square of the distance. Push the charges twice as far apart and the force drops to one quarter -- not one half.

board_events.text: Picture the aroma drifting out of a mithai shop. Stand at the counter and it is overpowering; walk to twice the distance and it is far weaker than half strength.
The smell spreads out over a sphere whose surface area grows as distance squared -- so its intensity must fall as one over distance squared.
That is why the r squared sits in the denominator. It is not an arbitrary choice -- it is geometry.
This is the famous inverse-square law -- the same mathematical shape Newton had found for gravity a century earlier.

segments.text: So what exactly did those torsion-balance measurements reveal? Two dependencies, and they are both simple.

The first: the force grows with the product of the two charges. Double either one of them, and the force doubles. Double both, and the force goes up four times. It is the product that matters, not the sum.

The second is the one that catches people out. The force falls off as the square of the distance. Push the charges twice as far apart and the force does not drop to one half -- it drops all the way to one quarter.
Look at why that has to be true. The same influence, spreading outward, has to cover a surface that grows as the distance squared -- so it gets diluted by exactly that factor.
Here is the everyday version. Picture the aroma drifting out of a mithai shop. Stand right at the counter and it is overpowering. Walk to twice that distance and it is far weaker than half strength.

Why? Because the smell spreads out over a sphere, and a sphere's surface area grows as the distance squared. The same amount of aroma has four times the area to cover, so its intensity falls to a quarter.
That is exactly why the r squared sits in the denominator of Coulomb's Law. It is not an arbitrary choice somebody made -- it is geometry, and it could hardly have come out any other way.

This is the famous inverse-square law. And notice that it is the very same mathematical shape Newton had found for gravity a full century earlier -- a coincidence worth holding onto, because we are about to make something of it.
तो उन torsion-balance measurements ने exactly क्या reveal किया? दो dependencies, और दोनों simple हैं।
पहली: force दोनों charges के product के साथ बढ़ता है। किसी भी एक को double करो, force double हो जाता है। दोनों को double करो, force चार गुना हो जाता है। Product matter करता है, sum नहीं।
दूसरी वो है जो लोगों को पकड़ लेती है। Force distance के square के हिसाब से गिरता है। Charges को दोगुना दूर करो और force आधा नहीं होता -- वो सीधा एक चौथाई हो जाता है।
देखो यह सच क्यों होना ही चाहिए। वही influence, बाहर की तरफ फैलते हुए, एक ऐसे surface को cover करना पड़ता है जो distance के square से बढ़ता है -- तो वो exactly उसी factor से dilute हो जाता है।
यह रहा everyday version। मिठाई की दुकान से आती खुशबू को सोचो। बिलकुल counter पर खड़े हो तो वो overpowering है। दोगुनी दूरी पर चलो और वो आधी strength से भी काफी कम है।
क्यों? क्योंकि खुशबू एक sphere पर फैलती है, और sphere का surface area distance के square से बढ़ता है। उतनी ही खुशबू को चार गुना area cover करना है, तो उसकी intensity एक चौथाई रह जाती है।
यही exactly वजह है कि Coulomb's Law के denominator में r squared बैठा है। यह किसी की बनाई arbitrary choice नहीं है -- यह geometry है, और यह शायद ही किसी और तरह से निकल सकता था।

यह है famous inverse-square law। और notice करो यह वही mathematical shape है जो Newton ने पूरे एक century पहले gravity के लिए पाया था -- यह coincidence पकड़ के रखो, क्योंकि हम अभी इससे कुछ बनाने वाले हैं।

sections.title: Newton's Third Law in Electrostatics

board_events.text: Newton's Third Law in Electrostatics
There is one more idea baked into Coulomb's Law, and it is beautifully democratic.
The force the first charge feels from the second is exactly equal and opposite to the force the second feels from the first -- no matter which charge is bigger.

board_events.text: Look at the arrows: they are the same length. The nine-times-bigger charge is not pushed nine times harder.
The reason is built into the formula. The product of the two charges is identical whichever one you call 'first' -- the expression is symmetric.
Exam trap: candidates guess the bigger charge pushes harder. It does not. This is tested almost every year.
It is like two kids in a tug-of-war: the rope tension on each child is identical even if one is twice the other's size. Newton's third law, showing up in electrostatics.

segments.text: There is one more idea baked into Coulomb's Law, and I would call it beautifully democratic.
It concerns what happens when the two charges are wildly unequal -- which is where most students' intuition quietly goes wrong.
The force the first charge feels from the second is exactly equal and opposite to the force the second feels from the first. And this holds no matter which charge is bigger.
Look carefully at this picture. On the left is a charge Q. On the right is a charge nine times larger. And the two force arrows are drawn the same length, because they genuinely are the same size.
That should feel slightly wrong the first time you see it. The nine-times-bigger charge is not pushed nine times harder. It feels exactly what the small charge feels.

The reason is sitting right in the formula. The force depends on the product of the two charges -- and a product does not care about order. Multiply Q by nine Q, or nine Q by Q, and you get the same number either way. The expression is perfectly symmetric.
<whisper> This is an exam trap that gets set almost every single year. Candidates reason that the bigger charge must push harder, and they lose the mark. It does not.

Think of two kids in a tug-of-war. The rope tension pulling on each child is identical, even if one kid is twice the other's size. That is Newton's third law -- and Coulomb's Law obeys it automatically, without anyone having to bolt it on.
Coulomb's Law में एक और idea baked है, और मैं इसे beautifully democratic कहूँगा।
यह उस situation से related है जब दोनों charges wildly unequal हों -- और यहीं ज़्यादातर students की intuition चुपचाप गलत हो जाती है।
पहला charge दूसरे से जो force feel करता है, वो exactly equal और opposite है उस force के जो दूसरा पहले से feel करता है। और यह चलता है चाहे कोई भी charge बड़ा हो।
इस picture को ध्यान से देखो। बाईं तरफ है charge Q। दाईं तरफ है नौ गुना बड़ा charge। और दोनों force arrows same length के बने हैं, क्योंकि वो genuinely same size के हैं।
पहली बार देखने पर यह थोड़ा गलत लगना चाहिए। नौ गुना बड़ा charge नौ गुना ज्यादा push नहीं होता। वो exactly उतना ही feel करता है जितना छोटा charge करता है।

वजह सीधे formula में बैठी है। Force दोनों charges के product पर depend करता है -- और product को order की परवाह नहीं होती। Q को नौ Q से multiply करो, या नौ Q को Q से, दोनों तरह same number आता है। Expression perfectly symmetric है।
<whisper> यह एक exam trap है जो लगभग हर साल set होता है। Candidates सोचते हैं कि बड़ा charge ज्यादा push करता होगा, और mark गँवा देते हैं। ऐसा नहीं होता।

दो बच्चों की tug-of-war सोचो। रस्सी का tension हर बच्चे पर identical होता है, चाहे एक बच्चा दूसरे से दोगुना size का हो। यही है Newton's third law -- और Coulomb's Law इसे automatically obey करता है, बिना किसी के इसे अलग से जोड़े।

sections.title: Coulomb Force versus Gravity, and Why Matter Seems Inert

board_events.text: Coulomb Force versus Gravity
Coulomb's Law mirrors Newton's law of gravitation closely. Both are central, inverse-square forces -- swap charges for masses and k for G, and the algebra looks identical.
But two deep differences set them apart.
First: gravity is only ever attractive -- masses never repel. Electric charges do both, depending on sign.
Second: the electric force is staggeringly stronger. Between two protons, Coulomb repulsion outmuscles gravitational attraction by a factor of around ten to the power thirty six.
That is why, at the scale of atoms and molecules, gravity is utterly irrelevant and electric forces run the show.
So a natural puzzle: if the electric force is this monstrous, why are we not flung across the room every time we walk past a charged object?

Because ordinary matter is almost perfectly neutral. Positive and negative charges cancel to extraordinary precision. The giant force is always there -- it is just hiding behind near-perfect cancellation.

segments.text: It is worth pausing to compare Coulomb's Law with the other great inverse-square law you already know.

Coulomb's Law mirrors Newton's law of gravitation remarkably closely. Both are central forces, meaning they act along the line joining the two objects. Both are inverse-square. Swap charges for masses, swap k for G, and the algebra looks essentially identical.
But two deep differences set them apart, and both matter.
The first: gravity is only ever attractive. Masses never repel each other. Electric charges do both, and which one you get depends entirely on the signs.

The second difference is the staggering one. The electric force is vastly stronger. Take two protons: the Coulomb repulsion between them outmuscles their gravitational attraction by a factor of around ten to the power thirty six. That is a one followed by thirty six zeros.
This is why, down at the scale of atoms and molecules, gravity is completely irrelevant. Chemistry, materials, biology -- electric forces run the entire show, and gravity does not get a vote.
<curious> Which raises a natural puzzle. If the electric force really is this monstrous, why are we not flung across the room every time we walk past a charged object?

Because ordinary matter is almost perfectly neutral. Every object packs in nearly equal amounts of positive and negative charge, and their pushes and pulls cancel to extraordinary precision. We only notice electric forces when that delicate balance gets disturbed -- a comb rubbed on hair, a balloon on a sweater, the crackle of a synthetic shirt on a dry winter day. The giant force is always there. It is just hiding behind near-perfect cancellation.
थोड़ा रुककर Coulomb's Law को उस दूसरे great inverse-square law से compare करना worth है जो तुम पहले से जानते हो।

Coulomb's Law, Newton के law of gravitation को remarkably closely mirror करता है। दोनों central forces हैं, मतलब वो दोनों objects को जोड़ने वाली line के along act करते हैं। दोनों inverse-square हैं। Charges की जगह masses रखो, k की जगह G रखो, और algebra essentially identical लगता है।
लेकिन दो deep differences उन्हें अलग करते हैं, और दोनों matter करते हैं।
पहला: gravity सिर्फ attractive होता है। Masses कभी एक दूसरे को repel नहीं करते। Electric charges दोनों करते हैं, और कौन सा मिलेगा यह पूरी तरह signs पर depend करता है।

दूसरा difference staggering है। Electric force vastly ज्यादा strong है। दो protons लो: उनके बीच Coulomb repulsion, उनके gravitational attraction को roughly ten to the power thirty six के factor से outmuscle करता है। यह एक के बाद छत्तीस zeros हैं।
यही वजह है कि atoms और molecules के scale पर gravity completely irrelevant है। Chemistry, materials, biology -- electric forces पूरा show चलाते हैं, और gravity को vote तक नहीं मिलता।
<curious> जिससे एक natural puzzle खड़ा होता है। अगर electric force सच में इतना monstrous है, तो हम हर बार किसी charged object के पास से गुज़रते वक्त room के पार क्यों नहीं उछल जाते?

क्योंकि ordinary matter almost perfectly neutral होता है। हर object में लगभग बराबर मात्रा में positive और negative charge भरा होता है, और उनके pushes और pulls extraordinary precision से cancel हो जाते हैं। हमें electric forces सिर्फ तब दिखते हैं जब वो delicate balance disturb होता है -- बालों पर rub किया comb, sweater पर balloon, dry winter day में synthetic shirt की crackle। वो giant force हमेशा वहाँ है। बस near-perfect cancellation के पीछे छुपा हुआ है।

board_events.text: Building the Vector Form
Coulomb's measurements gave two proportionalities. Combining them and inserting a constant k gives the scalar law -- but a force has direction, so we must point it.

board_events.caption: Position vectors, the separation vector, and how the sign of the product sets the direction

board_events.text: Let the charges sit at position vectors $\vec{r}_1$ and $\vec{r}_2$. Define the separation vector pointing from one to two.
The force acts along the line joining the charges -- this is what makes it a central force. Attach the magnitude to that direction.

If $q_1 q_2 \gt 0$ the prefactor is positive and the force points along $\hat{r}_{21}$, away from $q_1$: repulsion. If $q_1 q_2 \lt 0$ it flips the vector: attraction. One equation, no separate cases.
Swap the labels and, since $\hat{r}_{12} = -\hat{r}_{21}$, you get exactly the opposite vector -- Newton's third law falls straight out of the algebra.

segments.text: Now let's turn those two dependencies into the equation you will actually write in an exam.

Coulomb's measurements gave us two proportionalities: force goes as the product of the charges, and force goes as one over r squared. Combine them and insert a constant k, and you have the scalar law. But a force has direction as well as size -- so we still have to point it somewhere.
Here is the setup. The two charges sit somewhere in space, measured from an origin O. What we need is a vector that points from one charge to the other.
Let the charges sit at position vectors r one and r two. The separation vector pointing from charge one to charge two is just the difference between them.
So r two one equals r two minus r one, and dividing that by its own magnitude gives us r hat two one -- a unit vector, pure direction, length one.

Now, the force acts along the line joining the charges. Nothing in the setup picks out any other direction. That property has a name: we call this a central force. So we attach the magnitude we already have to this direction.
And that gives the vector form of Coulomb's Law: F two one equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times q one q two over r squared, times the unit vector r hat two one.

<excited> Here is what makes this equation so elegant. If the product q one q two is positive -- like charges -- the prefactor is positive, so the force points along r hat two one, away from charge one. That is repulsion. If the product is negative -- unlike charges -- the prefactor flips the whole vector around, pointing it back towards charge one. That is attraction. One single equation handles both cases, with no separate rules to remember.

And one last bonus. Swap the labels to get the force on charge one instead. Since r hat one two is just the negative of r hat two one, you get exactly the opposite vector. Newton's third law falls straight out of the algebra -- we never had to assume it.
अब उन दो dependencies को उस equation में बदलते हैं जो तुम actually exam में लिखोगे।

Coulomb की measurements ने हमें दो proportionalities दीं: force charges के product के हिसाब से चलता है, और force one over r squared के हिसाब से चलता है। इन्हें combine करो और एक constant k डालो, तो scalar law मिल जाता है। लेकिन force में size के साथ direction भी होती है -- तो हमें अभी भी उसे कहीं point करना है।
यह रहा setup। दोनों charges space में कहीं बैठे हैं, एक origin O से measure किए गए। हमें चाहिए एक vector जो एक charge से दूसरे की तरफ point करे।
मान लो charges position vectors r one और r two पर बैठे हैं। Charge one से charge two की तरफ point करने वाला separation vector बस उनका difference है।
तो r two one equals r two minus r one, और उसे उसकी अपनी magnitude से divide करने पर मिलता है r hat two one -- एक unit vector, pure direction, length one।

अब, force charges को जोड़ने वाली line के along act करता है। Setup में कुछ भी किसी और direction को pick नहीं करता। इस property का एक नाम है: हम इसे central force कहते हैं। तो हम जो magnitude पहले से रखते हैं, उसे इस direction से जोड़ देते हैं।
और इससे मिलता है Coulomb's Law का vector form: F two one equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times q one q two over r squared, times unit vector r hat two one।

<excited> यहाँ देखो इस equation को इतना elegant क्या बनाता है। अगर product q one q two positive है -- like charges -- तो prefactor positive है, तो force r hat two one के along point करता है, charge one से दूर। यह repulsion है। अगर product negative है -- unlike charges -- तो prefactor पूरे vector को पलट देता है, उसे charge one की तरफ वापस point कर देता है। यह attraction है। एक ही equation दोनों cases handle कर लेता है, बिना अलग rules याद रखे।

और एक last bonus। Labels swap करके charge one पर force निकालो। क्योंकि r hat one two बस r hat two one का negative है, तुम्हें exactly opposite vector मिलता है। Newton's third law सीधा algebra से निकल आता है -- हमें उसे assume करना ही नहीं पड़ा।

sections.title: The Superposition Principle

board_events.text: The Superposition Principle
Coulomb's Law only ever knows about two charges. So what happens when there are three, or ten?

board_events.text: Experiment confirms the answer: the total force on any one charge is the vector sum of the individual two-body forces, each calculated as if the others were not there.
The crucial physical claim: the forces do not interfere with one another. A third charge does not modify the force between the first two -- it simply adds its own.
This is why you must add as vectors, never as numbers. Adding magnitudes is one of the most common JEE Main errors.
For a continuous charge distribution, this sum becomes an integral over infinitesimal charge elements -- the same principle, taken to the limit.

segments.text: Coulomb's Law, as we have written it, only ever knows about two charges. So what do we do when there are three, or ten, or a whole charged rod?
This is not a small gap. Almost every real problem has more than two charges in it, so we need a rule for combining them.

Look at the middle charge here. It feels a separate pull or push from each of the other three, and each of those arrows is worked out independently. Then they add head to tail to give the green resultant.
Experiment confirms the rule: the total force on any one charge is the vector sum of the individual two-body forces, with each one calculated exactly as if the other charges were not there at all.

Written out, the net force on charge one is the sum of F one two, F one three, and so on -- or compactly, q one over four pi epsilon nought, times the sum over j of q j over r one j squared, times the corresponding unit vector.

Sit with the physical claim inside that formula, because it is not obvious. The forces do not interfere with one another. Bringing in a third charge does not modify the force between the first two -- it simply adds a new force of its own. Nature did not have to work this way, but it does.

<whisper> And here is the consequence that costs marks: you must add these as vectors, never as plain numbers. Adding magnitudes directly is one of the single most common errors in JEE Main, and we will see it bite in a worked example shortly.

One last extension. For a continuous charge distribution -- a rod, a ring, a sheet -- this sum becomes an integral over infinitesimal charge elements. It is the same principle, just taken to the limit.
Coulomb's Law, जैसा हमने लिखा है, सिर्फ दो charges के बारे में जानता है। तो क्या करें जब तीन हों, या दस, या एक पूरा charged rod?
यह कोई छोटा gap नहीं है। लगभग हर real problem में दो से ज्यादा charges होते हैं, तो हमें उन्हें combine करने का एक rule चाहिए।
यहाँ बीच वाले charge को देखो। वो बाकी तीनों से अलग-अलग pull या push feel करता है, और उनमें से हर arrow independently निकाला जाता है। फिर वो head to tail add होकर green resultant देते हैं।
Experiment इस rule को confirm करता है: किसी भी एक charge पर total force, individual two-body forces का vector sum होता है, और हर एक को exactly ऐसे निकाला जाता है जैसे बाकी charges वहाँ हैं ही नहीं।

लिखकर देखें तो charge one पर net force है F one two, F one three, वगैरह का sum -- या compactly, q one over four pi epsilon nought, times sum over j of q j over r one j squared, times corresponding unit vector।

उस formula के अंदर छुपे physical claim के साथ थोड़ा बैठो, क्योंकि वो obvious नहीं है। Forces एक दूसरे में interfere नहीं करते। एक तीसरा charge लाने से पहले दोनों के बीच का force modify नहीं होता -- वो बस अपना एक नया force add कर देता है। Nature को ऐसे काम करना ज़रूरी नहीं था, लेकिन वो करती है।

<whisper> और यह रहा वो consequence जो marks काटता है: इन्हें vectors की तरह add करना है, plain numbers की तरह कभी नहीं। Magnitudes को सीधा add कर देना JEE Main की सबसे common errors में से एक है, और हम इसे थोड़ी देर में एक worked example में काटते हुए देखेंगे।
एक last extension। Continuous charge distribution के लिए -- एक rod, एक ring, एक sheet -- यह sum एक integral बन जाता है infinitesimal charge elements पर। वही principle है, बस limit तक ले जाया गया।

sections.title: Limiting Conditions and the Effect of a Medium

board_events.text: When Coulomb's Law Applies -- and What a Medium Does
Coulomb's Law in its simple form is not a free pass. It applies strictly under three conditions.

One: the charges must be point charges -- their physical size tiny compared to the separation r. Useful loophole: a uniformly charged sphere acts, from the outside, as if all its charge sat at the centre.
Two: the charges must be at rest. Moving charges produce extra magnetic forces that this law ignores entirely.
Three: we are working in vacuum or air. Inside a material medium the force gets reduced, and the formula needs a correction.

board_events.text: When charges sit inside a material, its molecules polarise -- their own internal charges shift slightly to oppose the field -- and this screening weakens the force by the factor K.
Because K is never less than one, a medium can only reduce the force, never amplify it.
The law has been tested from subatomic separations of about ten to the power minus fifteen metres right up to laboratory scales -- part of why we trust it so deeply.

segments.text: Before we start calculating, we need to be honest about when this law actually applies.
Coulomb's Law in its simple form is not a free pass you can use anywhere. It holds strictly under three conditions, and exam questions love to violate them quietly.

Condition one: the charges must be point charges, meaning their physical size is tiny compared to the separation between them. There is one very useful loophole here though -- a uniformly charged sphere acts, from the outside, exactly as if all its charge were concentrated at its centre. So spheres are usually fine.
Condition two: the charges must be at rest. This is electrostatics. Moving charges produce additional magnetic forces, and this law knows nothing about them.
Condition three: we are working in vacuum, or in air, which is close enough. Put the same charges inside a material medium and the force gets reduced -- the formula needs a correction factor.
And this picture shows you why that reduction happens, which is worth understanding rather than memorising.

When charges sit inside a material, the molecules of that material polarise. Their own internal charges shift slightly, lining up to oppose the field between our two charges. That screening partly shields each charge from the other, weakening the force by a factor K, the dielectric constant.

<curious> Notice a consequence worth locking in: because K is never less than one, a medium can only ever reduce the force. It can never amplify it. If your answer has a medium making a force stronger, something has gone wrong.

One closing note on how much we should trust all this. The law has been tested from subatomic separations of about ten to the power minus fifteen metres, right up to large laboratory scales. That enormous range holding up is a large part of why we rely on it so completely.
Calculations शुरू करने से पहले, हमें honest होना पड़ेगा कि यह law actually कब apply होता है।
Coulomb's Law अपने simple form में कोई free pass नहीं है जो कहीं भी use कर लो। यह strictly तीन conditions के तहत चलता है, और exam questions उन्हें चुपचाप violate करना पसंद करते हैं।

Condition one: charges point charges होने चाहिए, मतलब उनका physical size उनके बीच की separation के comparison में tiny हो। हालाँकि यहाँ एक बहुत useful loophole है -- एक uniformly charged sphere, बाहर से, exactly ऐसे act करता है जैसे उसका सारा charge centre पर concentrated हो। तो spheres usually चल जाते हैं।
Condition two: charges at rest होने चाहिए। यह electrostatics है। Moving charges additional magnetic forces produce करते हैं, और यह law उनके बारे में कुछ नहीं जानता।
Condition three: हम vacuum में काम कर रहे हैं, या air में, जो काफी करीब है। वही charges किसी material medium के अंदर रखो और force कम हो जाता है -- formula को एक correction factor चाहिए।
और यह picture दिखाती है वो reduction होता क्यों है, जो memorise करने से बेहतर है समझना।

जब charges किसी material के अंदर बैठते हैं, उस material के molecules polarise हो जाते हैं। उनके अपने internal charges थोड़ा shift हो जाते हैं, हमारे दोनों charges के बीच के field को oppose करने के लिए line up हो जाते हैं। यह screening हर charge को दूसरे से partly shield कर देती है, force को K factor से कमज़ोर कर देती है, जिसे dielectric constant कहते हैं।

<curious> एक consequence notice करो जो lock करने लायक है: क्योंकि K कभी one से कम नहीं होता, medium सिर्फ force को कम ही कर सकता है। वो उसे कभी amplify नहीं कर सकता। अगर तुम्हारे answer में medium force को strong बना रहा है, तो कुछ गलत हुआ है।

एक closing note कि हमें इस सब पर कितना trust करना चाहिए। यह law roughly ten to the power minus fifteen metres की subatomic separations से लेकर बड़े laboratory scales तक test किया जा चुका है। इतनी enormous range पर टिके रहना ही बड़ी वजह है कि हम इस पर इतना completely rely करते हैं।

sections.title: Formulas and Constants for Coulomb's Law

board_events.text: Coulomb's Law -- Formulas and Constants
That is the magnitude form. Use absolute values here, and decide attraction or repulsion separately from the signs.
The vector form, where $\hat{r}_{21}$ points from $q_1$ towards $q_2$. Substitute charges with their signs and direction takes care of itself.

Constants: $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}$ C squared per newton per metre squared, with dimensional formula $[M^{-1}L^{-3}T^{4}A^{2}]$. And $k \approx 9.0 \times 10^{9}$ newton metre squared per coulomb squared, dimensions $[ML^{3}T^{-4}A^{-2}]$.
K is a pure number, dimensionless, never below one. It equals one for vacuum and about one point zero zero zero six for air.

One coulomb is enormous: two one-coulomb charges one metre apart in vacuum would repel with about nine times ten to the power nine newton -- roughly the weight of a million tonnes. Real work happens in microcoulombs and nanocoulombs.

segments.text: Let's collect every formula from this subtopic in one place, with the constants you will need alongside them.
First, the magnitude form: F equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times the absolute value of q one q two, over r squared. Or equivalently, k times the same thing.

Notice the absolute-value bars. When you only want the size of the force, use magnitudes, and work out attraction or repulsion separately from the physics of the signs. Mixing the two produces phantom negative forces.
Second, the vector form, which we built up in an earlier section: F two one equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times q one q two over r squared, times r hat two one.

Here r hat two one points from charge one towards charge two. Substitute the charges complete with their signs, and the direction takes care of itself -- no separate cases for attraction and repulsion.

Third, the medium correction: the force in a medium equals the vacuum force divided by K. And K, the dielectric constant, is also called the relative permittivity -- it is the permittivity of the medium divided by the permittivity of free space.

Now the constants. Epsilon nought, the permittivity of free space, is eight point eight five four times ten to the power minus twelve, in coulomb squared per newton per metre squared. Its dimensional formula is M to the minus one, L to the minus three, T to the fourth, A squared. And k is about nine times ten to the power nine newton metre squared per coulomb squared, with dimensions M L cubed T to the minus four A to the minus two.

K itself is a pure number -- dimensionless, and never below one. It equals exactly one for vacuum, and about one point zero zero zero six for air, which is why we treat air as vacuum without a second thought.

<excited> One last piece of number sense that puts the whole chapter in perspective. One coulomb is an enormous charge. Two one-coulomb charges placed just one metre apart in vacuum would repel each other with about nine times ten to the power nine newton -- roughly the weight of a million tonnes. That is why all real work in this chapter happens in microcoulombs and nanocoulombs.
चलिए इस subtopic के हर formula को एक जगह इकट्ठा करते हैं, साथ में वो constants जो तुम्हें चाहिए होंगे।
पहला, magnitude form: F equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times absolute value of q one q two, over r squared। या equivalently, k times वही चीज़।

Absolute-value bars notice करो। जब तुम्हें सिर्फ force का size चाहिए, magnitudes use करो, और attraction या repulsion अलग से signs की physics से निकालो। दोनों को mix करने पर phantom negative forces बन जाते हैं।
दूसरा, vector form, जो हमने पिछले section में build किया: F two one equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times q one q two over r squared, times r hat two one।

यहाँ r hat two one, charge one से charge two की तरफ point करता है। Charges को उनके signs के साथ substitute करो, और direction अपने आप संभल जाती है -- attraction और repulsion के लिए अलग cases नहीं चाहिए।

तीसरा, medium correction: medium में force equals vacuum force divided by K। और K, dielectric constant, को relative permittivity भी कहते हैं -- यह medium की permittivity divided by free space की permittivity है।

अब constants। Epsilon nought, permittivity of free space, है eight point eight five four times ten to the power minus twelve, coulomb squared per newton per metre squared में। इसका dimensional formula है M to the minus one, L to the minus three, T to the fourth, A squared। और k है roughly nine times ten to the power nine newton metre squared per coulomb squared, dimensions M L cubed T to the minus four A to the minus two।
K खुद एक pure number है -- dimensionless, और कभी one से कम नहीं। यह vacuum के लिए exactly one है, और air के लिए लगभग one point zero zero zero six, इसीलिए हम air को बिना सोचे vacuum मान लेते हैं।

<excited> एक last number sense जो पूरे chapter को perspective में रख देता है। एक coulomb एक enormous charge है। दो one-coulomb charges सिर्फ एक metre दूर vacuum में रखे जाएँ तो वो roughly nine times ten to the power nine newton से repel करेंगे -- लगभग दस लाख टन का weight। इसीलिए इस chapter का सारा real काम microcoulombs और nanocoulombs में होता है।

board_events.text: That evaluates to $F = 2.4$ N. The charges carry opposite signs, so the force is attractive, directed along the line joining them.
Example 2 -- NEET Speed Trap
Two charges repel with force $F$ at separation $r$ in vacuum. They are immersed in kerosene, dielectric constant $K = 4$. What separation restores the force to $F$?
The trap: students divide the separation by K, giving $r/4$. Wrong -- the medium weakens force by K, but distance enters as $r^2$, so you compensate by root K only.
Bring them closer to $r/2$. Mental check: halving the distance quadruples the force, exactly cancelling the division by four from the medium.

segments.text: Time to put the law to work. Two examples here -- a straight board-level calculation, and a NEET trap that catches a lot of people.
First: two point charges, plus four microcoulomb and minus six microcoulomb, sit thirty centimetres apart in vacuum. Find the magnitude and the nature of the force between them.
Start by looking at the setup. The signs are opposite, so before calculating anything we already know the force pulls them together -- both arrows point inward.

Now the magnitude. Use the absolute-value form: k times four microcoulomb times six microcoulomb, divided by zero point three zero metres squared. Notice the conversions -- microcoulombs to coulombs, and centimetres to metres, done before anything else.

Work that through and the force comes out to two point four newton. And the nature: the charges carry opposite signs, so it is attractive, directed along the line joining them. Always state both -- magnitude and nature -- for full marks.
Now the NEET speed trap, and this one is genuinely well designed.

Two charges repel with force F at separation r in vacuum. They are then immersed in kerosene, which has dielectric constant K equal to four. By how much must the separation change so that the force returns to its original value F?

<whisper> Here is the trap. Many students see K equals four and divide the separation by four, giving r over four. That is wrong. The medium weakens the force by K, but distance enters the formula as r squared -- so to compensate you only need root K, not K.

Do it as a ratio and it falls out in one line. In vacuum the force is k q squared over r squared. In kerosene at a new separation r dash, it is k q squared over K r dash squared. Set them equal, the k and q squared cancel, and you get r dash equals r over root K, which is r over two.

So bring them closer, to half the original separation. And here is the mental check that confirms it: halving the distance quadruples the force, which exactly cancels the division by four that the medium imposed. The numbers agree.
अब law को काम पर लगाने का समय। यहाँ दो examples हैं -- एक सीधा board-level calculation, और एक NEET trap जो बहुत लोगों को पकड़ लेता है।
पहला: दो point charges, plus four microcoulomb और minus six microcoulomb, vacuum में thirty centimetres दूर रखे हैं। उनके बीच force की magnitude और nature निकालो।
Setup देखने से शुरू करो। Signs opposite हैं, तो कुछ भी calculate करने से पहले ही हम जानते हैं कि force उन्हें साथ खींचेगा -- दोनों arrows अंदर की तरफ point करते हैं।

अब magnitude। Absolute-value form use करो: k times four microcoulomb times six microcoulomb, divided by zero point three zero metres squared। Conversions notice करो -- microcoulombs से coulombs, और centimetres से metres, सबसे पहले किए गए।

इसे हल करो तो force आता है two point four newton। और nature: charges opposite signs रखते हैं, तो यह attractive है, उन्हें जोड़ने वाली line के along। हमेशा दोनों बताओ -- magnitude और nature -- full marks के लिए।
अब NEET speed trap, और यह genuinely well designed है।

दो charges vacuum में separation r पर force F से repel करते हैं। फिर उन्हें kerosene में डुबोया जाता है, जिसका dielectric constant K equals four है। Separation कितना बदलना पड़ेगा ताकि force वापस original value F पर आ जाए?

<whisper> यह रहा trap। बहुत students K equals four देखकर separation को चार से divide कर देते हैं, r over four दे देते हैं। यह गलत है। Medium force को K से कमज़ोर करता है, लेकिन distance formula में r squared की तरह आता है -- तो compensate करने के लिए सिर्फ root K चाहिए, K नहीं।

इसे ratio की तरह करो और यह एक line में निकल आता है। Vacuum में force है k q squared over r squared। Kerosene में नई separation r dash पर, यह है k q squared over K r dash squared। दोनों बराबर रखो, k और q squared cancel हो जाते हैं, और मिलता है r dash equals r over root K, जो है r over two।

तो उन्हें पास लाओ, original separation के आधे पर। और यह रहा mental check जो इसे confirm करता है: distance आधी करने से force चार गुना हो जाता है, जो exactly उस division by four को cancel कर देता है जो medium ने लगाया था। Numbers आपस में agree करते हैं।

board_events.text: A corner charge feels two such forces, with sixty degrees between them -- the triangle's interior angle. Resolve them, do not add them as numbers.
