segments.text: This is a classic JEE Main problem because it combines two things at once -- superposition, and then an equilibrium condition.

Three identical charges of two microcoulomb sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle with side ten centimetres. Part a: find the net electrostatic force on any one charge. Part b: what charge placed at the centroid would hold the whole system in equilibrium?

Start with the picture, because the geometry is the whole problem. Focus on the top vertex. It is pushed by each of the other two charges, along the two sides, away from them. Those two red arrows are what we need to combine.

First get the size of one pairwise force. k times Q squared over a squared, with Q as two microcoulomb and a as zero point one zero metre, gives three point six newton. Each of the two forces has exactly this magnitude, since all three charges are identical and all sides are equal.

Now the crucial step, and the one that separates correct answers from wrong ones. The corner charge feels two forces of three point six newton each, with sixty degrees between them, because that is the triangle's interior angle. You must resolve these as vectors. Adding them as numbers to get seven point two would be exactly the error we warned about in the superposition section.

For two equal vectors F at an angle of sixty degrees, the resultant is two F cos of half that angle, which is two F cos thirty, which simplifies to root three times F. So the net force is root three times three point six, about six point two four newton.

And its direction: radially outward, straight away from the centroid along the median. Which immediately tells us what part b needs. To cancel an outward push, the centroid charge must pull each corner inward -- so q nought has to be negative. We have the sign before we have the number.

For the magnitude: the centroid sits a distance a over root three from each vertex, so d squared is a squared over three. That means the centroid's force on a corner charge is three k q nought Q over a squared. Set that equal to the root three F we need to cancel, and the a squared and k cancel out, leaving three times q nought equals root three Q. So q nought is Q over root three, about one point one five microcoulomb.

<whisper> So the answers are: net force about six point two four newton outward, and q nought about minus one point one five microcoulomb at the centroid. And one flag worth adding, because examiners like it: this equilibrium is unstable. Nudge any charge and the system runs away. Students routinely find the number and forget to check the stability.
यह एक classic JEE Main problem है क्योंकि यह एक साथ दो चीज़ें combine करता है -- superposition, और फिर equilibrium condition।

तीन identical charges, दो microcoulomb के, एक equilateral triangle के corners पर बैठे हैं जिसकी side दस centimetre है। Part a: किसी भी एक charge पर net electrostatic force निकालो। Part b: centroid पर कौन सा charge रखने से पूरा system equilibrium में रहेगा?
Picture से शुरू करो, क्योंकि geometry ही पूरी problem है। Top vertex पर focus करो। उसे बाकी दोनों charges push करते हैं, दोनों sides के along, उनसे दूर। वो दो red arrows ही हमें combine करने हैं।

पहले एक pairwise force का size निकालो। k times Q squared over a squared, Q दो microcoulomb और a zero point one zero metre के साथ, देता है three point six newton। दोनों forces की exactly यही magnitude है, क्योंकि तीनों charges identical हैं और सारी sides बराबर हैं।

अब crucial step, और वही जो सही answers को गलत से अलग करता है। Corner charge तीन point छह newton के दो forces feel करता है, जिनके बीच साठ degrees हैं, क्योंकि यही triangle का interior angle है। इन्हें vectors की तरह resolve करना है। इन्हें numbers की तरह जोड़कर seven point two निकालना exactly वही error होगी जिसकी हमने superposition section में चेतावनी दी थी।

साठ degrees पर दो equal vectors F के लिए, resultant होता है two F cos of आधा angle, यानी two F cos thirty, जो simplify होकर root three times F बन जाता है। तो net force है root three times three point six, लगभग six point two four newton।

और उसकी direction: radially outward, centroid से सीधा दूर, median के along। जो तुरंत बता देता है कि part b को क्या चाहिए। एक outward push को cancel करने के लिए, centroid charge को हर corner को अंदर खींचना होगा -- तो q nought negative होना ही चाहिए। Number से पहले हमारे पास sign आ गया।

Magnitude के लिए: centroid हर vertex से a over root three की दूरी पर बैठता है, तो d squared है a squared over three। इसका मतलब centroid का force एक corner charge पर है three k q nought Q over a squared। इसे उस root three F के बराबर रखो जिसे cancel करना है, और a squared तथा k cancel हो जाते हैं, बचता है three times q nought equals root three Q। तो q nought है Q over root three, लगभग one point one five microcoulomb।

<whisper> तो answers हैं: net force लगभग six point two four newton outward, और q nought लगभग minus one point one five microcoulomb centroid पर। और एक flag जोड़ने लायक है, क्योंकि examiners को यह पसंद है: यह equilibrium unstable है। किसी भी charge को हल्का सा हिलाओ और system भाग जाता है। Students अक्सर number निकाल लेते हैं और stability check करना भूल जाते हैं।

sections.title: Worked Example: Force From a Charged Rod by Integration

board_events.text: Example 4 -- JEE Advanced Level

A thin rod of length $L$ carries total charge $Q$ uniformly. A point charge $q$ lies on the rod's axis, a distance $d$ from the near end. Find the force on $q$, then verify it reduces correctly as the rod shrinks to a point.

board_events.text: The rod is not a point charge, so Coulomb's Law cannot be applied in one shot. Slice it into elements and superpose.
Every element pushes along the same axis, so the forces add as plain scalars -- that symmetry is the gift in this problem. Let x run from $d$ to $d+L$.
Now the deep step -- the limiting check. Let the rod collapse to a point, so $L$ tends to zero.
That is exactly the point-charge Coulomb's Law. The result passes the sanity test. For $q = 1\ \mu\text{C}$, $Q = 5\ \mu\text{C}$, $d = 0.10$ m, $L = 0.30$ m, the force is about $1.125$ N.

segments.text: This one steps up to JEE Advanced, and it is the first time in this chapter we will need calculus.

A thin rod of length L carries a total charge Q spread uniformly along it. A point charge q sits on the rod's axis, a distance d from the near end. Find the force on q -- and then verify your result behaves correctly when the rod shrinks to a point.
Here is the setup. The point charge is on the left. The rod stretches away to the right, and we have highlighted one thin slice of it -- an element of width dx, sitting a distance x from the charge.

The reason we need this slicing is important. The rod is not a point charge, so we cannot apply Coulomb's Law in one shot. But each infinitesimal element is small enough to count as a point charge -- so we apply the law to each element and superpose.

Set up the pieces. The linear charge density lambda is Q over L. An element of width dx carries charge dq equal to lambda dx. And the force it exerts on q is k q dq over x squared, which becomes k q lambda dx over x squared.

Now here is the gift in this problem. Every single element lies on the same axis as the charge, so every force it produces points along that same line. There is no vector resolution to do -- the contributions add as plain scalars. Then x simply runs from d at the near end to d plus L at the far end.

Integrate one over x squared and you get minus one over x, evaluated between those limits. That gives one over d minus one over d plus L. Combine those fractions and the L in the numerator cancels against the L hidden inside lambda -- leaving the beautifully clean result: F equals k q Q over d times d plus L.
<excited> And now the deep step, the one that separates a good solution from a complete one. Test the formula by letting the rod collapse to a point -- that is, let L tend to zero.
Put L equals zero into the answer and the denominator becomes d times d, which is d squared.

That is exactly the point-charge Coulomb's Law we started the subtopic with. The result passes the sanity test, which confirms the integration was set up correctly. Run the numbers for a one microcoulomb charge, a five microcoulomb rod, d of zero point one zero metre and L of zero point three zero metre, and the force comes out to about one point one two five newton.
यह JEE Advanced level पर जाता है, और इस chapter में पहली बार हमें calculus चाहिए होगी।

L लंबाई का एक thin rod है जिस पर total charge Q uniformly फैला है। एक point charge q rod के axis पर बैठा है, near end से d दूरी पर। q पर force निकालो -- और फिर verify करो कि तुम्हारा result सही behave करता है जब rod सिकुड़कर एक point बन जाए।
यह रहा setup। Point charge बाईं तरफ है। Rod दाईं तरफ फैला है, और हमने उसका एक thin slice highlight किया है -- dx चौड़ाई का एक element, charge से x दूरी पर बैठा।

इस slicing की ज़रूरत क्यों है, यह important है। Rod एक point charge नहीं है, तो हम Coulomb's Law को एक ही बार में apply नहीं कर सकते। लेकिन हर infinitesimal element इतना छोटा है कि उसे point charge माना जा सके -- तो हम law को हर element पर apply करके superpose करते हैं।

Pieces set up करो। Linear charge density lambda है Q over L। dx चौड़ाई का element charge dq रखता है, जो lambda dx के बराबर है। और q पर उसका force है k q dq over x squared, जो बन जाता है k q lambda dx over x squared।

अब यह रहा इस problem का gift। हर एक element charge के same axis पर है, तो वो जो भी force देता है वो उसी line के along point करता है। कोई vector resolution नहीं करना -- contributions plain scalars की तरह add हो जाते हैं। फिर x simply near end पर d से लेकर far end पर d plus L तक चलता है।

One over x squared को integrate करो तो मिलता है minus one over x, उन limits के बीच evaluate किया गया। इससे मिलता है one over d minus one over d plus L। इन fractions को combine करो और numerator का L, lambda के अंदर छुपे L से cancel हो जाता है -- बचता है यह beautifully clean result: F equals k q Q over d times d plus L।
<excited> और अब deep step, वही जो एक अच्छे solution को complete solution से अलग करता है। Formula को test करो rod को एक point में collapse करके -- यानी L को zero की तरफ ले जाओ।
Answer में L equals zero रखो और denominator बन जाता है d times d, जो है d squared।

यह exactly वही point-charge Coulomb's Law है जिससे हमने subtopic शुरू किया था। Result sanity test pass कर लेता है, जो confirm करता है कि integration सही set up हुआ था। एक microcoulomb charge, पाँच microcoulomb rod, d zero point one zero metre और L zero point three zero metre के लिए numbers चलाओ, तो force आता है लगभग one point one two five newton।

sections.title: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Coulomb's Law

board_events.text: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Coulomb's Law
Pitfall: plugging in signs where you should not. For magnitude, use the absolute value of the product and decide attraction or repulsion separately. Signs belong in the vector form.

Pitfall: treating force as a scalar in superposition. With three or more charges the individual forces must be added as vectors -- saying the equilateral-triangle resultant is $2F$ instead of $\sqrt{3}F$ is among the most common JEE Main errors.
Pitfall: confusing K with root K. Force scales as one over K, but the distance needed to restore the force scales as root K. Tie the factor to what is actually being asked.
Pitfall: unit slips. Distances arrive in centimetres, charges in microcoulomb or nanocoulomb. Forgetting to convert is the single biggest source of 'right method, wrong answer'.
Pro-tip: for multiple-charge problems, do not compute each force fully. Write everything as multiples of one reference force, add the geometry, and substitute numbers only at the very end.
And always run the dimensional or limiting check, the way we let $L$ tend to zero in the rod problem. If a formula does not collapse to the point-charge result, it is wrong.
Coulomb's Law tells us the force between charges. But it leaves a question open: how does one charge know the other is there at all? That question leads us to the electric field.

segments.text: Let's close this subtopic by collecting the mistakes that cost the most marks -- and the habits that save them.

First pitfall: plugging in signs where you should not. When you only want the magnitude of a force, use the absolute value of the product and decide attraction or repulsion separately from the physics. Signs belong in the vector form. Mixing the two produces phantom negative forces that mean nothing.

Second pitfall, and the expensive one: treating force as a scalar during superposition. With three or more charges, the individual Coulomb forces must be added as vectors, not as numbers. Saying the equilateral-triangle resultant is two F instead of root three F is among the most common errors in all of JEE Main -- and we walked straight through that example so you would recognise it.

Third pitfall: confusing K with root K. The force scales as one over K. But the distance you would need to restore the force scales as root K. Students routinely apply the wrong one. Tie the factor to what the question is actually asking for.

Fourth pitfall, and the most avoidable of all: unit slips. Distances arrive in centimetres, charges in microcoulomb or nanocoulomb. Forgetting to convert -- one centimetre is ten to the minus two metres, one microcoulomb is ten to the minus six coulomb -- is the single biggest source of right method, wrong answer.

<curious> Now the pro-tip that will genuinely speed you up. For almost any multiple-charge problem, do not compute each force fully at the start. Write everything as multiples of a single reference force -- something like k q squared over a squared -- then add the geometry, and substitute actual numbers only at the very end. You will cut the arithmetic roughly in half and dodge most calculator slips.

And always run the dimensional or limiting check, exactly the way we let L tend to zero in the rod problem. If a formula does not collapse to the point-charge result when it should, it is wrong, and you have caught it before the examiner did.

One last thought to carry forward. Coulomb's Law tells us the force between two charges very precisely. But it quietly leaves a question open: how does one charge know the other is there at all, across empty space? That question is what leads us to the electric field, and that is where we go next.
इस subtopic को बंद करते हैं वो mistakes इकट्ठा करके जो सबसे ज्यादा marks काटती हैं -- और वो habits जो उन्हें बचाती हैं।

पहला pitfall: signs वहाँ डालना जहाँ नहीं डालने चाहिए। जब सिर्फ force की magnitude चाहिए, product की absolute value use करो और attraction या repulsion अलग से physics से तय करो। Signs vector form में जाते हैं। दोनों mix करने पर phantom negative forces बनते हैं जिनका कोई मतलब नहीं।

दूसरा pitfall, और महँगा वाला: superposition में force को scalar मानना। तीन या ज्यादा charges के साथ, individual Coulomb forces vectors की तरह add होने चाहिए, numbers की तरह नहीं। Equilateral-triangle का resultant root three F की जगह two F कहना पूरे JEE Main की सबसे common errors में से एक है -- और हम उस example से सीधा गुज़रे ताकि तुम उसे पहचान सको।

तीसरा pitfall: K को root K से confuse करना। Force one over K के हिसाब से scale करता है। लेकिन force restore करने के लिए जो distance चाहिए वो root K के हिसाब से scale करती है। Students अक्सर गलत वाला apply कर देते हैं। Factor को इससे बाँधो कि question actually क्या पूछ रहा है।

चौथा pitfall, और सबसे ज्यादा avoidable: unit slips। Distances centimetres में आती हैं, charges microcoulomb या nanocoulomb में। Convert करना भूल जाना -- एक centimetre है ten to the minus two metres, एक microcoulomb है ten to the minus six coulomb -- यही सबसे बड़ी वजह है right method, wrong answer की।

<curious> अब वो pro-tip जो तुम्हें genuinely तेज़ करेगा। लगभग किसी भी multiple-charge problem में, शुरू में हर force पूरा मत निकालो। सब कुछ एक single reference force के multiples में लिखो -- कुछ जैसे k q squared over a squared -- फिर geometry जोड़ो, और actual numbers बिलकुल आखिर में substitute करो। तुम arithmetic लगभग आधी कर दोगे और ज़्यादातर calculator slips से बच जाओगे।

और हमेशा dimensional या limiting check चलाओ, exactly जैसे हमने rod problem में L को zero की तरफ ले जाया। अगर कोई formula वहाँ point-charge result में collapse नहीं होता जहाँ होना चाहिए, तो वो गलत है, और तुमने उसे examiner से पहले पकड़ लिया।

एक last सोच आगे ले जाने के लिए। Coulomb's Law हमें दो charges के बीच का force बहुत precisely बता देता है। लेकिन वो चुपचाप एक सवाल खुला छोड़ देता है: एक charge को यह पता कैसे चलता है कि दूसरा वहाँ है भी, खाली space के पार? यही सवाल हमें electric field तक ले जाता है, और वहीं हम अगली बार जाएँगे।

sections.title: How Does One Charge Know the Other Is There?

board_events.text: How Does One Charge Know the Other Is There?
Coulomb's Law told us the force between two charges. But that picture has something slightly uncomfortable about it.
How does charge A 'know' that charge B is sitting three metres away? They never touch, and nothing visible passes between them.
Physicists resolved this discomfort with one of the most powerful ideas in all of science -- the field.

board_events.text: The trick is to split the interaction into two stages. A charge does not reach out and grab another charge directly.
Instead it modifies the space around it -- setting up an electric field everywhere, a kind of invisible tension filling the region.
Any second charge that wanders in simply responds to the field at its own location. Neither charge ever needs to know about the other.

segments.text: <curious> We finished the last subtopic with a question hanging in the air, and now it is time to answer it.

Coulomb's Law told us exactly how strong the force between two charges is. That was real progress. But if you look closely at the picture it gives us, something about it should feel slightly uncomfortable.

How does charge A know that charge B is sitting three metres away? They never touch. Nothing visible passes between them. And yet A somehow adjusts its behaviour based on something happening across the room. Stated plainly, that is a strange claim about the world.
Physicists resolved this discomfort with what I would call one of the most powerful ideas in all of science. The idea of a field.

Look at how it restructures the problem. On the left, a single charge sitting alone, with arrows filling the space around it. On the right, a second charge arriving and feeling a push from the arrows already there.
The trick is to split the interaction into two separate stages. A charge does not reach out across space and grab another charge directly. That is the part we quietly stop believing.

Instead, a charge modifies the space around it. It sets up an electric field everywhere -- a sort of invisible tension filling the whole region, present at every point, whether or not anything is there to feel it.

Then any second charge that wanders in simply responds to the field at its own location. And that is the beautiful part: the source charge and the second charge never need to know about each other at all. Each one only ever deals with the field at the point where it happens to sit.
<curious> हमने पिछला subtopic एक सवाल हवा में छोड़कर खत्म किया था, और अब उसका जवाब देने का समय है।
Coulomb's Law ने हमें exactly बता दिया कि दो charges के बीच force कितना strong है। वो real progress थी। लेकिन अगर तुम उस picture को ध्यान से देखो जो वो देता है, तो कुछ थोड़ा uncomfortable लगना चाहिए।

Charge A को कैसे पता चलता है कि charge B तीन metre दूर बैठा है? वो कभी touch नहीं करते। उनके बीच कुछ visible नहीं गुज़रता। और फिर भी A किसी तरह अपना behaviour उस चीज़ के हिसाब से adjust कर लेता है जो room के पार हो रही है। सीधे-सीधे कहें तो यह दुनिया के बारे में एक अजीब claim है।
Physicists ने इस discomfort को हल किया उस idea से जिसे मैं पूरे science के सबसे powerful ideas में से एक कहूँगा। Field का idea।
देखो यह problem को कैसे restructure करता है। बाईं तरफ, एक अकेला charge, जिसके चारों तरफ की space arrows से भरी है। दाईं तरफ, एक दूसरा charge आता है और पहले से मौजूद arrows से push feel करता है।
Trick है interaction को दो अलग stages में बाँटना। एक charge space के पार हाथ बढ़ाकर दूसरे charge को सीधा नहीं पकड़ता। यही वो हिस्सा है जिस पर हम चुपचाप विश्वास करना छोड़ देते हैं।

इसके बजाय, एक charge अपने चारों तरफ की space को modify कर देता है। वो हर जगह एक electric field set up कर देता है -- एक तरह का invisible tension जो पूरे region को भर देता है, हर point पर मौजूद, चाहे उसे feel करने वाला कोई हो या न हो।

फिर जो भी दूसरा charge वहाँ आता है, वो simply अपनी जगह के field को respond करता है। और यही beautiful हिस्सा है: source charge और दूसरे charge को एक दूसरे के बारे में जानने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं। हर एक सिर्फ उस field से deal करता है जो उसकी अपनी जगह पर है।

board_events.text: Picture a still pond. Drop a stone and ripples spread outward, filling the whole surface. A leaf floating far away bobs up and down.
Not because it feels the stone directly -- but because it responds to the ripple that has arrived at its spot.
We define the field at a point as the force per unit positive charge that a tiny test charge would feel there.
Because the field is a property of space set up by the source, it exists whether or not a test charge is actually present.
The test charge must be vanishingly small. A real one would itself disturb the source distribution, so this definition is strictly a limiting one as $q_0$ tends to zero.

segments.text: The field idea is intuitive once you have the right picture in your head, so let me give you the one that works best.
Here it is. A stone dropped into a still pond, ripples spreading outward across the whole surface, and a leaf floating far away.
Picture that pond. You drop the stone, and ripples spread outward, filling the entire surface. Some distance away, a leaf floating on the water starts to bob up and down.

Now, why does the leaf move? Not because it feels the stone directly -- the stone is metres away and sank long ago. The leaf responds to the ripple that has arrived at its own spot. The stone created the disturbance; the leaf reacts to the local disturbance. The electric field is exactly that ever-present disturbance a charge creates in space.
So let's make it quantitative. We define the electric field at a point as the force per unit positive charge that a tiny test charge would feel if you placed it there.
In symbols: E equals F over q nought. Take the force the test charge feels, divide by the size of that test charge, and what is left describes the space itself rather than the test charge.

<excited> And that division is the whole point. Because we divided out the test charge, the field is a property of the space, set up by the source alone. It exists at every point whether or not any test charge is actually sitting there. The pond has ripples even where there is no leaf.

One honest caveat on the definition. The test charge must be vanishingly small. A real test charge, being a charge itself, would push the source charges around and change the very field we are trying to measure. So strictly, this definition is a limiting one -- we let q nought tend to zero, and take the limit of the ratio.
Field का idea intuitive हो जाता है जब सही picture दिमाग में हो, तो मैं तुम्हें वही देता हूँ जो सबसे अच्छा काम करती है।
यह रही। एक शांत तालाब में गिराया गया पत्थर, ripples जो पूरे surface पर फैल रही हैं, और दूर तैरता हुआ एक पत्ता।
उस तालाब को सोचो। तुम पत्थर गिराते हो, और ripples बाहर की तरफ फैलती हैं, पूरे surface को भर देती हैं। कुछ दूरी पर, पानी पर तैरता एक पत्ता ऊपर-नीचे हिलने लगता है।

अब, पत्ता हिलता क्यों है? इसलिए नहीं कि वो पत्थर को सीधा feel करता है -- पत्थर metres दूर है और कब का डूब चुका है। पत्ता उस ripple को respond करता है जो उसकी अपनी जगह पर पहुँची है। पत्थर ने disturbance बनाई; पत्ता local disturbance पर react करता है। Electric field exactly वही ever-present disturbance है जो एक charge space में बनाता है।
तो चलो इसे quantitative बनाते हैं। हम किसी point पर electric field को define करते हैं per unit positive charge force के रूप में, जो एक tiny test charge वहाँ रखने पर feel करेगा।
Symbols में: E equals F over q nought। Test charge जो force feel करता है वो लो, उस test charge के size से divide करो, और जो बचता है वो space को describe करता है, test charge को नहीं।

<excited> और वही division पूरी बात है। क्योंकि हमने test charge को divide करके हटा दिया, field अब space की property है, अकेले source से बनी हुई। वो हर point पर exist करती है चाहे वहाँ कोई test charge बैठा हो या न हो। तालाब में ripples वहाँ भी हैं जहाँ कोई पत्ता नहीं।

Definition पर एक honest caveat। Test charge vanishingly small होना चाहिए। एक real test charge, खुद charge होने के नाते, source charges को इधर-उधर धकेल देगा और वही field बदल देगा जिसे हम measure करने की कोशिश कर रहे हैं। तो strictly, यह definition एक limiting definition है -- हम q nought को zero की तरफ ले जाते हैं, और ratio की limit लेते हैं।

board_events.text: Like Coulomb forces, fields obey superposition. The field from many sources is just the vector sum of the individual fields.
Each source contributes as if the others were absent -- and the contributions add as vectors, never as numbers.

segments.text: Now let's work out what the field of the simplest possible source actually looks like.

Put a single point charge Q alone in space. We already know the Coulomb force it would exert on a test charge sitting a distance r away. Divide that force by the test charge, exactly as the definition tells us to -- and watch what happens. The test charge cancels out and disappears from the expression entirely.

What remains is the field of a point charge: E equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times Q over r squared, in the radial direction. Notice there is no trace of any test charge left. This is a statement purely about Q and about space.

And here is what that looks like. Around a positive charge the arrows point outward in every direction. Around a negative charge they point inward. In both cases the arrows shrink as you move away, because of that one over r squared.

The direction comes from a convention worth stating clearly: the field points away from a positive charge and towards a negative one. Why? Because the field is defined by the force on a positive test charge, and a positive test charge is pushed away from positive and pulled towards negative. Fix that convention once and you never have to re-derive it.
Now, what if there is more than one source charge? Look at this arrangement -- a positive charge and a negative charge, and the point P where we want the total field.

Just like Coulomb forces, fields obey superposition. The field at any point due to many sources is simply the vector sum of the individual fields, each one calculated as if the other sources were not there.
Written out: the net field is the sum over all sources i of one over four pi epsilon nought, times q i over r i squared, times the corresponding unit vector.

<whisper> And the same warning applies as before, because it costs the same marks. The contributions add as vectors, never as plain numbers. In the picture, the arrow from the positive source points away from it, the arrow from the negative source points towards it, and only after adding them head to tail do you get the true net field.
अब निकालते हैं कि सबसे simple source का field actually कैसा दिखता है।

Space में एक अकेला point charge Q रखो। हम पहले से जानते हैं कि वो r दूरी पर बैठे test charge पर कितना Coulomb force लगाएगा। उस force को test charge से divide करो, exactly जैसा definition कहती है -- और देखो क्या होता है। Test charge cancel होकर expression से पूरी तरह गायब हो जाता है।

जो बचता है वो है point charge का field: E equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times Q over r squared, radial direction में। Notice करो किसी test charge का कोई निशान नहीं बचा। यह purely Q के बारे में और space के बारे में statement है।

और यह रहा वो कैसा दिखता है। Positive charge के चारों तरफ arrows हर direction में बाहर की ओर point करते हैं। Negative charge के चारों तरफ वो अंदर की ओर point करते हैं। दोनों cases में दूर जाने पर arrows छोटे होते जाते हैं, उसी one over r squared की वजह से।

Direction एक convention से आती है जिसे साफ कहना ज़रूरी है: field positive charge से दूर point करता है और negative की तरफ। क्यों? क्योंकि field को positive test charge पर force से define किया गया है, और positive test charge positive से दूर धकेला जाता है और negative की तरफ खींचा जाता है। यह convention एक बार fix कर लो और फिर कभी दोबारा derive नहीं करना पड़ेगा।
अब, अगर एक से ज्यादा source charge हों तो? इस arrangement को देखो -- एक positive charge और एक negative charge, और वो point P जहाँ हमें total field चाहिए।

Coulomb forces की तरह ही, fields भी superposition obey करते हैं। कई sources की वजह से किसी point पर field simply individual fields का vector sum होता है, हर एक ऐसे निकाला गया जैसे बाकी sources हैं ही नहीं।
लिखकर: net field है सभी sources i पर sum, one over four pi epsilon nought, times q i over r i squared, times corresponding unit vector।

<whisper> और वही warning फिर से लागू है, क्योंकि यह उतने ही marks काटती है। Contributions vectors की तरह add होते हैं, plain numbers की तरह कभी नहीं। Picture में, positive source से arrow उससे दूर point करता है, negative source से arrow उसकी तरफ, और इन्हें head to tail जोड़ने के बाद ही सही net field मिलता है।

board_events.text: Rule one: field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges.
Rule two: the tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the field there.
Rule three: closely spaced lines mean a stronger field. The density of lines carries the magnitude.
Rule four: two field lines can never cross each other.
The reason for rule four is airtight: at a crossing point the field would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible.
That last rule is a favourite exam target, usually disguised as 'lines can cross where the field is strong'. They cannot cross anywhere.

segments.text: Drawing a little arrow at every single point in space gets crowded very fast. So we use a cleaner picture that carries exactly the same information -- field lines.
The idea is to trace continuous curves through space that follow the field, rather than sampling it point by point with arrows.

Look at these three panels. On the left, lines running between a positive and a negative charge. In the middle, lines radiating out from a single positive charge. At the bottom, the one configuration that is forbidden.

Rule one: field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges. Positive charges are sources, negative charges are sinks. If a line seems to come from nowhere, there is a positive charge off the edge of your diagram.

Rule two: the tangent to a field line at any point gives you the direction of the field at that point. That is what makes these curves useful rather than decorative -- you can read the direction off them anywhere along their length.

Rule three: closely spaced lines mean a stronger field. Notice in the middle panel how the lines are packed tightly near the charge and spread apart further out -- that spreading is the one over r squared falloff, drawn geometrically.
Rule four, and this is the one exams love: two field lines can never cross each other. Not anywhere, not under any circumstances.

<curious> And the reason is completely airtight, which is why it is worth understanding rather than memorising. Suppose two lines did cross. At the crossing point, rule two says the tangent gives the field direction -- but there would be two different tangents, so the field would have to point in two directions at once. A field has one value at each point. So crossing is simply impossible.

Watch for how this gets tested. The trap is usually phrased as 'field lines can cross where the field is strong', which sounds plausible because students remember that lines crowd together in strong-field regions. Crowding is not crossing. They can get arbitrarily close, and they still never touch.
Space के हर एक point पर एक छोटा arrow बनाना बहुत जल्दी crowded हो जाता है। तो हम एक cleaner picture use करते हैं जो exactly वही information रखती है -- field lines।
Idea यह है कि space में continuous curves trace की जाएँ जो field को follow करें, बजाय इसके कि arrows से point-by-point sample किया जाए।
इन तीन panels को देखो। बाईं तरफ, एक positive और एक negative charge के बीच चलती lines। बीच में, एक अकेले positive charge से बाहर निकलती lines। नीचे, वो एक configuration जो forbidden है।

Rule one: field lines positive charges पर शुरू होती हैं और negative charges पर खत्म। Positive charges sources हैं, negative charges sinks। अगर कोई line कहीं से भी न आती दिखे, तो तुम्हारे diagram के किनारे से बाहर कोई positive charge है।

Rule two: किसी भी point पर field line की tangent तुम्हें उस point पर field की direction देती है। यही इन curves को useful बनाता है, decorative नहीं -- तुम उनकी पूरी लंबाई में कहीं से भी direction पढ़ सकते हो।

Rule three: पास-पास lines मतलब stronger field। बीच वाले panel में notice करो lines charge के पास कैसे tightly packed हैं और दूर जाकर फैल जाती हैं -- वो फैलना ही one over r squared falloff है, geometrically बना हुआ।
Rule four, और यही वो है जो exams को पसंद है: दो field lines कभी एक दूसरे को cross नहीं कर सकतीं। कहीं भी नहीं, किसी भी हालत में नहीं।

<curious> और वजह completely airtight है, इसीलिए इसे रटने से बेहतर है समझना। मान लो दो lines cross कर गईं। Crossing point पर, rule two कहता है tangent field direction देती है -- लेकिन वहाँ दो अलग tangents होंगी, तो field को एक साथ दो directions में point करना पड़ेगा। Field की हर point पर एक ही value होती है। तो crossing simply impossible है।

देखो यह कैसे test होता है। Trap आमतौर पर ऐसे लिखा जाता है कि 'field lines वहाँ cross कर सकती हैं जहाँ field strong हो', जो plausible लगता है क्योंकि students को याद रहता है कि strong-field regions में lines crowd करती हैं। Crowding, crossing नहीं है। वो कितनी भी पास आ जाएँ, फिर भी कभी touch नहीं करतीं।

sections.title: Field Formulas, Units and Dimensions

board_events.text: Electric Field -- Formulas, Units and Dimensions
The defining relation. SI unit: newton per coulomb, equivalently volt per metre. Dimensional formula $[MLT^{-3}A^{-1}]$.
Field due to a point charge $Q$ at distance $r$ -- directed away from a positive $Q$, towards a negative $Q$.
Superposition for several sources. And running it backwards gives the force on any charge placed in a known field.
Watch the sign: for a positive $q$ the force is along $\vec{E}$; for a negative $q$ it is exactly opposite to $\vec{E}$. This flip is examined constantly.
Field lines summary: start on positive, end on negative; tangent gives direction; line density gives strength; lines never cross.

segments.text: Let's gather the field formulas in one place, with the units and dimensions you will be asked for directly.
First, the defining relation: E equals F over q nought. Everything else in this subtopic descends from this one line.

Its SI unit is newton per coulomb, which you will also see written as volt per metre -- the two are genuinely the same unit, and you should be comfortable with both. The dimensional formula is M L T to the minus three, A to the minus one. Derive it if you ever forget: force divided by charge is M L T to the minus two, over A T.
Second, the field due to a point charge: one over four pi epsilon nought, times Q over r squared, in the radial direction.

And with it, the direction rule: the field points away from a positive Q, and towards a negative Q. Get in the habit of writing the direction down alongside the magnitude, because board questions award marks for it separately.
Third, superposition for several sources: sum the individual contributions as vectors, each one calculated independently.
And now something we have not yet written explicitly. Run the defining relation backwards. If you already know the field at a point, you can immediately get the force on any charge you place there.
F equals q E. That is a small equation doing a great deal of work -- it is how the field idea actually pays for itself in problems.

<whisper> Watch the sign here, because this is examined constantly. For a positive charge, the force points along the field. For a negative charge, the force points exactly opposite to the field. The magnitude uses the size of q, but the direction flips.
And finally, the field-line rules in one breath: they start on positive and end on negative, the tangent gives the direction, the density of lines gives the strength, and they never cross.
चलिए field के सारे formulas एक जगह इकट्ठा करते हैं, उन units और dimensions के साथ जो सीधे पूछे जाते हैं।
पहला, defining relation: E equals F over q nought। इस subtopic में बाकी सब कुछ इसी एक line से निकलता है।

इसकी SI unit है newton per coulomb, जिसे तुम volt per metre भी लिखा देखोगे -- दोनों genuinely एक ही unit हैं, और तुम्हें दोनों के साथ comfortable होना चाहिए। Dimensional formula है M L T to the minus three, A to the minus one। कभी भूल जाओ तो derive कर लो: force divided by charge है M L T to the minus two, over A T।
दूसरा, point charge की वजह से field: one over four pi epsilon nought, times Q over r squared, radial direction में।
और इसके साथ direction rule: field positive Q से दूर point करता है, और negative Q की तरफ। Magnitude के साथ direction लिखने की आदत डालो, क्योंकि board questions उसके अलग से marks देते हैं।
तीसरा, कई sources के लिए superposition: individual contributions को vectors की तरह जोड़ो, हर एक independently निकाला गया।
और अब कुछ जो हमने अभी तक explicitly नहीं लिखा। Defining relation को उल्टा चलाओ। अगर तुम्हें किसी point पर field पहले से पता है, तो वहाँ रखे किसी भी charge पर force तुरंत निकाल सकते हो।
F equals q E। यह एक छोटा equation है जो बहुत काम करता है -- यही वो तरीका है जिससे field का idea problems में अपनी कीमत वसूल करता है।

<whisper> यहाँ sign पर ध्यान दो, क्योंकि यह लगातार examine होता है। Positive charge के लिए, force field के along point करता है। Negative charge के लिए, force exactly field के opposite point करता है। Magnitude q के size से आती है, लेकिन direction पलट जाती है।
और आखिर में, field-line rules एक साँस में: वो positive पर शुरू होती हैं और negative पर खत्म, tangent direction देती है, lines की density strength देती है, और वो कभी cross नहीं करतीं।

board_events.text: The denominator is $0.04$, so $E = 9 \times 10^{5}$ N/C, directed radially outward, away from the positive charge.
For part b, use $F = |q_0| E$ -- take the magnitude of the charge, then settle the direction from its sign separately.
Since $q_0$ is negative, the force points opposite to the field -- back towards $Q$. This is attraction, and the sign flip is the whole examinable point.

segments.text: Let's put the field machinery to work on a standard board-level question. It comes in two parts, and the second part is where the marks quietly hide.

A point charge of plus four microcoulomb sets up an electric field. Part a: find the field magnitude at a point twenty centimetres away. Part b: find the force acting on a charge of minus three nanocoulomb placed at that point.

Here is the setup. The source charge is on the left, the point P is twenty centimetres to its right, and notice that the field arrow at P and the force arrow on the negative charge point in opposite directions. That opposition is the heart of part b.

Part a first. Straight into the point-charge field formula: nine times ten to the power nine, times four microcoulomb, divided by zero point two zero metres squared. Convert first -- twenty centimetres is zero point two zero metres, and four microcoulomb is four times ten to the minus six coulomb.

The denominator works out to zero point zero four, and the whole thing gives nine times ten to the power five newton per coulomb. The direction is radially outward, away from the positive charge. State both -- magnitude and direction -- because the direction carries its own mark.

Now part b, and here is the method I want you to adopt. Use F equals the magnitude of q nought, times E. Take the size of the charge for the number, and settle the direction separately from the sign. Trying to carry a negative sign through the arithmetic is how people end up with a force that appears to point nowhere sensible.
So: three nanocoulomb, which is three times ten to the minus nine coulomb, times nine times ten to the power five newton per coulomb. That gives two point seven times ten to the minus three newton.

<whisper> And now the direction, which is the whole examinable point of this question. Because q nought is negative, the force points exactly opposite to the field. The field at P points away from Q, so the force on this negative charge points back towards Q. In other words, it is attracted -- exactly as an unlike charge should be. If you wrote the magnitude and stopped, you left a mark on the table.
चलिए field की machinery को एक standard board-level question पर लगाते हैं। यह दो parts में आता है, और दूसरे part में ही marks चुपचाप छुपे रहते हैं।

Plus four microcoulomb का एक point charge एक electric field set up करता है। Part a: बीस centimetre दूर एक point पर field की magnitude निकालो। Part b: उस point पर रखे minus three nanocoulomb charge पर लगने वाला force निकालो।

यह रहा setup। Source charge बाईं तरफ है, point P उसके बीस centimetre दाईं तरफ है, और notice करो कि P पर field arrow और negative charge पर force arrow opposite directions में point करते हैं। वही opposition part b का दिल है।

पहले part a। सीधा point-charge field formula में: nine times ten to the power nine, times four microcoulomb, divided by zero point two zero metres squared। पहले convert करो -- बीस centimetre है zero point two zero metres, और four microcoulomb है four times ten to the minus six coulomb।

Denominator निकलता है zero point zero four, और पूरा calculation देता है nine times ten to the power five newton per coulomb। Direction है radially outward, positive charge से दूर। दोनों बताओ -- magnitude और direction -- क्योंकि direction का अपना mark होता है।

अब part b, और यहाँ वो method है जो मैं चाहता हूँ तुम अपनाओ। F equals magnitude of q nought, times E use करो। Number के लिए charge का size लो, और direction sign से अलग तय करो। Arithmetic में negative sign साथ ले जाने की कोशिश ही वो तरीका है जिससे लोगों को ऐसा force मिल जाता है जो कहीं sensible point ही नहीं करता।
तो: three nanocoulomb, यानी three times ten to the minus nine coulomb, times nine times ten to the power five newton per coulomb। इससे मिलता है two point seven times ten to the minus three newton।

<whisper> और अब direction, जो इस question का पूरा examinable point है। क्योंकि q nought negative है, force exactly field के opposite point करता है। P पर field Q से दूर point करता है, तो इस negative charge पर force वापस Q की तरफ point करता है। दूसरे शब्दों में, वो attract हो रहा है -- exactly जैसा unlike charge को होना चाहिए। अगर तुमने सिर्फ magnitude लिखकर छोड़ दिया, तो एक mark मेज़ पर छोड़ आए।

</svg>
board_events.caption: A ring element and its diametrically opposite twin, with perpendicular components cancelling

board_events.text: Every element $dq$ is the same distance $\sqrt{x^2+R^2}$ from P, so each produces a field of the same magnitude. Only their directions differ.
Here is the symmetry payoff: for every element there is a diametrically opposite one. Their components perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs -- only the axial components survive.
Two checks. At the centre, $x = 0$ gives $E = 0$, correct by symmetry. Far away, $x \gg R$ gives $E \to kQ/x^2$ -- the ring looks like a point charge.
The axial field is maximum at $x = R/\sqrt{2}$. The field grows away from the centre, peaks there, then decays -- a hallmark JEE Advanced result.

segments.text: Now a JEE Advanced problem that shows why the field idea plus symmetry is so much more powerful than brute-force calculation.

A thin ring of radius R carries a total charge Q spread uniformly around it. Part a: derive the electric field at a point P on the axis, a distance x from the centre. Part b: find the distance x at which that axial field is a maximum.

Look carefully at the setup, because the picture does most of the work. The ring is seen edge-on. P sits out along the axis. And I have drawn one element at the top of the ring, plus its mirror twin at the bottom.

Start with what is the same for every element. Every single piece of the ring is exactly the same distance from P -- the square root of x squared plus R squared, by Pythagoras. So every element produces a field at P of exactly the same magnitude. Only their directions differ.

<excited> And here is the symmetry payoff that makes this problem tractable. For every element, there is a diametrically opposite one on the far side of the ring. Look at the two arrows from the top and bottom elements. Their components perpendicular to the axis point in exactly opposite directions and cancel in pairs. Only the components along the axis survive, and those all point the same way, so they simply add.

So instead of a brutal vector integral, we integrate only the axial component, which is dE times cos alpha, where cos alpha is x over the square root of x squared plus R squared. Everything except dq is constant across the ring, so it comes straight out of the integral and what is left is just the total charge Q. The result: E equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times Q x, over x squared plus R squared, all to the power three halves.

Always sanity-check a result like this at both extremes. At the centre, put x equals zero: the numerator vanishes, so E equals zero. Correct -- by symmetry, every element is cancelled by its opposite twin at the centre. Far away, when x is much bigger than R, the R squared becomes negligible and the expression collapses to k Q over x squared. Also correct -- from far enough away, the ring just looks like a point charge.

Now part b. The field is zero at the centre and dies away to zero far off, so somewhere in between it must peak. Differentiate and set the derivative to zero. Only the numerator matters for finding where it vanishes, and that numerator is R squared minus two x squared.

Set that to zero and you get R squared equals two x squared, so x equals R over root two. That is the answer, and it is a hallmark JEE Advanced result worth memorising: the axial field of a ring grows as you move away from the centre, peaks at R over root two, and then decays.
अब एक JEE Advanced problem जो दिखाती है कि field का idea plus symmetry, brute-force calculation से कितना ज्यादा powerful है।

R radius का एक thin ring है जिस पर total charge Q uniformly फैला है। Part a: axis पर centre से x दूरी पर स्थित point P पर electric field derive करो। Part b: वो दूरी x निकालो जहाँ यह axial field maximum हो।
Setup को ध्यान से देखो, क्योंकि picture ही ज्यादातर काम कर देती है। Ring edge-on दिख रहा है। P axis के along बाहर बैठा है। और मैंने ring के ऊपर एक element बनाया है, साथ में नीचे उसका mirror twin।

उससे शुरू करो जो हर element के लिए same है। Ring का हर एक टुकड़ा P से exactly same दूरी पर है -- square root of x squared plus R squared, Pythagoras से। तो हर element P पर exactly same magnitude का field बनाता है। सिर्फ उनकी directions अलग हैं।

<excited> और यह रहा वो symmetry payoff जो इस problem को tractable बना देता है। हर element के लिए, ring के दूसरी तरफ एक diametrically opposite element होता है। ऊपर और नीचे वाले elements से आते दोनों arrows देखो। Axis के perpendicular उनके components exactly opposite directions में point करते हैं और जोड़ों में cancel हो जाते हैं। सिर्फ axis के along components बचते हैं, और वो सब एक ही तरफ point करते हैं, तो simply जुड़ जाते हैं।

तो एक brutal vector integral की जगह, हम सिर्फ axial component integrate करते हैं, जो है dE times cos alpha, जहाँ cos alpha है x over square root of x squared plus R squared। dq के अलावा सब कुछ पूरे ring पर constant है, तो वो सीधा integral से बाहर आ जाता है और जो बचता है वो बस total charge Q है। Result: E equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times Q x, over x squared plus R squared, whole to the power three halves।

ऐसे result को हमेशा दोनों extremes पर sanity-check करो। Centre पर, x equals zero रखो: numerator गायब हो जाता है, तो E equals zero। सही -- symmetry से, centre पर हर element अपने opposite twin से cancel हो जाता है। दूर, जब x, R से बहुत बड़ा हो, R squared negligible हो जाता है और expression collapse होकर k Q over x squared बन जाता है। यह भी सही -- काफी दूर से ring बस एक point charge जैसा दिखता है।

अब part b। Field centre पर zero है और दूर जाकर भी zero हो जाता है, तो बीच में कहीं उसे peak करना ही होगा। Differentiate करो और derivative को zero रखो। कहाँ vanish होता है यह ढूँढने के लिए सिर्फ numerator matter करता है, और वो numerator है R squared minus two x squared।

उसे zero रखो तो मिलता है R squared equals two x squared, यानी x equals R over root two। यही answer है, और यह एक hallmark JEE Advanced result है जो याद रखने लायक है: ring का axial field centre से दूर जाने पर बढ़ता है, R over root two पर peak करता है, और फिर decay हो जाता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for the Electric Field

board_events.text: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for the Electric Field
Pitfall: adding field magnitudes instead of vectors. Fields from several sources superpose as vectors -- resolve into components before you add anything.
Pitfall: losing the direction flip for a negative charge. In $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$, a positive charge is pushed along the field and a negative charge exactly opposite to it.
Pitfall: thinking the field needs a test charge to exist. The field is a property of space set up by the source -- it is there whether or not anything is present to feel it.
Pitfall: claiming field lines cross where the field is strong. Crowding is not crossing. Lines never cross anywhere, because the field cannot have two directions at one point.
Pro-tip: for any symmetric distribution -- ring, arc, line -- do not integrate blindly. First ask which components cancel by symmetry. Spotting the cancellation is worth more marks than the calculus.
And always sanity-check a derived field at its limits: it should vanish where symmetry demands, and collapse to $kQ/r^2$ when viewed from far enough away.
We now have the field of a single charge. Next we meet the most important arrangement of two -- equal and opposite, a small distance apart. The electric dipole.

segments.text: Let's close the field subtopic with the errors that cost the most marks, and the habits that prevent them.

First pitfall: adding field magnitudes instead of vectors. This is the same error we met with forces, and it reappears here because the temptation is identical. Fields from several sources superpose as vectors. Resolve into components first, then add. Never sum the sizes and hope.

Second pitfall: losing the direction flip for a negative charge. In F equals q E, a positive charge is pushed along the field, and a negative charge is pushed exactly opposite to it. We saw this in the worked example, where a negative test charge ended up attracted back towards the source. Half the marks in these questions live in that direction.

Third pitfall, and this one is conceptual rather than computational: thinking the field somehow needs a test charge in order to exist. It does not. The field is a property of space, set up by the source charge alone. We use a test charge to define and measure it, but then we divide the test charge out -- and what remains describes the space itself. The pond has ripples even where no leaf is floating.

Fourth pitfall: claiming field lines can cross where the field is strong. Crowding is not crossing. Lines can get arbitrarily close together in a strong-field region, and they still never touch, because the field cannot point in two directions at a single point.

<curious> Now the pro-tip, and this one genuinely changes how fast you solve problems. For any field due to a symmetric distribution -- a ring, an arc, a line of charge -- do not start integrating blindly. First ask a single question: which components cancel by symmetry? On a ring's axis, only the axial components survive, and that one observation collapses a hard vector integral into a one-line scalar one. Spotting the cancellation is worth more marks than the calculus that follows it.

And pair that with a habit from the last subtopic: always sanity-check a derived field at its limits. It should vanish wherever symmetry demands it, as the ring's field did at the centre. And it should collapse to k Q over r squared when you back far enough away, because everything looks like a point charge from far enough off.

So we now know the field of a single point charge, and how to add fields from several. Next we meet the single most important arrangement of two charges in all of physics -- equal and opposite, held a small distance apart. The electric dipole.
Field subtopic को बंद करते हैं उन errors के साथ जो सबसे ज्यादा marks काटती हैं, और उन habits के साथ जो उन्हें रोकती हैं।

पहला pitfall: fields की magnitudes जोड़ना vectors की जगह। यह वही error है जो हमें forces में मिली थी, और यहाँ फिर आती है क्योंकि temptation बिलकुल वैसी ही है। कई sources के fields vectors की तरह superpose होते हैं। पहले components में resolve करो, फिर जोड़ो। Sizes जोड़कर उम्मीद मत करो।

दूसरा pitfall: negative charge के लिए direction flip खो देना। F equals q E में, positive charge field के along धकेला जाता है, और negative charge exactly उसके opposite। हमने यह worked example में देखा, जहाँ negative test charge वापस source की तरफ attract हो गया। इन questions के आधे marks उसी direction में रहते हैं।

तीसरा pitfall, और यह computational से ज्यादा conceptual है: यह सोचना कि field को exist करने के लिए किसी test charge की ज़रूरत है। नहीं है। Field space की property है, अकेले source charge से बनी। हम test charge इसे define और measure करने के लिए use करते हैं, लेकिन फिर test charge को divide करके हटा देते हैं -- और जो बचता है वो खुद space को describe करता है। तालाब में ripples वहाँ भी हैं जहाँ कोई पत्ता नहीं तैर रहा।

चौथा pitfall: यह कहना कि field lines वहाँ cross कर सकती हैं जहाँ field strong हो। Crowding, crossing नहीं है। Strong-field region में lines कितनी भी पास आ सकती हैं, फिर भी कभी touch नहीं करतीं, क्योंकि field एक ही point पर दो directions में point नहीं कर सकता।

<curious> अब pro-tip, और यह genuinely बदल देता है कि तुम problems कितनी तेज़ी से हल करते हो। किसी भी symmetric distribution के field के लिए -- ring, arc, charge की line -- आँख बंद करके integrate करना शुरू मत करो। पहले एक सवाल पूछो: symmetry से कौन से components cancel हो रहे हैं? Ring के axis पर, सिर्फ axial components बचते हैं, और वो एक observation एक कठिन vector integral को एक line के scalar integral में collapse कर देता है। Cancellation पकड़ लेना, उसके बाद आने वाली calculus से ज्यादा marks का है।

और इसके साथ पिछले subtopic की एक habit जोड़ो: derived field को हमेशा उसकी limits पर sanity-check करो। जहाँ symmetry माँगे वहाँ वो vanish होना चाहिए, जैसे ring का field centre पर हुआ। और काफी दूर जाने पर उसे k Q over r squared में collapse होना चाहिए, क्योंकि पर्याप्त दूरी से हर चीज़ point charge जैसी दिखती है।

तो अब हम एक single point charge का field जानते हैं, और कई fields जोड़ना भी। अगली बार हम मिलेंगे पूरी physics के दो charges के सबसे important arrangement से -- equal और opposite, थोड़ी सी दूरी पर रखे हुए। Electric dipole।

board_events.text: What Is an Electric Dipole?
Meet a special and enormously important arrangement: two equal and opposite charges, $+q$ and $-q$, held a small distance $2a$ apart.

But zero total charge does not mean zero effect. The two charges sit at different places, and that separation is what makes a dipole matter.

board_events.text: A water molecule is a dipole. The membranes of every cell in your body hold dipole layers.
And the behaviour of insulators in an electric field is the behaviour of countless tiny dipoles -- which is exactly the screening we met with dielectrics.

segments.text: Now we meet the single most important arrangement of two charges in all of physics.

Take two equal and opposite charges -- plus q and minus q -- and hold them a small distance apart. Call that separation two a. That arrangement is an electric dipole, and it deserves a whole subtopic of its own.
Here it is. The negative charge on one side, the positive on the other, the centre marked O halfway between, and a green arrow running from minus to plus that we will name in a moment.

<curious> Now at first glance this looks almost trivial, and I want you to feel that objection properly. Add up the charge: plus q and minus q give exactly zero. From a distance the whole thing is neutral. So why should we care at all?

Here is why. Zero total charge does not mean zero effect. The two charges are not sitting on top of each other -- they sit at different places. And that separation is the entire reason a dipole matters. A neutral object with its positive and negative charge separated behaves very differently from a genuinely empty region of space.
And this is not an artificial arrangement invented for exams. Look at a water molecule.

The oxygen atom pulls the shared electrons closer to itself, leaving the oxygen end slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. The molecule is neutral overall, but its charge is separated -- so water is a permanent dipole. The membranes of every cell in your body hold dipole layers too.

And there is one more connection worth making explicitly. Remember dielectric screening from the Coulomb's Law subtopic, where a medium weakened the force by a factor K? That was this. The behaviour of an insulator in a field is the collective behaviour of countless tiny dipoles, all turning to line up. We are now going to understand precisely why they turn.
अब हम मिलते हैं पूरी physics के दो charges के सबसे important arrangement से।

दो equal और opposite charges लो -- plus q और minus q -- और उन्हें थोड़ी सी दूरी पर पकड़ो। उस separation को two a कहो। वो arrangement एक electric dipole है, और यह अपने आप में एक पूरे subtopic का हकदार है।
यह रहा। एक तरफ negative charge, दूसरी तरफ positive, बीचोंबीच centre O marked, और minus से plus की तरफ जाता एक green arrow जिसे हम अभी नाम देंगे।

<curious> अब पहली नज़र में यह almost trivial लगता है, और मैं चाहता हूँ तुम उस objection को ठीक से महसूस करो। Charge जोड़ो: plus q और minus q मिलकर exactly zero देते हैं। दूर से पूरी चीज़ neutral है। तो हमें परवाह क्यों करनी चाहिए?

यह रही वजह। Zero total charge का मतलब zero effect नहीं होता। दोनों charges एक दूसरे के ऊपर नहीं बैठे हैं -- वो अलग-अलग जगहों पर हैं। और वही separation पूरी वजह है कि dipole matter करता है। एक neutral object जिसका positive और negative charge separated हो, वो space के सच में खाली region से बहुत अलग behave करता है।
और यह exams के लिए बनाया गया कोई artificial arrangement नहीं है। एक water molecule देखो।

Oxygen atom shared electrons को अपनी तरफ ज्यादा खींच लेता है, जिससे oxygen वाला सिरा थोड़ा negative और hydrogen वाला सिरा थोड़ा positive रह जाता है। Molecule overall neutral है, लेकिन उसका charge separated है -- तो पानी एक permanent dipole है। तुम्हारे शरीर की हर cell की membranes भी dipole layers रखती हैं।

और एक connection explicitly बनाने लायक है। Coulomb's Law subtopic में dielectric screening याद है, जहाँ medium force को K factor से कमज़ोर कर देता था? वो यही था। Field में insulator का behaviour, अनगिनत tiny dipoles का collective behaviour है, जो सब line up होने के लिए घूम जाते हैं। अब हम exactly समझने वाले हैं कि वो घूमते क्यों हैं।

sections.title: The Dipole Moment Vector

board_events.text: The Dipole Moment Vector
The key descriptor of a dipole is its dipole moment -- a vector, written $\vec{p}$.
Direction: $\vec{p}$ points from the negative charge to the positive charge. Remember it as 'p points minus to plus'.
SI unit: coulomb metre. Dimensional formula $[LTA]$ -- a length times a charge.
Think of it as an arrow that captures both 'how much charge' and 'how far apart' in a single quantity.
Two molecules with the same $p$ behave identically at a distance -- even if one has large charges close together and the other small charges far apart.
That is why $p$ is the right descriptor. From far away, nature only ever asks for the product, never for $q$ and $2a$ separately.

segments.text: To describe a dipole we need more than just saying two charges are near each other. We need one quantity that captures the whole arrangement.
That quantity is the dipole moment, and it is a vector. We write it as p with an arrow over it.
Its magnitude is q times two a -- the size of either charge, multiplied by the full separation between them. Not the half-separation: the full two a. That is a slip worth guarding against.

<whisper> And its direction, which examiners test directly: p points from the negative charge to the positive charge. The memory line is simply, p points minus to plus. Notice that this is the opposite of the direction electrons actually move, so it catches people out.
The SI unit follows straight from the definition: charge times distance, so coulomb metre. And the dimensional formula is L T A -- a length multiplied by a charge, since charge itself is A T.
Now think about what this arrow is really doing for us. It packages two separate facts -- how much charge is involved, and how far apart that charge is spread -- into a single quantity.

<excited> And here is the remarkable consequence. Two dipoles with the same value of p behave absolutely identically at a distance. One might have large charges very close together; the other small charges spread far apart. If the products match, then from far away nothing whatsoever distinguishes them.

That is precisely why p is the right descriptor to invent. From a distance, nature only ever asks for the product q times two a. It never asks for q and two a separately. So we define the one combination that matters and work with that from here on.
एक dipole को describe करने के लिए सिर्फ यह कहना काफी नहीं कि दो charges पास-पास हैं। हमें एक quantity चाहिए जो पूरा arrangement पकड़ ले।
वो quantity है dipole moment, और यह एक vector है। हम इसे p लिखते हैं, ऊपर arrow के साथ।
इसकी magnitude है q times two a -- किसी भी एक charge का size, पूरी separation से multiply किया हुआ। Half-separation नहीं: पूरा two a। यह एक slip है जिससे बचना चाहिए।

<whisper> और इसकी direction, जो examiners सीधे test करते हैं: p negative charge से positive charge की तरफ point करता है। Memory line simply यह है, p points minus to plus। Notice करो यह उस direction का उल्टा है जिसमें electrons actually move करते हैं, इसलिए यह लोगों को पकड़ लेता है।
SI unit सीधे definition से आती है: charge times distance, यानी coulomb metre। और dimensional formula है L T A -- एक length multiplied by charge, क्योंकि charge खुद A T है।
अब सोचो यह arrow हमारे लिए असल में कर क्या रहा है। यह दो अलग facts को -- कितना charge शामिल है, और वो charge कितनी दूर तक फैला है -- एक single quantity में पैक कर देता है।

<excited> और यह रहा remarkable consequence। एक ही p value वाले दो dipoles दूर से बिलकुल identically behave करते हैं। एक में बड़े charges बहुत पास-पास हो सकते हैं; दूसरे में छोटे charges दूर-दूर फैले। अगर products match करते हैं, तो दूर से उनमें कुछ भी फर्क नहीं किया जा सकता।

यही exactly वजह है कि p सही descriptor है। दूर से, nature सिर्फ product q times two a माँगती है। वो q और two a अलग-अलग कभी नहीं माँगती। तो हम वही एक combination define कर लेते हैं जो matter करता है और आगे उसी के साथ काम करते हैं।

board_events.caption: Point P on the dipole axis, with the fields from the near and far charges pointing opposite ways

board_events.text: Place $-q$ at A and $+q$ at B, separated by $2a$, centre O. Take P on the axis, distance $r$ from O, on the $+q$ side.
The $+q$ charge is at distance $(r-a)$ from P, and its field points away from $+q$, along $\vec{p}$. The $-q$ charge is at $(r+a)$, and its field points towards $-q$, opposite to $\vec{p}$.
They are antiparallel, so the net field is their difference. Combining the fractions, the numerator becomes $4ar$ and the denominator $(r^2-a^2)^2$.
The far field falls as $1/r^3$, faster than a point charge's $1/r^2$ -- because at a distance the two charges nearly cancel, leaving only a residual that dies off quickly.

segments.text: Now let's actually calculate the field a dipole produces. There are two directions the board asks about, and we take the axial one first.
Here is the setup. The dipole lies along a horizontal line, and our field point P sits out along that same line, beyond the positive charge.

Place minus q at point A and plus q at point B, separated by two a, with the centre marked O. Then take P on the axis, a distance r from O, on the plus q side. Note carefully that r is measured from the centre, not from either charge -- that is where sign errors creep in.

Now work out each field separately. The plus q charge is nearer -- at distance r minus a from P -- and its field points away from it, which is along p. The minus q charge is further -- at distance r plus a -- and its field points towards it, which is opposite to p. So the two contributions are antiparallel, and the nearer one is stronger.
Because they oppose each other, the net field is their difference: q over four pi epsilon nought, times the bracket, one over r minus a all squared, minus one over r plus a all squared.

Now combine those two fractions over a common denominator. The numerator becomes r plus a all squared minus r minus a all squared, and if you expand that carefully, the r squared and a squared terms cancel and you are left with four a r. The denominator is r squared minus a squared, all squared.

Substitute q times two a equals p, and the result is the axial field: one over four pi epsilon nought, times two p r, over r squared minus a squared all squared. Then for a far point, where r is much greater than a, the a squared is negligible and r squared minus a squared becomes just r squared -- giving the compact form, two p over r cubed.

<curious> Now read what that result is telling you physically. The field falls off as one over r cubed, which is faster than a single point charge's one over r squared. And there is a good reason. At a distance, the plus q and minus q very nearly cancel each other out. What survives is only a small residual difference -- and that residual dies away much more quickly than either charge alone would.
अब actually calculate करते हैं कि एक dipole कैसा field बनाता है। Board दो directions के बारे में पूछता है, और हम पहले axial वाली लेते हैं।
यह रहा setup। Dipole एक horizontal line के along है, और हमारा field point P उसी line पर बाहर बैठा है, positive charge के आगे।

Minus q को point A पर रखो और plus q को point B पर, two a की दूरी पर, centre O marked के साथ। फिर P को axis पर लो, O से r दूरी पर, plus q वाली तरफ। ध्यान से notice करो कि r centre से मापा गया है, किसी charge से नहीं -- यहीं sign errors घुसती हैं।

अब हर field अलग से निकालो। Plus q charge नज़दीक है -- P से r minus a दूरी पर -- और उसका field उससे दूर point करता है, जो p के along है। Minus q charge दूर है -- r plus a दूरी पर -- और उसका field उसकी तरफ point करता है, जो p के opposite है। तो दोनों contributions antiparallel हैं, और नज़दीक वाला ज्यादा strong है।
क्योंकि वो एक दूसरे को oppose करते हैं, net field उनका difference है: q over four pi epsilon nought, times bracket, one over r minus a whole squared, minus one over r plus a whole squared।

अब उन दोनों fractions को common denominator पर combine करो। Numerator बनता है r plus a whole squared minus r minus a whole squared, और अगर उसे ध्यान से expand करो, r squared और a squared terms cancel हो जाते हैं और बचता है four a r। Denominator है r squared minus a squared, whole squared।

q times two a equals p substitute करो, और result है axial field: one over four pi epsilon nought, times two p r, over r squared minus a squared whole squared। फिर far point के लिए, जहाँ r, a से बहुत बड़ा है, a squared negligible है और r squared minus a squared बस r squared बन जाता है -- देता है compact form, two p over r cubed।

<curious> अब पढ़ो कि यह result physically क्या बता रहा है। Field one over r cubed के हिसाब से गिरता है, जो एक single point charge के one over r squared से तेज़ है। और इसकी अच्छी वजह है। दूर से, plus q और minus q लगभग पूरी तरह एक दूसरे को cancel कर देते हैं। जो बचता है वो सिर्फ एक छोटा residual difference है -- और वो residual किसी अकेले charge से कहीं ज्यादा तेज़ी से मर जाता है।

board_events.text: Now put P on the equatorial line -- the perpendicular bisector -- a distance $r$ from the centre O.
Each charge is now the same distance $\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$ from P, so the two field magnitudes are exactly equal. Only their directions differ.

Resolve each into components parallel and perpendicular to the dipole axis. By symmetry the perpendicular components cancel, while the components along the axis add -- both pointing opposite to $\vec{p}$.

<text x="330" y="292" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Both fall off as one over r cubed — faster than a point charge, because the charges nearly cancel</text>
</svg>
board_events.caption: The axial field is twice the equatorial field at equal distance, and they point opposite ways

board_events.text: Two facts, both exam gold: $E_{\text{axial}} = 2E_{\text{equatorial}}$ at the same distance, and the equatorial field points opposite to $\vec{p}$ while the axial field points along it.

segments.text: Now the second direction the board asks about -- the equatorial line, also called broadside-on.
Look at how the geometry changes. P now sits directly above the centre of the dipole, on the perpendicular bisector, so it is no longer in line with the charges.
Put P on the equatorial line, a distance r from the centre O. That is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining the charges.

And immediately something helpful happens. Each charge is now exactly the same distance from P -- the square root of r squared plus a squared, straight from Pythagoras. So the two field magnitudes are precisely equal. Unlike the axial case, neither one dominates. Only their directions differ.

So resolve each field into two components: one parallel to the dipole axis, one perpendicular to it. By symmetry, the perpendicular components are equal and opposite, so they cancel exactly. The components along the axis both survive, and here is the key point -- they both point in the same direction, opposite to p. So they add.

That gives twice E plus times cos theta, where cos theta is a over the square root of r squared plus a squared. Multiply it out and the q times two a in the numerator is just p again, leaving p over r squared plus a squared, to the power three halves.

And for a far point, where r is much greater than a, that collapses to p over r cubed -- pointing opposite to p. Note that the one over r cubed falloff appears here too, for exactly the same cancellation reason as before.
Now put the two results side by side, because the comparison is where the marks are.

<whisper> Two facts, and both are exam gold. First: at the same distance, the axial field is exactly twice the equatorial field. Second: the directions are opposite -- the axial field points along p, while the equatorial field points against it. Most students remember one of these two facts and lose marks on the other. Learn them as a pair.
अब दूसरी direction जिसके बारे में board पूछता है -- equatorial line, जिसे broadside-on भी कहते हैं।
देखो geometry कैसे बदलती है। P अब dipole के centre के सीधा ऊपर बैठा है, perpendicular bisector पर, तो वो अब charges के साथ एक line में नहीं है।
P को equatorial line पर रखो, centre O से r दूरी पर। यह charges को जोड़ने वाली line का perpendicular bisector है।

और तुरंत कुछ helpful होता है। अब हर charge P से exactly same दूरी पर है -- square root of r squared plus a squared, सीधा Pythagoras से। तो दोनों field magnitudes बिलकुल बराबर हैं। Axial case के उलट, कोई भी dominate नहीं करता। सिर्फ उनकी directions अलग हैं।

तो हर field को दो components में resolve करो: एक dipole axis के parallel, एक उसके perpendicular। Symmetry से, perpendicular components equal और opposite हैं, तो वो exactly cancel हो जाते हैं। Axis के along components दोनों बचते हैं, और यही key point है -- वो दोनों एक ही direction में point करते हैं, p के opposite। तो वो जुड़ जाते हैं।

इससे मिलता है twice E plus times cos theta, जहाँ cos theta है a over square root of r squared plus a squared। Multiply करो और numerator में q times two a फिर से बस p है, बचता है p over r squared plus a squared, to the power three halves।

और far point के लिए, जहाँ r, a से बहुत बड़ा है, यह collapse होकर p over r cubed बन जाता है -- p के opposite point करता हुआ। Notice करो one over r cubed falloff यहाँ भी आता है, exactly उसी cancellation की वजह से जो पहले थी।
अब दोनों results को साथ-साथ रखो, क्योंकि comparison में ही marks हैं।

<whisper> दो facts, और दोनों exam gold हैं। पहला: same दूरी पर, axial field exactly equatorial field का दोगुना है। दूसरा: directions opposite हैं -- axial field p के along point करता है, जबकि equatorial field उसके against। ज़्यादातर students इन दोनों में से एक fact याद रखते हैं और दूसरे पर marks गँवा देते हैं। इन्हें जोड़े में सीखो।

sections.title: Derivation: Torque on a Dipole in a Uniform Field

board_events.text: Derivation: Torque on a Dipole in a Uniform Field
A dipole is like a compass needle made of charge. Drop a compass needle into a magnetic field and it does not get pushed across the table -- it rotates to line up.

board_events.svg:
<svg font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" viewBox="-49 -12 766 414" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

</svg>
board_events.caption: Equal and opposite forces on the two charges forming a couple, with perpendicular separation 2a sine theta

board_events.text: In a uniform field $\vec{E}$, the charge $+q$ feels $+q\vec{E}$ and $-q$ feels $-q\vec{E}$. These are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero -- the dipole will not translate.
But the two forces do not share a line of action. They form a couple, and a couple produces a torque.
With the dipole axis at angle $\theta$ to $\vec{E}$, the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action is $2a\sin\theta$.
The torque is maximum at $\theta = 90^\circ$, when $\vec{p}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{E}$, and zero at $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$.

segments.text: We now know what field a dipole produces. The reverse question is just as important: what does a field do to a dipole?

The picture I want in your head is a compass needle. Drop a compass needle into the Earth's magnetic field and it does not go flying across the table. It stays put and rotates until it lines up. A dipole in a uniform electric field does exactly this -- it feels no net push, only a twist.
Here is why, drawn out. A uniform field, shown by the evenly spaced parallel lines, and a dipole sitting at an angle to it.

In a uniform field E, the positive charge feels a force plus q E, pointing along the field. The negative charge feels minus q E, pointing against it. Those two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they add to exactly zero. The net force vanishes, and the dipole will not translate anywhere.

<excited> But look more carefully at the picture, because zero net force is not the end of the story. The two forces do not act along the same line. One acts up here, the other acts down there. In mechanics that arrangement has a name -- it is a couple. And a couple produces a pure torque, a twist with no push.

To get its size, we need the perpendicular distance between those two lines of action. With the dipole axis at an angle theta to the field, that distance is two a sine theta -- you can read it straight off the figure as the vertical gap between the two force arrows.
So the torque is force times perpendicular distance: q E times two a sine theta. Group the q with the two a and that is just p, giving torque equals p E sine theta.

In vector form, this twist is captured exactly by tau equals p cross E. The cross product does everything for us at once -- it gives the right magnitude, p E sine theta, and it gives the correct axis of rotation.

Read off the two extremes, because both get examined. The torque is maximum at theta equals ninety degrees, when p is perpendicular to E and the forces have the most leverage. And it is zero at theta equals zero or one hundred and eighty degrees, when the dipole is lined up along the field and the two forces act along the same line.
अब हम जानते हैं कि dipole कैसा field बनाता है। उल्टा सवाल उतना ही important है: field, dipole के साथ क्या करता है?

जो picture मैं तुम्हारे दिमाग में चाहता हूँ वो है एक compass needle। Compass needle को Earth के magnetic field में डालो और वो मेज़ के पार उड़ नहीं जाती। वो अपनी जगह रहती है और घूमकर line up हो जाती है। Uniform electric field में dipole exactly यही करता है -- उसे कोई net push नहीं मिलता, सिर्फ एक twist।
यह रही वजह, बनाकर दिखाई गई। एक uniform field, evenly spaced parallel lines से दिखाया गया, और एक dipole उससे कोण बनाकर बैठा हुआ।

Uniform field E में, positive charge plus q E force feel करता है, field के along point करता हुआ। Negative charge minus q E feel करता है, उसके against। वो दोनों forces size में बराबर और direction में opposite हैं, तो वो जुड़कर exactly zero हो जाते हैं। Net force गायब हो जाता है, और dipole कहीं translate नहीं करेगा।

<excited> लेकिन picture को और ध्यान से देखो, क्योंकि zero net force कहानी का अंत नहीं है। दोनों forces एक ही line के along act नहीं करते। एक यहाँ ऊपर act करता है, दूसरा वहाँ नीचे। Mechanics में उस arrangement का एक नाम है -- वो एक couple है। और couple एक pure torque बनाता है, बिना push वाला twist।

इसका size निकालने के लिए, हमें उन दो lines of action के बीच perpendicular distance चाहिए। Dipole axis के field से theta कोण पर होने पर, वो distance है two a sine theta -- तुम इसे figure से सीधा पढ़ सकते हो, दोनों force arrows के बीच का vertical gap।
तो torque है force times perpendicular distance: q E times two a sine theta। q को two a के साथ group करो और वो बस p है, देता है torque equals p E sine theta।

Vector form में, यह twist exactly capture होता है tau equals p cross E से। Cross product हमारे लिए एक साथ सब कुछ कर देता है -- यह सही magnitude देता है, p E sine theta, और यह rotation का सही axis भी देता है।

दोनों extremes पढ़ लो, क्योंकि दोनों examine होते हैं। Torque maximum है theta equals ninety degrees पर, जब p, E के perpendicular हो और forces को सबसे ज्यादा leverage मिले। और यह zero है theta equals zero या one hundred and eighty degrees पर, जब dipole field के along line up हो और दोनों forces एक ही line पर act करें।

sections.title: Energy, Stability, and Non-Uniform Fields

board_events.text: Energy, Stability, and Non-Uniform Fields
Rotating a dipole against the torque costs work, so a dipole in a field has potential energy that depends on its orientation.

board_events.text: Torque vanishes at both $\theta = 0^\circ$ and $\theta = 180^\circ$ -- but only $\theta = 0^\circ$ is stable. Nudge it there and the torque pushes it back.
At $\theta = 180^\circ$ the torque is also zero, but any nudge swings it right around. That is unstable equilibrium -- the maximum of the energy curve.
