board_events.caption: In a non-uniform field the two charges sit in different field strengths, so a net force survives

board_events.text: A dipole feels zero net force ONLY in a uniform field. In a non-uniform field the ends sit in different field strengths and a net force survives -- this is why a charged comb attracts neutral bits of paper.

segments.text: If a field twists a dipole, then turning that dipole against the twist must cost work. So a dipole in a field carries potential energy that depends purely on which way it is facing.
Let's write that energy down, and then read the whole physics of stability straight off it.

The potential energy is U equals minus p dot E, which is minus p E cos theta. Watch that minus sign -- it is the single most common sign error in this entire subtopic, and dropping it inverts every conclusion that follows.
Now plot that against angle, and the physics becomes visual. The curve is a valley at theta equals zero, rising to a peak at one hundred and eighty degrees, then falling back.

Here is the key reading. The torque vanishes at both ends -- at theta equals zero and at theta equals one hundred and eighty degrees -- so both are equilibrium positions. But they are not the same kind of equilibrium. At theta equals zero, with p lined up along E, the energy is at its minimum, minus p E. Nudge the dipole away from there and the torque pushes it straight back. That is stable.

At one hundred and eighty degrees, the torque is also zero, so it will sit there in principle. But the energy is at its maximum, plus p E. Give it the tiniest nudge and it swings right around to the other side. That is unstable equilibrium -- balanced on a peak rather than resting in a valley.

And if you want the work to rotate from one angle to another, just take the energy difference: W equals p E, times cos theta one minus cos theta two. That single line handles every rotation question they can set.
<curious> One last piece, and it resolves something from the very first subtopic. Everything so far assumed a uniform field. What happens in a non-uniform one?

Look at the picture. The field is crowded near the comb and spreads out further away. The dipole's two ends now sit in genuinely different field strengths, so the two forces no longer cancel. A net force survives, equal to p times the rate of change of E with distance, and it pulls the dipole towards the stronger field.

So remember the condition precisely: a dipole feels zero net force only in a uniform field. And this is not a technicality. It is exactly why a comb rubbed on your hair picks up neutral bits of paper. The comb's field polarises each scrap into a tiny dipole, and because that field is non-uniform, the scrap is pulled in. We can finally explain the trick we opened this chapter with.

अगर field एक dipole को घुमाता है, तो उस dipole को twist के against घुमाने में काम लगना ही चाहिए। तो field में रखा dipole potential energy रखता है जो purely इस पर depend करती है कि वो किस तरफ मुँह किए है।
चलिए वो energy लिखते हैं, और फिर stability की पूरी physics सीधा उसी से पढ़ते हैं।

Potential energy है U equals minus p dot E, यानी minus p E cos theta। उस minus sign पर ध्यान दो -- यह पूरे subtopic की सबसे common sign error है, और इसे छोड़ देने पर आगे के हर conclusion उल्टे हो जाते हैं।
अब इसे angle के against plot करो, और physics visual हो जाती है। Curve theta equals zero पर एक valley है, one hundred and eighty degrees पर peak तक उठती है, फिर वापस गिरती है।

यह रही key reading। Torque दोनों सिरों पर गायब हो जाता है -- theta equals zero पर और theta equals one hundred and eighty degrees पर -- तो दोनों equilibrium positions हैं। लेकिन वो एक ही तरह के equilibrium नहीं हैं। Theta equals zero पर, जहाँ p, E के along line up है, energy अपने minimum पर है, minus p E। Dipole को वहाँ से हिलाओ और torque उसे सीधा वापस धकेल देता है। यह stable है।

One hundred and eighty degrees पर, torque भी zero है, तो principle में वो वहाँ बैठ जाएगा। लेकिन energy अपने maximum पर है, plus p E। ज़रा सा भी धक्का दो और वो घूमकर दूसरी तरफ चला जाता है। यह unstable equilibrium है -- valley में आराम करने के बजाय चोटी पर balanced।

और अगर एक angle से दूसरे तक घुमाने का work चाहिए, तो बस energy का difference लो: W equals p E, times cos theta one minus cos theta two। यह एक line हर rotation question संभाल लेती है जो वो पूछ सकते हैं।
<curious> एक आखिरी टुकड़ा, और यह पहले ही subtopic की एक चीज़ हल कर देता है। अब तक सब कुछ uniform field मानकर चला। Non-uniform field में क्या होता है?

Picture देखो। Field comb के पास crowded है और दूर जाकर फैल जाता है। Dipole के दोनों सिरे अब genuinely अलग field strengths में बैठे हैं, तो दोनों forces अब cancel नहीं होते। एक net force बच जाता है, जो p times E के distance के साथ बदलने की दर के बराबर है, और वो dipole को stronger field की तरफ खींचता है।

तो condition ठीक से याद रखो: dipole को zero net force सिर्फ uniform field में मिलता है। और यह कोई technicality नहीं है। यही exactly वजह है कि बालों पर rub किया comb कागज़ के neutral टुकड़े उठा लेता है। Comb का field हर टुकड़े को एक tiny dipole में polarise कर देता है, और क्योंकि वो field non-uniform है, टुकड़ा खिंच आता है। आखिरकार हम वो trick explain कर सकते हैं जिससे हमने यह chapter शुरू किया था।

sections.title: Dipole Formulas at a Glance

board_events.text: Dipole Formulas at a Glance
Directed from $-q$ to $+q$. SI unit coulomb metre; dimensional formula $[LTA]$.
Golden ratio: at the same large distance, $E_{\text{axial}} = 2E_{\text{eq}}$. Axial points along $\vec{p}$; equatorial points opposite to $\vec{p}$.
Units and dimensions: torque in newton metre, $[ML^2T^{-2}]$. Energy in joule. Both $E$ expressions in newton per coulomb, $[MLT^{-3}A^{-1}]$.

segments.text: Let's collect every dipole formula in one place. This is your complete toolkit for the subtopic.
Start with the dipole moment itself: p equals q times two a, as a vector.
Directed from minus q to plus q -- always state the direction, not just the size. Its SI unit is coulomb metre, and the dimensional formula is L T A.

Next, the axial field, in both its exact and its far-field form. Exactly, it is two p r over r squared minus a squared, all squared. And when r is much greater than a, that simplifies to two p over r cubed.
Then the equatorial field. Exactly, p over r squared plus a squared, to the power three halves. And in the far field, simply p over r cubed.

<whisper> Here is the relationship worth burning into memory, because it saves you from ever needing the full expressions in a hurry. At the same large distance, the axial field is exactly twice the equatorial field. And the directions: axial points along p, equatorial points opposite to p. Two facts, always learned together.
Now the torque on a dipole sitting in an external field: tau equals p cross E, with magnitude p E sine theta.

Its potential energy is minus p dot E, which is minus p E cos theta -- and mind that leading minus sign. From it, the work to rotate from theta one to theta two is p E times cos theta one minus cos theta two.

And finally, the one that only applies in a non-uniform field: the net force equals p times d E by d r, pointing towards the stronger field when p is aligned with E. In a uniform field this term is zero, which is why the dipole only twists there.

The units and dimensions you may be asked for directly: torque in newton metre, dimensions M L squared T to the minus two. Energy in joule. And both field expressions in newton per coulomb, dimensions M L T to the minus three, A to the minus one.
चलिए हर dipole formula एक जगह इकट्ठा करते हैं। यह इस subtopic के लिए तुम्हारा complete toolkit है।
Dipole moment से शुरू करो: p equals q times two a, vector के रूप में।
Minus q से plus q की तरफ directed -- हमेशा direction बताओ, सिर्फ size नहीं। इसकी SI unit है coulomb metre, और dimensional formula है L T A।

अगला, axial field, इसके exact और far-field दोनों forms में। Exactly, यह है two p r over r squared minus a squared, whole squared। और जब r, a से बहुत बड़ा हो, यह simplify होकर two p over r cubed बन जाता है।
फिर equatorial field। Exactly, p over r squared plus a squared, to the power three halves। और far field में, simply p over r cubed।

<whisper> यह रहा वो relationship जिसे memory में जलाकर रख लेना चाहिए, क्योंकि यह तुम्हें जल्दबाज़ी में पूरे expressions की ज़रूरत से बचा देता है। Same बड़ी दूरी पर, axial field exactly equatorial field का दोगुना है। और directions: axial p के along, equatorial p के opposite। दो facts, हमेशा साथ में सीखे जाने वाले।
अब external field में बैठे dipole पर torque: tau equals p cross E, magnitude p E sine theta के साथ।

इसकी potential energy है minus p dot E, यानी minus p E cos theta -- और उस शुरुआती minus sign का ध्यान रखो। इससे, theta one से theta two तक घुमाने का work है p E times cos theta one minus cos theta two।

और आखिर में, वो जो सिर्फ non-uniform field में लागू होता है: net force equals p times d E by d r, stronger field की तरफ point करता हुआ जब p, E के साथ aligned हो। Uniform field में यह term zero है, इसीलिए वहाँ dipole सिर्फ घूमता है।

वो units और dimensions जो सीधे पूछे जा सकते हैं: torque newton metre में, dimensions M L squared T to the minus two। Energy joule में। और दोनों field expressions newton per coulomb में, dimensions M L T to the minus three, A to the minus one।

sections.title: Worked Example: The Two-to-One Ratio Speed Trap

board_events.text: Example 2 -- NEET Speed Trap

At a fixed distance $r \gg a$ from a short dipole, the axial field is $E_a$ and the equatorial field is $E_e$. A student computes $E_a = 1.8 \times 10^{4}$ N/C. Find $E_e$ at the same distance, and its direction relative to $\vec{p}$.

board_events.text: The trap: students who half-remember the formulas write $E_e = E_a$, forgetting the factor of two -- or they get the direction backwards.
Lock in two facts and this needs no formula at all: $E_{\text{axial}} = 2E_{\text{equatorial}}$, and the equatorial field points opposite to $\vec{p}$.
So $E_e = 9 \times 10^{3}$ N/C, directed antiparallel to $\vec{p}$.
Notice what we never did: we never used $p$, never used $r$, never plugged into a formula. The two-to-one ratio was the entire shortcut.

segments.text: This is a NEET speed trap, which means it is designed to be solved in about fifteen seconds -- if you know the right two facts, and to waste two minutes if you do not.

At a fixed distance r, much greater than a, from a short dipole, the axial field is E a and the equatorial field is E e. A student has already computed E a to be one point eight times ten to the power four newton per coulomb. Find E e at the same distance, and say which direction it points relative to p.
Look at this comparison figure, because it contains the whole answer. The axial arrow is twice as long as the equatorial one, and the two point in opposite directions.

<whisper> Here is the trap, and it catches people two different ways. Students who half-remember the formulas notice that both far fields go as p over r cubed and conclude that E e equals E a -- forgetting that the axial expression carries a factor of two. Others get the size right but reverse the direction.

Lock in two facts and this question needs no formula whatsoever. First: the axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance. Second: the equatorial field points opposite to p, while the axial field points along it.
So E e is simply E a over two. One point eight times ten to the power four, divided by two, gives nine times ten to the power three newton per coulomb.
And the direction: antiparallel to p. State both parts, because in a NEET question the direction is often what separates the correct option from the distractor.

Now notice what we never did. We never used the value of p. We never used the value of r. We never substituted into either field formula. The two-to-one ratio was the entire shortcut, and that is precisely the kind of recognition these speed traps are testing.
यह एक NEET speed trap है, मतलब यह लगभग पंद्रह seconds में हल होने के लिए बनाया गया है -- अगर तुम्हें सही दो facts पता हों, और दो minute बर्बाद करने के लिए अगर न पता हों।

एक short dipole से fixed दूरी r पर, जो a से बहुत बड़ी है, axial field है E a और equatorial field है E e। एक student ने पहले ही E a निकाल लिया है, one point eight times ten to the power four newton per coulomb। उसी दूरी पर E e निकालो, और बताओ वो p के relative किस direction में point करता है।
इस comparison figure को देखो, क्योंकि इसमें पूरा जवाब है। Axial arrow equatorial से दोगुना लंबा है, और दोनों opposite directions में point करते हैं।

<whisper> यह रहा trap, और यह लोगों को दो अलग तरीकों से पकड़ता है। जो students formulas आधे याद रखते हैं वो notice करते हैं कि दोनों far fields p over r cubed के हिसाब से चलते हैं और conclude कर लेते हैं कि E e equals E a -- यह भूलकर कि axial expression में two का factor है। बाकी size सही कर लेते हैं लेकिन direction उल्टी कर देते हैं।

दो facts lock कर लो और इस question को किसी formula की ज़रूरत ही नहीं। पहला: same दूरी पर axial field, equatorial field का दोगुना है। दूसरा: equatorial field p के opposite point करता है, जबकि axial उसके along।
तो E e simply E a over two है। One point eight times ten to the power four, divided by two, देता है nine times ten to the power three newton per coulomb।
और direction: p के antiparallel। दोनों हिस्से बताओ, क्योंकि NEET question में अक्सर direction ही correct option को distractor से अलग करती है।

अब notice करो हमने क्या कभी नहीं किया। हमने p की value कभी use नहीं की। हमने r की value कभी use नहीं की। हमने किसी field formula में कुछ substitute नहीं किया। Two-to-one ratio ही पूरा shortcut था, और यही वो recognition है जो ये speed traps test करते हैं।

board_events.text: The product $pE$ is $10^{-4}$, and $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$, so the torque is $5 \times 10^{-5}$ N m.
For part b, recall that stable equilibrium means $\vec{p}$ aligned with $\vec{E}$ -- so $\theta_1 = 0^\circ$, and we rotate to $\theta_2 = 90^\circ$.
Sanity check: rotating away from the stable position should cost positive work -- and it does. If your answer came out negative, you dropped the minus sign in $U$.

segments.text: Now a JEE Main problem that puts torque and energy together in one question -- a very common pairing.

A dipole of moment five times ten to the minus nine coulomb metre sits in a uniform field of two times ten to the power four newton per coulomb. Part a: find the torque when p makes thirty degrees with E. Part b: find the work needed to rotate the dipole from its stable equilibrium position to ninety degrees.
Picture the situation. A uniform field, the dipole sitting at an angle to it, and the two equal and opposite forces forming a couple that twists it.
Part a is a direct substitution. Torque equals p E sine theta: five times ten to the minus nine, times two times ten to the power four, times sine thirty degrees.

Do the p E product first -- it is ten to the minus four, and it will reappear in part b, so it is worth having. Sine thirty degrees is zero point five. Multiply and the torque is five times ten to the minus five newton metre.

<curious> Part b is where the thinking is, and it hinges on one phrase in the question: stable equilibrium. From our energy curve, we know the stable position is where p is aligned with E -- the valley of the curve, at theta equals zero. So theta one is zero degrees, and we are rotating to theta two equals ninety degrees. Recognising that stable means zero, not one hundred and eighty, is the whole examinable step.
Now use the work formula: W equals p E, times cos theta one minus cos theta two. Cos zero is one, and cos ninety is zero. So the bracket is simply one minus zero, and the work is just p E.
And we already have p E from part a -- it is ten to the minus four. So the work is one times ten to the minus four joule.

Always close with the sanity check. We rotated the dipole away from its most stable, lowest-energy position, so the work should come out positive -- and it does. If your answer had come out negative, that is the signature of dropping the minus sign in U equals minus p E cos theta, which is the most common error in this entire subtopic.
अब एक JEE Main problem जो torque और energy को एक ही question में जोड़ देता है -- बहुत common pairing है।

Five times ten to the minus nine coulomb metre moment वाला एक dipole two times ten to the power four newton per coulomb के uniform field में बैठा है। Part a: torque निकालो जब p, E के साथ thirty degrees बनाए। Part b: dipole को stable equilibrium position से ninety degrees तक घुमाने के लिए ज़रूरी work निकालो।
Situation की कल्पना करो। एक uniform field, dipole उससे कोण बनाकर बैठा हुआ, और दो equal तथा opposite forces एक couple बनाते हुए जो उसे twist करता है।
Part a एक सीधा substitution है। Torque equals p E sine theta: five times ten to the minus nine, times two times ten to the power four, times sine thirty degrees।

पहले p E का product कर लो -- यह है ten to the minus four, और यह part b में फिर आएगा, तो इसे रखना फायदेमंद है। Sine thirty degrees है zero point five। Multiply करो और torque है five times ten to the minus five newton metre।

<curious> Part b में असली सोच है, और वो question के एक शब्द पर टिकी है: stable equilibrium। हमारे energy curve से, हम जानते हैं कि stable position वहाँ है जहाँ p, E के साथ aligned हो -- curve की valley, theta equals zero पर। तो theta one है zero degrees, और हम theta two equals ninety degrees तक घुमा रहे हैं। यह पहचानना कि stable का मतलब zero है, one hundred and eighty नहीं, यही पूरा examinable step है।
अब work formula use करो: W equals p E, times cos theta one minus cos theta two। Cos zero है one, और cos ninety है zero। तो bracket simply one minus zero है, और work बस p E है।
और p E हमारे पास part a से पहले से है -- वो है ten to the minus four। तो work है one times ten to the minus four joule।

हमेशा sanity check के साथ बंद करो। हमने dipole को उसकी सबसे stable, lowest-energy position से दूर घुमाया, तो work positive आना चाहिए -- और वो आता है। अगर तुम्हारा answer negative आया होता, तो वो U equals minus p E cos theta में minus sign छोड़ देने का signature है, जो पूरे subtopic की सबसे common error है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Dipoles

board_events.text: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Dipoles
Pitfall: confusing $1/r^2$ with $1/r^3$. A point charge's field is $1/r^2$; a dipole's far field is $1/r^3$. Anchor it -- a dipole is less far-reaching because its charges cancel.

Pitfall: forgetting the axial-to-equatorial factor of two. $E_{\text{axial}} = 2E_{\text{equatorial}}$ at equal distance, AND the directions are opposite. Many students remember one fact but not both.
Pitfall: assuming 'no net force' always. That is true only in a uniform field. In a non-uniform field $F = p\,dE/dr$ is not zero -- which is how a charged rod picks up paper bits.
Pitfall: sign errors in potential energy. $U = -pE\cos\theta$. The stable position at $\theta = 0$ is the energy minimum $-pE$, not a maximum. Draw the curve once and it is fixed for good.
Pro-tip: for dipole numericals at $r \gg a$, always use the compact $kp/r^3$ forms rather than the full two-charge expressions -- faster and far less error-prone.
And remember that $p$ points from minus to plus. That single convention fixes the direction of the axial field, the sign of the torque, and the sign of the energy all at once.
We have now handled charges we can point at. Next we face objects with charge smeared continuously along a line, over a surface, or through a volume.

segments.text: Let's close the dipole subtopic with the four errors that cost the most marks, and the habits that prevent them.

First pitfall, and the single most common dipole error: confusing one over r squared with one over r cubed. A point charge's field falls as one over r squared. A dipole's far field falls as one over r cubed. Anchor it with the reason rather than the fact -- a dipole is less far-reaching precisely because its two charges nearly cancel at a distance.

Second pitfall: forgetting the axial-to-equatorial factor of two. At equal distance, the axial field is twice the equatorial field, and the directions are opposite. Notice that is two separate facts. Many students confidently remember one of them and lose the mark on the other, so always rehearse them as a pair.

Third pitfall: assuming there is never a net force on a dipole. That is true only in a uniform field. In a non-uniform field, the force p times d E by d r is genuinely non-zero. And this is not an edge case -- it is the entire explanation for why a charged rod or comb picks up neutral bits of paper.

Fourth pitfall: sign errors in the potential energy. U equals minus p E cos theta, with that leading minus sign. The stable position at theta equals zero is the energy minimum, minus p E -- not a maximum. Draw the U versus theta curve once, properly, and this is fixed for good.

<curious> Now the pro-tip that speeds you up most. For any dipole numerical where r is much greater than a -- and in exam questions it almost always is, because they say 'short dipole' -- go straight to the compact k p over r cubed forms. Do not start from the full two-charge expressions with r minus a and r plus a in them. The compact forms are faster and far less error-prone, and the question is signalling that they are valid.

And one convention that pays for itself repeatedly: p points from minus to plus. Fix that single fact and it simultaneously settles the direction of the axial field, the sense of the torque, and the sign of the energy. Three things from one convention.

So far, every charge in this chapter has been one we can point at -- a sphere, a rod treated as points, two charges making a dipole. Next we face objects where the charge is smeared out continuously: along a line, over a surface, or through a whole volume. That is continuous charge distribution.
Dipole subtopic को बंद करते हैं उन चार errors के साथ जो सबसे ज्यादा marks काटती हैं, और उन habits के साथ जो उन्हें रोकती हैं।

पहला pitfall, और dipole की सबसे common error: one over r squared को one over r cubed से confuse करना। Point charge का field one over r squared के हिसाब से गिरता है। Dipole का far field one over r cubed के हिसाब से। इसे fact की जगह वजह से anchor करो -- dipole कम दूर तक पहुँचता है ठीक इसलिए क्योंकि उसके दोनों charges दूरी पर लगभग cancel हो जाते हैं।

दूसरा pitfall: axial-to-equatorial का two का factor भूल जाना। बराबर दूरी पर, axial field equatorial का दोगुना है, और directions opposite हैं। Notice करो यह दो अलग facts हैं। बहुत students confidently एक याद रखते हैं और दूसरे पर mark गँवा देते हैं, तो इन्हें हमेशा जोड़े में दोहराओ।

तीसरा pitfall: यह मान लेना कि dipole पर कभी net force होता ही नहीं। यह सिर्फ uniform field में सच है। Non-uniform field में, force p times d E by d r genuinely non-zero है। और यह कोई edge case नहीं -- यही पूरी explanation है कि charged rod या comb कागज़ के neutral टुकड़े क्यों उठा लेता है।

चौथा pitfall: potential energy में sign errors। U equals minus p E cos theta, उस शुरुआती minus sign के साथ। Theta equals zero पर stable position energy minimum है, minus p E -- maximum नहीं। U versus theta curve एक बार ठीक से बना लो, और यह हमेशा के लिए fix हो जाता है।

<curious> अब वो pro-tip जो सबसे ज्यादा तेज़ करता है। किसी भी dipole numerical में जहाँ r, a से बहुत बड़ा हो -- और exam questions में लगभग हमेशा होता है, क्योंकि वो 'short dipole' कहते हैं -- सीधा compact k p over r cubed forms पर जाओ। r minus a और r plus a वाले पूरे two-charge expressions से शुरू मत करो। Compact forms तेज़ हैं और कहीं कम error-prone, और question खुद signal दे रहा है कि वो valid हैं।

और एक convention जो बार-बार अपनी कीमत वसूल करती है: p minus से plus की तरफ point करता है। यह एक fact fix कर लो और यह एक साथ axial field की direction, torque का sense, और energy का sign तय कर देता है। एक convention से तीन चीज़ें।

अब तक, इस chapter का हर charge ऐसा था जिस पर उँगली रखी जा सके -- एक sphere, points की तरह माना गया rod, dipole बनाते दो charges। अगली बार हम ऐसी objects से सामना करेंगे जहाँ charge continuously फैला हुआ है: एक line के along, एक surface पर, या पूरे volume में। यही है continuous charge distribution।

sections.title: Why We Stop Counting and Start Describing a Density

board_events.text: Why We Stop Counting and Start Describing
Real charged objects -- a metal wire, a plastic disc, a glass sphere -- do not carry a handful of point charges. They carry unimaginably many.
Recall from the first subtopic that one microcoulomb is already about six times ten to the power twelve electrons. Tracking each one with Coulomb's law is hopeless.

board_events.text: So we do what physicists always do with the very numerous: we stop counting individuals and start describing a density.
Just as a city's population is better described by people per square kilometre than by listing every resident.
The continuum description is an approximation -- but a superb one, because the charge quantum e is fantastically small compared with any everyday object.
At truly atomic scales it does break down, and there the graininess of charge matters again. For every object in this chapter, it does not.

segments.text: Every charge we have handled so far has been one we could point at. A sphere here, another sphere there, two charges making a dipole. Now that has to change.
Real charged objects -- a metal wire, a plastic disc, a glass sphere -- do not carry a handful of point charges sitting at labelled positions. They carry unimaginably many.

Cast your mind back to the very first subtopic, where we worked out that one microcoulomb is already about six times ten to the power twelve electrons. Six trillion. Now imagine writing Coulomb's law for each of them, and adding up six trillion vectors. That approach is not merely hard, it is hopeless.

So look at the shift we have to make. On the left, the impossible picture: individual charges we would have to track one by one. On the right, the workable one: a smooth description of how much charge sits per unit size.
This is what physicists always do when faced with the very numerous. We stop counting individuals, and we start describing a density.

You already accept this move everywhere else. A city's population is far better described by people per square kilometre than by a list of every resident's name. Nobody thinks that description is a cop-out -- it is simply the right level of description for the question being asked.

<curious> Now, is this exact? No, and it is worth being honest about that. The continuum description is an approximation, because charge really does come in discrete packets. But it is a superb approximation, precisely because the quantum e is fantastically small compared with any everyday object.

At truly atomic scales the approximation does break down, and there the graininess of charge starts to matter again. But for every wire, disc, and sphere in this chapter, treating charge as smoothly spread is not just convenient -- it is essentially exact.
अब तक हमने जितने charges संभाले, वो सब ऐसे थे जिन पर उँगली रखी जा सके। यहाँ एक sphere, वहाँ दूसरा, dipole बनाते दो charges। अब यह बदलना ही होगा।
असली charged objects -- एक metal wire, एक plastic disc, एक glass sphere -- मुट्ठी भर point charges नहीं रखते जो labelled positions पर बैठे हों। वो अनगिनत charges रखते हैं।

पहले subtopic पर वापस जाओ, जहाँ हमने निकाला था कि एक microcoulomb पहले से ही roughly six times ten to the power twelve electrons है। छह trillion। अब सोचो हर एक के लिए Coulomb's law लिखना, और छह trillion vectors जोड़ना। वो तरीका सिर्फ मुश्किल नहीं है, वो hopeless है।

तो देखो हमें कौन सा shift करना है। बाईं तरफ, impossible picture: individual charges जिन्हें एक-एक करके track करना पड़ेगा। दाईं तरफ, workable वाली: एक smooth description कि per unit size कितना charge बैठा है।
Physicists हमेशा यही करते हैं जब बहुत सारी चीज़ों से सामना हो। हम individuals गिनना बंद कर देते हैं, और एक density describe करना शुरू कर देते हैं।

यह move तुम हर जगह पहले से accept करते हो। एक शहर की आबादी को हर निवासी का नाम गिनाने से कहीं बेहतर बताया जाता है people per square kilometre से। कोई नहीं सोचता कि वो description कोई बहाना है -- वो बस पूछे गए सवाल के लिए सही level की description है।

<curious> अब, क्या यह exact है? नहीं, और इस पर honest होना ज़रूरी है। Continuum description एक approximation है, क्योंकि charge सच में discrete packets में आता है। लेकिन यह एक superb approximation है, ठीक इसलिए क्योंकि quantum e किसी भी everyday object के मुकाबले बहुत ही छोटा है।

सच में atomic scales पर यह approximation टूट जाती है, और वहाँ charge की graininess फिर से matter करने लगती है। लेकिन इस chapter के हर wire, disc, और sphere के लिए, charge को smoothly फैला मानना सिर्फ convenient नहीं -- वो essentially exact है।

There are three flavours of density, depending on the shape of the object.

board_events.caption: Linear density on a wire, surface density on a sheet, volume density in a solid body

board_events.text: Linear charge density, lambda -- for thin wires, rods, and rings. Charge per metre.
Surface charge density, sigma -- for sheets, discs, and shells. Charge per square metre.
Volume charge density, rho -- for solid bodies. Charge per cubic metre.
Imagine spreading a fixed amount of ghee over a roti. Describe it as grams per square centimetre, and you can find the ghee on any patch by multiplying density by that patch's area.

Charge works identically: pick any tiny piece, and its charge is density times the size of that piece. Crucially, that tiny $dq$ is small enough to treat as a point charge -- so Coulomb's law applies to it.

segments.text: So if we are describing a density, the next question is: density of what, per what? And the answer depends entirely on the shape of the object.
There are three flavours, and each one is matched to a geometry. Getting the match right is half the battle in these problems.
Look at the three cases side by side. A thin wire, where charge is spread along a length. A flat sheet, where it is spread over an area. And a solid body, where it fills a volume.

First, linear charge density, written lambda. This is for thin wires, rods, and rings -- anything where the charge is effectively spread along a line. Its units are charge per metre, so coulomb per metre.
Second, surface charge density, written sigma. This is for sheets, discs, and shells -- anything where charge is spread over an area. Units of charge per square metre.
Third, volume charge density, written rho. This is for solid bodies, where charge fills a three-dimensional region. Units of charge per cubic metre.

Here is the picture that makes this concrete. Imagine spreading a fixed amount of ghee over a roti. If you describe it as grams per square centimetre, then you can find the ghee sitting on any patch simply by multiplying that density by the patch's area. No need to track individual molecules of ghee.
Charge behaves in exactly the same way, and this line captures it: the charge on a tiny element is the density times the size of that element. Length for lambda, area for sigma, volume for rho.

<excited> And now here is why this matters so much. That tiny element dq is small enough that we can treat it as a point charge. Which means Coulomb's law applies to it, and everything we already know comes flooding back into play. We have turned an impossible object into an infinite collection of things we already understand.
तो अगर हम density describe कर रहे हैं, तो अगला सवाल है: किसकी density, किसके per? और जवाब पूरी तरह object के shape पर depend करता है।
तीन flavours हैं, और हर एक किसी geometry से match करता है। सही match पकड़ लेना इन problems की आधी लड़ाई है।
तीनों cases साथ-साथ देखो। एक thin wire, जहाँ charge एक length के along फैला है। एक flat sheet, जहाँ वो एक area पर फैला है। और एक solid body, जहाँ वो एक volume भरता है।

पहला, linear charge density, lambda लिखा जाता है। यह thin wires, rods, और rings के लिए है -- कुछ भी जहाँ charge effectively एक line के along फैला हो। इसकी units हैं charge per metre, यानी coulomb per metre।
दूसरा, surface charge density, sigma लिखा जाता है। यह sheets, discs, और shells के लिए है -- कुछ भी जहाँ charge एक area पर फैला हो। Units हैं charge per square metre।
तीसरा, volume charge density, rho लिखा जाता है। यह solid bodies के लिए है, जहाँ charge एक three-dimensional region भरता है। Units हैं charge per cubic metre।

यह रही वो picture जो इसे concrete बना देती है। सोचो एक रोटी पर तय मात्रा में घी फैलाना। अगर तुम उसे grams per square centimetre में describe करो, तो किसी भी टुकड़े पर बैठा घी सिर्फ उस density को टुकड़े के area से multiply करके निकाल सकते हो। घी के individual molecules track करने की ज़रूरत नहीं।
Charge exactly वैसे ही behave करता है, और यह line उसे पकड़ लेती है: किसी tiny element पर charge है density times उस element का size। Lambda के लिए length, sigma के लिए area, rho के लिए volume।

<excited> और अब यह रहा कि यह इतना क्यों matter करता है। वो tiny element dq इतना छोटा है कि हम उसे point charge मान सकते हैं। मतलब उस पर Coulomb's law लागू होता है, और जो कुछ हम पहले से जानते हैं वो सब वापस खेल में आ जाता है। हमने एक impossible object को उन चीज़ों के infinite collection में बदल दिया जिन्हें हम पहले से समझते हैं।

sections.title: The Universal Recipe: Chop, Write, Cancel, Integrate

board_events.text: The Universal Recipe
Every continuous-distribution problem in this chapter follows the same four steps. Learn the recipe once and you can attack any of them.

board_events.caption: The four-step recipe: chop into elements, write dE, cancel by symmetry, then integrate

board_events.text: Step one: pick an element $dq$ matched to the geometry -- $\lambda\,dl$ for a wire or arc, $\sigma\,dA$ for a disc, $\rho\,dV$ for a solid.
Step two: write the field $d\vec{E}$ from that element using Coulomb's law, since the element is effectively a point charge.
Step three: use symmetry to identify which components cancel, and keep only the surviving direction.
Step four: express everything in one variable and integrate over the whole object.

Step three is where the marks live. The integral is straightforward only when symmetry kills most components -- rings, discs, arcs, infinite lines and sheets. Without symmetry the vector integral can be brutal.

segments.text: Here is the good news about this entire subtopic: every problem in it follows the same four steps. Learn the recipe properly once, and you can attack any of them.
Rings, discs, arcs, rods -- they look like four different problems, but they are one problem wearing four costumes. So let's set out the method clearly.
Chop, write, cancel, integrate. Those four words are the whole subtopic, and notice that the third box is highlighted, because that is the one people skip.

Step one: pick an element dq matched to the geometry. Lambda d l for a wire or an arc, sigma d A for a disc, rho d V for a solid body. Match the density to the shape, and match the element to the density.
Step two: write the field d E produced by that single element, using Coulomb's law. We are allowed to do this precisely because the element is infinitesimal, so it counts as a point charge.

<excited> Step three, and this is the step that separates a two-line solution from a two-page one: use symmetry to work out which components cancel, and keep only the direction that survives. Ask this question before you write down a single integral sign.

Step four: express everything in terms of one variable, and integrate over the whole object. If step three was done properly, this is now a scalar integral rather than a vector one, and it is usually straightforward.

Written formally, the master formula is: E equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times the integral of d q over r squared, in the radial direction. But do not be intimidated by that expression -- in practice you almost never evaluate it as written. You use symmetry to simplify it first.

One honest caveat about when this works. The integral is genuinely straightforward only when symmetry kills most of the components -- rings, discs, arcs, infinite lines and sheets. Without enough symmetry, the vector integral can be brutal. Keep that limitation in mind, because it is exactly the gap that Gauss's law is going to fill in the next subtopic.
इस पूरे subtopic के बारे में अच्छी खबर यह है: इसकी हर problem एक ही चार steps को follow करती है। Recipe एक बार ठीक से सीख लो, और तुम इनमें से किसी पर भी हमला कर सकते हो।
Rings, discs, arcs, rods -- वो चार अलग problems लगती हैं, लेकिन वो एक ही problem है चार भेस में। तो चलिए method साफ-साफ रखते हैं।
Chop, write, cancel, integrate। यही चार शब्द पूरा subtopic हैं, और notice करो तीसरा box highlighted है, क्योंकि वही है जिसे लोग skip कर देते हैं।
Step one: geometry से match करता हुआ एक element dq चुनो। Wire या arc के लिए lambda d l, disc के लिए sigma d A, solid body के लिए rho d V। Density को shape से match करो, और element को density से।
Step two: उस single element से बनने वाला field d E लिखो, Coulomb's law से। हमें ऐसा करने की इजाज़त ठीक इसलिए है क्योंकि element infinitesimal है, तो वो point charge गिना जाता है।

<excited> Step three, और यही वो step है जो दो line के solution को दो page के solution से अलग करता है: symmetry से निकालो कि कौन से components cancel होते हैं, और सिर्फ बचने वाली direction रखो। एक भी integral sign लिखने से पहले यह सवाल पूछो।
Step four: सब कुछ एक variable में express करो, और पूरे object पर integrate करो। अगर step three ठीक से हुआ, तो अब यह vector की जगह scalar integral है, और आमतौर पर सीधा होता है।

Formally लिखें तो master formula है: E equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times integral of d q over r squared, radial direction में। लेकिन उस expression से डरो मत -- practice में तुम उसे लगभग कभी वैसे evaluate नहीं करते जैसा लिखा है। तुम पहले symmetry से उसे simplify करते हो।

यह कब काम करता है इस पर एक honest caveat। Integral genuinely सीधा तभी होता है जब symmetry ज़्यादातर components को मार दे -- rings, discs, arcs, infinite lines और sheets। पर्याप्त symmetry के बिना, vector integral brutal हो सकता है। यह limitation याद रखो, क्योंकि यही exactly वो gap है जिसे अगले subtopic में Gauss's law भरने वाला है।

We already know a ring's axial field from the previous subtopic, so we can reuse it directly rather than starting from scratch.
All contributions point along the axis -- the off-axis components cancel by the disc's circular symmetry -- so we integrate $r$ from zero to $R$.

<text x="525" y="274" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">field becomes k Q over x squared</text>
</svg>
board_events.caption: Up close the disc behaves as an infinite sheet; far away it behaves as a point charge

board_events.text: Two beautiful limits. Up close ($x \ll R$) the second term vanishes and $E = \sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ -- the infinite-sheet result. Far away ($x \gg R$) it collapses to $kQ/x^2$ with $Q = \sigma\pi R^2$.

segments.text: Let's run the recipe on a real case -- the field on the axis of a uniformly charged disc. This is one of the two derivations the board asks for here.
And here is the clever choice of element that makes it work. Instead of chopping the disc into tiny squares, we chop it into thin concentric rings, like the growth rings of a tree.

So treat the disc, with surface density sigma and radius R, as a nest of thin concentric rings. A ring of radius r and width d r has area two pi r d r -- circumference times width -- and therefore carries charge sigma times two pi r d r.

<curious> And now the payoff for that choice. We already derived a ring's axial field in the previous subtopic. So instead of starting from scratch, we can reuse that result directly. This is why the choice of element matters so much -- pick the right one and the hard work is already done.

So each ring contributes d E equal to one over four pi epsilon nought, times x sigma two pi r d r, over x squared plus r squared, to the power three halves. That is just the ring formula with the ring's charge substituted in.

Now step three, the symmetry step. Every one of these rings is circularly symmetric about the axis, so all the off-axis components cancel, exactly as they did for a single ring. Every contribution points straight along the axis. So we simply integrate r from zero at the centre out to R at the rim.

The integral looks awkward but yields to the substitution u equals x squared plus r squared. Working it through gives one over x minus one over the root of x squared plus R squared -- and the final result is sigma over two epsilon nought, times the bracket one minus x over root x squared plus R squared.
Now, this result is worth more than the algebra that produced it, because of what happens at its two extremes.

<excited> Look at both limits. First, up close, where x is much less than R. The second term goes to zero, and the field becomes simply sigma over two epsilon nought -- constant, independent of distance. That is exactly the infinite-sheet result, and it makes sense: stand close enough to any disc and it looks infinite. Second, far away, where x is much greater than R. Expand carefully and the whole thing collapses to k Q over x squared, with Q being sigma times pi R squared, the total charge. The disc has shrunk to a point charge. One formula, containing both a sheet and a point charge inside it.
चलिए recipe को एक असली case पर चलाते हैं -- uniformly charged disc के axis पर field। यह उन दो derivations में से एक है जो board यहाँ पूछता है।
और यह रहा element का वो clever choice जो इसे काम करने लायक बनाता है। Disc को छोटे squares में काटने के बजाय, हम उसे thin concentric rings में काटते हैं, पेड़ के growth rings की तरह।

तो disc को, surface density sigma और radius R के साथ, thin concentric rings के nest की तरह मानो। Radius r और width d r वाले ring का area है two pi r d r -- circumference times width -- और इसलिए वो charge रखता है sigma times two pi r d r।

<curious> और अब उस choice का फायदा। हमने पिछले subtopic में ring का axial field पहले ही derive कर लिया था। तो शुरू से शुरू करने के बजाय, हम वो result सीधा दोबारा इस्तेमाल कर सकते हैं। यही वजह है कि element का choice इतना matter करता है -- सही चुनो और मुश्किल काम पहले से हो चुका होता है।

तो हर ring contribute करता है d E, बराबर one over four pi epsilon nought, times x sigma two pi r d r, over x squared plus r squared, to the power three halves। यह बस ring का formula है जिसमें ring का charge substitute कर दिया गया।

अब step three, symmetry वाला step। इनमें से हर ring axis के बारे में circularly symmetric है, तो सारे off-axis components cancel हो जाते हैं, exactly जैसे एक अकेले ring के लिए हुए थे। हर contribution सीधा axis के along point करता है। तो हम simply r को centre पर zero से लेकर rim पर R तक integrate करते हैं।

Integral awkward लगता है लेकिन substitution u equals x squared plus r squared से हल हो जाता है। इसे चलाने पर मिलता है one over x minus one over root of x squared plus R squared -- और final result है sigma over two epsilon nought, times bracket one minus x over root x squared plus R squared।
अब, यह result उस algebra से ज्यादा कीमती है जिसने उसे बनाया, क्योंकि इसके दोनों extremes पर जो होता है वो खास है।

<excited> दोनों limits देखो। पहला, पास से, जहाँ x, R से बहुत कम है। दूसरा term zero हो जाता है, और field बन जाता है simply sigma over two epsilon nought -- constant, distance से independent। यह exactly infinite-sheet result है, और यह सही लगता है: किसी भी disc के काफी पास खड़े हो जाओ और वो infinite दिखने लगता है। दूसरा, दूर से, जहाँ x, R से बहुत बड़ा है। ध्यान से expand करो और पूरी चीज़ collapse होकर k Q over x squared बन जाती है, जहाँ Q है sigma times pi R squared, यानी total charge। Disc सिकुड़कर point charge बन गया। एक formula, जिसके अंदर एक sheet और एक point charge दोनों बैठे हैं।

board_events.text: Take a wire bent into a semicircle of radius $R$ and linear density $\lambda$, centred at O. An element subtending angle $d\theta$ has length $R\,d\theta$ and charge $\lambda R\,d\theta$.

board_events.text: A full ring would give exactly zero at its centre -- the two halves cancel. That single symmetry insight is behind a great many quick exam questions.

segments.text: Now the second derivation, and this one is a beautiful showcase of the symmetry step doing almost all of the work.
Look at the arrangement. A semicircular arc, its centre O sitting at the midpoint of the diameter, and I have drawn one element together with its mirror twin on the other side.

Take a wire bent into a semicircle of radius R, carrying linear density lambda, centred at O. An element that subtends an angle d theta at the centre has length R d theta, and therefore carries charge lambda R d theta.
Its field at the centre is one over four pi epsilon nought, times d q over R squared -- and substituting d q gives lambda d theta over R.

Notice something pleasant that just happened. One power of R cancelled: we had R squared in the denominator, but d q brought an R up in the numerator. And notice too that every single element sits at exactly the same distance R from the centre -- that is the special gift of working at the centre of a circular arc.

<excited> Now the symmetry step. Look at the element and its mirror twin. Their fields at O have components along the diameter that point in exactly opposite directions and cancel in pairs. What survives is only the components perpendicular to the diameter -- and those all point the same way, straight down and away from the arc. So they add.

So we integrate only the surviving component, which is d E sine theta, with theta running from zero to pi across the semicircle. The integral of sine theta over that range is exactly two. And the answer comes out remarkably clean: E equals two k lambda over R.
Now compare that with a case you should never confuse it with.

<whisper> Take a full ring instead of a half ring. Now every element has a diametrically opposite twin, and the cancellation is complete -- the field at the centre is exactly zero. For the semicircle, the cancellation is only partial, and two k lambda over R survives. That single symmetry insight sits behind a great many quick exam questions, and we will use it in the very next section.
अब दूसरी derivation, और यह symmetry step का एक beautiful showcase है जहाँ वो लगभग पूरा काम खुद कर देता है।
Arrangement देखो। एक semicircular arc, उसका centre O diameter के midpoint पर बैठा हुआ, और मैंने एक element के साथ दूसरी तरफ उसका mirror twin भी बनाया है।

R radius का एक semicircle में मोड़ा गया wire लो, जो linear density lambda रखता है, O पर centred। जो element centre पर d theta कोण बनाता है उसकी length है R d theta, और इसलिए वो charge रखता है lambda R d theta।
Centre पर उसका field है one over four pi epsilon nought, times d q over R squared -- और d q substitute करने पर मिलता है lambda d theta over R।

एक अच्छी बात notice करो जो अभी हुई। R की एक power cancel हो गई: denominator में R squared था, लेकिन d q numerator में एक R ले आया। और यह भी notice करो कि हर एक element centre से exactly same दूरी R पर है -- यही circular arc के centre पर काम करने का खास तोहफा है।

<excited> अब symmetry step। Element और उसके mirror twin को देखो। O पर उनके fields के diameter के along components exactly opposite directions में point करते हैं और जोड़ों में cancel हो जाते हैं। जो बचता है वो सिर्फ diameter के perpendicular components हैं -- और वो सब एक ही तरफ point करते हैं, सीधा नीचे और arc से दूर। तो वो जुड़ जाते हैं।

तो हम सिर्फ बचने वाला component integrate करते हैं, जो है d E sine theta, theta zero से pi तक semicircle पर चलता हुआ। उस range पर sine theta का integral exactly two है। और जवाब remarkably clean आता है: E equals two k lambda over R।
अब इसकी तुलना उस case से करो जिससे इसे कभी confuse नहीं करना चाहिए।

<whisper> आधे ring की जगह पूरा ring लो। अब हर element का एक diametrically opposite twin है, और cancellation पूरी हो जाती है -- centre पर field exactly zero है। Semicircle के लिए, cancellation सिर्फ आधी है, और two k lambda over R बच जाता है। वो एक symmetry insight बहुत सारे quick exam questions के पीछे बैठी है, और हम उसे अगले ही section में इस्तेमाल करेंगे।

sections.title: Densities, the Master Formula, and Standard Results

board_events.text: Densities, the Master Formula, and Standard Results
Units and dimensions: $\lambda$ in C/m, $[L^{-1}TA]$. $\sigma$ in C per square metre, $[L^{-2}TA]$. $\rho$ in C per cubic metre, $[L^{-3}TA]$.
For a uniform density this is just density times total size -- no integration needed.
Keep these three standard results at your fingertips. Ring at centre gives zero; ring axial field peaks at $x = R/\sqrt{2}$; the disc becomes a sheet up close and a point charge far away.

segments.text: Let's gather the formulas for this subtopic, including the standard results that are worth knowing cold rather than rederiving under time pressure.
First the three densities, each defined as charge per unit of the relevant size: lambda is d q by d l, sigma is d q by d A, and rho is d q by d V.

Their units and dimensions come up as direct one-mark questions, so learn them together. Lambda in coulomb per metre, dimensions L to the minus one, T, A. Sigma in coulomb per square metre, L to the minus two, T, A. And rho in coulomb per cubic metre, L to the minus three, T, A. Notice the pattern -- only the power of length changes.
To get the total charge, integrate the density over the whole object.

And for a uniform density -- which is most exam questions -- this reduces to simply density times total size. No integration needed at all. That is worth knowing, because students sometimes set up an unnecessary integral for a one-line question.
The master formula for the field is the integral of d q over r squared in the radial direction. As we said, you rarely evaluate this as written -- symmetry simplifies it first.
Now the three standard results. First, the ring on its axis: k Q x over x squared plus R squared, to the power three halves. We derived this in the field subtopic.
Second, the disc on its axis: sigma over two epsilon nought, times one minus x over root x squared plus R squared.
Third, the semicircular arc at its centre: two k lambda over R.

<whisper> Keep these three at your fingertips, along with three facts that hang off them. A full ring gives exactly zero at its centre. The ring's axial field peaks at x equals R over root two. And the disc becomes an infinite sheet up close and a point charge far away. Those facts turn multi-step problems into single lines.
चलिए इस subtopic के formulas इकट्ठा करते हैं, उन standard results समेत जिन्हें time pressure में दोबारा derive करने से बेहतर है cold याद रखना।
पहले तीनों densities, हर एक relevant size के per unit charge के रूप में defined: lambda है d q by d l, sigma है d q by d A, और rho है d q by d V।

उनकी units और dimensions सीधे one-mark questions के रूप में आते हैं, तो उन्हें साथ में सीखो। Lambda coulomb per metre में, dimensions L to the minus one, T, A। Sigma coulomb per square metre में, L to the minus two, T, A। और rho coulomb per cubic metre में, L to the minus three, T, A। Pattern notice करो -- सिर्फ length की power बदलती है।
Total charge निकालने के लिए, density को पूरे object पर integrate करो।

और uniform density के लिए -- जो ज़्यादातर exam questions होते हैं -- यह घटकर simply density times total size रह जाता है। कोई integration नहीं चाहिए। यह जानना ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि students कभी-कभी एक line के question के लिए बेवजह integral set up कर बैठते हैं।
Field का master formula है radial direction में d q over r squared का integral। जैसा हमने कहा, तुम इसे लिखे हुए रूप में शायद ही evaluate करते हो -- symmetry पहले उसे simplify कर देती है।
अब तीन standard results। पहला, ring अपने axis पर: k Q x over x squared plus R squared, to the power three halves। हमने यह field subtopic में derive किया था।
दूसरा, disc अपने axis पर: sigma over two epsilon nought, times one minus x over root x squared plus R squared।
तीसरा, semicircular arc अपने centre पर: two k lambda over R।

<whisper> इन तीनों को उँगलियों पर रखो, साथ में उन तीन facts के जो इनसे लटके हैं। पूरा ring अपने centre पर exactly zero देता है। Ring का axial field x equals R over root two पर peak करता है। और disc पास से infinite sheet और दूर से point charge बन जाता है। ये facts multi-step problems को single lines में बदल देते हैं।

sections.title: Worked Examples: Total Charge on a Rod, and the Ring-versus-Arc Trap

board_events.text: Example 1 -- CBSE Board Level
A thin rod of length fifty centimetres carries a uniform linear charge density $\lambda = 4\ \mu\text{C/m}$. Find the total charge on the rod.
For a uniform density, total charge is simply density times size -- no integral required. Recognising that is the whole question.
Example 2 -- NEET Speed Trap
A uniformly charged full ring and a uniformly charged semicircular arc have the same radius $R$ and the same $\lambda$. What is the electric field at the centre of each?

board_events.caption: The full ring cancelling to zero at its centre, against the arc leaving a surviving field

board_events.text: The trap: students reflexively set up an integral for both. Symmetry settles the ring instantly, with no calculation at all.

For the full ring, every element has a diametrically opposite twin pushing the opposite way, so all contributions cancel: $E = 0$. For the semicircle the cancellation is incomplete, leaving $E = 2k\lambda/R$.

segments.text: Two quick examples now, and together they make a point about when to calculate and when to think.
First, a board-level question. A thin rod of length fifty centimetres carries a uniform linear charge density of four microcoulomb per metre. Find the total charge on the rod.
Total charge is lambda times L: four times ten to the minus six, times zero point five zero metres. That gives two point zero times ten to the minus six coulomb, or two point zero microcoulomb.

Notice what made that a one-line answer. Because the density is uniform, total charge is simply density times size -- there is no integral to do. Recognising that is genuinely the whole question, and students who reach for the integral sign have already lost time they did not need to spend.
Now the NEET speed trap, which pushes that same lesson much harder.
A uniformly charged full ring and a uniformly charged semicircular arc have the same radius R and carry the same linear density lambda. What is the electric field at the centre of each?
Look at the two cases side by side, because the picture answers the question faster than any algebra could.
<whisper> Here is the trap. Students see a curved charged object and reflexively start setting up an integral for both cases. But symmetry settles the ring instantly, with no calculation whatsoever.

For the full ring, every element has a diametrically opposite twin pushing exactly the opposite way. All contributions cancel in pairs, so the field at the centre is exactly zero. For the semicircle, that cancellation is incomplete -- only the components along the diameter cancel -- and what survives is two k lambda over R. Full ring gives zero, half ring gives two k lambda over R. No integration needed for either, once you have seen it.
अब दो quick examples, और मिलकर वो एक बात बनाते हैं: कब calculate करना है और कब सोचना है।
पहला, एक board-level question। पचास centimetre लंबा एक thin rod uniform linear charge density चार microcoulomb per metre रखता है। Rod पर total charge निकालो।
Total charge है lambda times L: four times ten to the minus six, times zero point five zero metres। इससे मिलता है two point zero times ten to the minus six coulomb, यानी two point zero microcoulomb।

Notice करो किस चीज़ ने इसे एक line का जवाब बनाया। क्योंकि density uniform है, total charge simply density times size है -- कोई integral करना ही नहीं। यह पहचान लेना ही genuinely पूरा question है, और जो students integral sign की तरफ हाथ बढ़ाते हैं वो पहले ही वो समय गँवा चुके हैं जो खर्च करने की ज़रूरत नहीं थी।
अब NEET speed trap, जो उसी सबक को कहीं ज्यादा ज़ोर से धकेलता है।
एक uniformly charged पूरा ring और एक uniformly charged semicircular arc, दोनों की radius R same है और linear density lambda भी same। हर एक के centre पर electric field क्या है?
दोनों cases साथ-साथ देखो, क्योंकि picture इस सवाल का जवाब किसी भी algebra से तेज़ दे देती है।

<whisper> यह रहा trap। Students एक curved charged object देखते हैं और reflexively दोनों cases के लिए integral set up करना शुरू कर देते हैं। लेकिन symmetry ring को तुरंत settle कर देती है, बिना किसी calculation के।

पूरे ring के लिए, हर element का एक diametrically opposite twin है जो exactly उल्टी तरफ धकेलता है। सारे contributions जोड़ों में cancel हो जाते हैं, तो centre पर field exactly zero है। Semicircle के लिए, वो cancellation अधूरी है -- सिर्फ diameter के along components cancel होते हैं -- और जो बचता है वो है two k lambda over R। पूरा ring zero देता है, आधा ring two k lambda over R। एक बार देख लेने के बाद, किसी के लिए भी integration नहीं चाहिए।

sections.title: Worked Example: Axial Field of a Charged Disc

board_events.text: Example 3 -- JEE Main Level
A disc of radius $R = 10$ cm carries uniform surface charge density $\sigma = 8.85 \times 10^{-7}$ C per square metre. Find the electric field on its axis at a distance $x = R$ from the centre.
Handle the bracket first. With $x = R$, the fraction becomes $R$ over $\sqrt{2R^2}$, which is one over root two -- and the radius cancels entirely.
Notice the numbers were chosen so that $\sigma$ and $\varepsilon_0$ share the same leading digits -- they cancel cleanly, leaving a round prefactor.
The field is about $1.46 \times 10^{4}$ N/C, directed along the axis away from the disc. Sanity check: it is well below the close-up ceiling of $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, as it must be.

segments.text: Now a JEE Main problem that simply applies the disc result we derived -- but it rewards anyone who handles the algebra in the right order.

A disc of radius ten centimetres carries a uniform surface charge density of eight point eight five times ten to the minus seven coulomb per square metre. Find the electric field on its axis at a distance x equal to R from the centre.
Start by writing down the disc formula: sigma over two epsilon nought, times one minus x over the root of x squared plus R squared.

<curious> Now here is the move that makes this easy. Handle the bracket first, before touching any numbers. We are told x equals R, so substitute that in: the fraction becomes R over the root of R squared plus R squared, which is R over the root of two R squared. And now watch -- the R cancels completely, top and bottom. The answer will not depend on the radius at all.

What is left is one over root two, which is about zero point seven zero seven. Notice we never needed the ten centimetres. That was a distractor, and students who convert it and carry it through the algebra do a lot of unnecessary work.

Now the prefactor. Sigma over two epsilon nought is eight point eight five times ten to the minus seven, divided by twice eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve. That gives five point zero times ten to the power four newton per coulomb.

Notice how kindly that came out. The problem-setter chose sigma to share its leading digits with epsilon nought, so the eight point eight five cancels top and bottom, leaving only the powers of ten. Whenever you see numbers that suspiciously echo a physical constant, expect them to cancel.

Now multiply the two pieces. Five times ten to the fourth, times one minus zero point seven zero seven, which is zero point two nine three. That gives about one point four six times ten to the power four newton per coulomb.

And the direction: along the axis, pointing away from the disc, since the charge is positive. One last sanity check worth doing -- our answer is comfortably below five times ten to the fourth, which is the ceiling value sigma over two epsilon nought that the field would reach right at the surface. It must be smaller than that, and it is.
अब एक JEE Main problem जो बस उसी disc result को apply करती है जो हमने derive किया -- लेकिन यह उसे इनाम देती है जो algebra सही क्रम में संभाले।

दस centimetre radius का एक disc uniform surface charge density eight point eight five times ten to the minus seven coulomb per square metre रखता है। उसके axis पर centre से x equals R दूरी पर electric field निकालो।
Disc formula लिखने से शुरू करो: sigma over two epsilon nought, times one minus x over root of x squared plus R squared।

<curious> अब यह रहा वो move जो इसे आसान बना देता है। किसी भी number को छूने से पहले bracket संभालो। हमें बताया गया है x equals R, तो वो substitute करो: fraction बन जाता है R over root of R squared plus R squared, यानी R over root of two R squared। और अब देखो -- R पूरी तरह cancel हो जाता है, ऊपर और नीचे। जवाब radius पर बिलकुल depend नहीं करेगा।

जो बचता है वो है one over root two, यानी लगभग zero point seven zero seven। Notice करो हमें दस centimetre की ज़रूरत ही नहीं पड़ी। वो एक distractor था, और जो students उसे convert करके algebra में साथ ले चलते हैं वो बहुत बेवजह मेहनत करते हैं।

अब prefactor। Sigma over two epsilon nought है eight point eight five times ten to the minus seven, divided by twice eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve। इससे मिलता है five point zero times ten to the power four newton per coulomb।

Notice करो यह कितनी मेहरबानी से निकला। Problem बनाने वाले ने sigma ऐसा चुना कि उसके leading digits epsilon nought से मिलें, तो eight point eight five ऊपर-नीचे cancel हो जाता है, सिर्फ powers of ten बचते हैं। जब भी ऐसे numbers दिखें जो शक़ के साथ किसी physical constant की नकल कर रहे हों, उम्मीद रखो कि वो cancel होंगे।

अब दोनों टुकड़े multiply करो। Five times ten to the fourth, times one minus zero point seven zero seven, यानी zero point two nine three। इससे मिलता है लगभग one point four six times ten to the power four newton per coulomb।

और direction: axis के along, disc से दूर point करता हुआ, क्योंकि charge positive है। एक आखिरी sanity check करने लायक है -- हमारा जवाब five times ten to the fourth से आराम से नीचे है, जो वो ceiling value sigma over two epsilon nought है जिस तक field surface पर पहुँचता। उससे छोटा होना ही चाहिए, और है।

board_events.text: Element at angle $\theta$, running from zero to $\pi/2$: $dq = \lambda R\,d\theta$, giving field magnitude $k\lambda\,d\theta/R$ at O, with components $(-\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)$.
Unlike the symmetric semicircle, here BOTH components survive. There is no mirror element to cancel anything, so you must integrate each direction separately.
Both integrals evaluate to one, so both components have the same magnitude $k\lambda/R$. That equality is the symmetry of the quarter arc about its own bisector.
Check: two perpendicular quarter arcs would combine to give the semicircle's $2k\lambda/R$ along the axis -- consistent with the previous derivation.

segments.text: Now the JEE Advanced version, and it is a deliberate variation on the arc we just did -- designed to catch anyone who memorised the semicircle result without understanding where it came from.
A wire is bent into a quarter circle of radius R, sitting in the first quadrant, carrying uniform linear density lambda. Find the magnitude of the electric field at the centre O.
Look at the geometry. The arc occupies only one quadrant, from the x axis round to the y axis, and O is the centre of that circle.

Set up as before. An element at angle theta, with theta now running from zero to pi over two, carries charge lambda R d theta. Its field at O has magnitude k lambda d theta over R, exactly as in the semicircle case. And it points away from the element, which gives it components minus cos theta and minus sin theta.

<whisper> But now here is the crucial difference, and it is the entire point of the problem. In the semicircle, every element had a mirror twin that cancelled its horizontal component. In a quarter arc, there is no such twin. Both components survive. So you cannot lean on symmetry to kill one direction -- you must integrate each direction separately.
So do exactly that. E x is minus k lambda over R, times the integral of cos theta from zero to pi over two. And E y is minus k lambda over R, times the integral of sin theta over the same range.

Both of those integrals evaluate to exactly one, so both components come out with the same magnitude, k lambda over R. And that equality is not a coincidence -- it reflects the fact that a quarter arc is still symmetric about its own bisector, the forty five degree line. It has lost the symmetry that killed a component, but it kept the symmetry that makes the two components equal.
So the resultant is the root of E x squared plus E y squared, which is root two times k lambda over R. Its direction is along the bisector of the quarter arc, pointing away from the arc.

<excited> And here is the consistency check that ties this back to the previous derivation. Take two perpendicular quarter arcs and put them together -- you get a semicircle. Their bisector-directed fields combine, and the components perpendicular to the semicircle's axis cancel, leaving exactly two k lambda over R along the axis. That is precisely the semicircle result we derived earlier. The two answers agree, which is how you know both are right.
अब JEE Advanced वाला version, और यह उसी arc पर एक जानबूझकर की गई variation है जो हमने अभी की -- उन लोगों को पकड़ने के लिए बनाई गई जिन्होंने semicircle का result बिना समझे रट लिया।
एक wire को R radius के quarter circle में मोड़ा गया है, जो first quadrant में बैठा है, uniform linear density lambda के साथ। Centre O पर electric field की magnitude निकालो।
Geometry देखो। Arc सिर्फ एक quadrant घेरता है, x axis से घूमकर y axis तक, और O उस circle का centre है।

पहले की तरह set up करो। Theta कोण पर एक element, जहाँ theta अब zero से pi over two तक चलता है, charge lambda R d theta रखता है। O पर उसके field की magnitude है k lambda d theta over R, exactly semicircle case जैसी। और वो element से दूर point करता है, जिससे उसके components बनते हैं minus cos theta और minus sin theta।

<whisper> लेकिन अब यह रहा crucial difference, और यही पूरी problem का मकसद है। Semicircle में, हर element का एक mirror twin था जो उसका horizontal component cancel कर देता था। Quarter arc में, ऐसा कोई twin नहीं है। दोनों components बच जाते हैं। तो तुम एक direction मारने के लिए symmetry पर भरोसा नहीं कर सकते -- हर direction अलग से integrate करनी होगी।
तो exactly वही करो। E x है minus k lambda over R, times cos theta का integral zero से pi over two तक। और E y है minus k lambda over R, times sin theta का integral उसी range पर।

उन दोनों integrals की value exactly one निकलती है, तो दोनों components same magnitude के साथ आते हैं, k lambda over R। और वो बराबरी कोई coincidence नहीं है -- यह इस बात को दिखाती है कि quarter arc अभी भी अपने खुद के bisector, यानी पैंतालीस degree line, के बारे में symmetric है। उसने वो symmetry खोई जो एक component को मार देती थी, लेकिन वो symmetry रखी जो दोनों components को बराबर बनाती है।
तो resultant है E x squared plus E y squared का root, यानी root two times k lambda over R। इसकी direction quarter arc के bisector के along है, arc से दूर point करती हुई।

<excited> और यह रहा वो consistency check जो इसे पिछली derivation से जोड़ देता है। दो perpendicular quarter arcs लो और उन्हें साथ रखो -- तुम्हें एक semicircle मिल जाता है। उनके bisector वाले fields मिलते हैं, और semicircle के axis के perpendicular components cancel हो जाते हैं, बचता है exactly two k lambda over R axis के along। यही ठीक वही semicircle result है जो हमने पहले derive किया था। दोनों जवाब agree करते हैं, और इसी से पता चलता है कि दोनों सही हैं।

sections.title: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Continuous Distributions

board_events.text: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Continuous Distributions
Pitfall: adding magnitudes instead of vectors. Field contributions are vectors -- always resolve into components and use symmetry to cancel before integrating.
Pitfall: treating an extended body as a point too early. $E = kQ/r^2$ is valid only far away, or for spherical symmetry. Near a disc, rod, or ring you must integrate.
Pitfall: mixing up the densities. Lambda is per length, sigma per area, rho per volume. Match the density to the geometry, and the element $dq$ to the density.
Pitfall: forgetting the ring-versus-arc distinction. Full ring centre gives zero; semicircle centre gives $2k\lambda/R$. Do not let one overwrite the other.

Pro-tip: before integrating anything, ask which components cancel. For a full loop, often everything cancels. For a disc on its axis, only the axial part survives -- turning a vector integral into a one-variable scalar one.
And sanity-check every result with a limit: a disc should become an infinite sheet up close, and a point charge far away.
Notice the tension building. Our method works beautifully when there is symmetry, and becomes brutal when there is not.
Next we meet a law that turns that same symmetry into a shortcut so powerful it replaces the integration entirely -- Gauss's law.

segments.text: Let's close this subtopic with the four errors that cost the most marks here, and the two habits that prevent nearly all of them.

First pitfall: adding magnitudes instead of vectors. Field contributions from different elements are vectors, and they point in different directions. Always resolve into components and use symmetry to cancel before you integrate anything. Never sum the sizes of d E blindly.

Second pitfall: treating an extended body as a point charge too early. The formula k Q over r squared is valid only when you are far away, or when the distribution is spherically symmetric. Near a disc, a rod, or a ring, you have to integrate. Collapsing the object to a point at the start is a tempting shortcut that produces a confidently wrong answer.

Third pitfall: mixing up the densities. Lambda is per length, sigma is per area, rho is per volume. Match the density to the geometry, and then match the element d q to the density you chose. Most set-up errors in this subtopic trace back to this one step.

Fourth pitfall: forgetting the ring-versus-arc distinction. A full ring gives exactly zero at its centre. A semicircle gives two k lambda over R. These two live very close together in memory, and one tends to overwrite the other under exam pressure. Rehearse them as a contrasting pair, never separately.

<curious> Now the pro-tip, and it is the same one we have been building towards all through this subtopic. Before you integrate anything at all, ask one question: which components cancel? For a full loop, very often everything cancels and the answer is simply zero. For a disc on its axis, only the axial part survives, which turns a hard vector integral into a one-variable scalar one. That single question saves more marks than all the calculus that follows it.

And pair it with the habit from earlier subtopics: sanity-check every result at its limits. A disc should become an infinite sheet when you stand very close, and a point charge when you back far away. If your formula does not do both, it is wrong, and you have caught it yourself.

Now, before we move on, notice the tension that has been building through this whole subtopic. Our method works beautifully when the object has symmetry -- rings, discs, arcs all fell out cleanly. But we admitted at the start that without enough symmetry, the vector integral becomes genuinely brutal.

So here is the question to carry forward. We keep using symmetry to rescue a hard integral. What if, instead, there were a law that used symmetry to avoid the integral altogether? That law exists, it is one of the four Maxwell equations, and it is where we go next. Gauss's law.
इस subtopic को बंद करते हैं उन चार errors के साथ जो यहाँ सबसे ज्यादा marks काटती हैं, और उन दो habits के साथ जो इनमें से लगभग सब रोक देती हैं।

पहला pitfall: vectors की जगह magnitudes जोड़ना। अलग-अलग elements के field contributions vectors हैं, और वो अलग directions में point करते हैं। कुछ भी integrate करने से पहले हमेशा components में resolve करो और symmetry से cancel करो। d E के sizes आँख बंद करके कभी मत जोड़ो।

दूसरा pitfall: extended body को बहुत जल्दी point charge मान लेना। Formula k Q over r squared सिर्फ तब valid है जब तुम दूर हो, या जब distribution spherically symmetric हो। Disc, rod, या ring के पास, तुम्हें integrate करना ही पड़ेगा। शुरू में ही object को point में collapse कर देना एक लुभावना shortcut है जो confidently गलत जवाब देता है।

तीसरा pitfall: densities को आपस में गड्ड-मड्ड करना। Lambda है per length, sigma है per area, rho है per volume। Density को geometry से match करो, और फिर element d q को चुनी हुई density से match करो। इस subtopic की ज़्यादातर set-up errors इसी एक step पर जाकर मिलती हैं।

चौथा pitfall: ring-versus-arc का फर्क भूल जाना। पूरा ring अपने centre पर exactly zero देता है। Semicircle देता है two k lambda over R। ये दोनों memory में बहुत पास-पास रहते हैं, और exam pressure में एक दूसरे को overwrite कर देता है। इन्हें हमेशा एक contrasting जोड़े की तरह दोहराओ, अलग-अलग कभी नहीं।

<curious> अब pro-tip, और यह वही है जिसकी तरफ हम पूरे subtopic में बढ़ रहे थे। कुछ भी integrate करने से पहले, एक सवाल पूछो: कौन से components cancel हो रहे हैं? पूरे loop के लिए, अक्सर सब कुछ cancel हो जाता है और जवाब simply zero है। Disc के axis पर, सिर्फ axial हिस्सा बचता है, जो एक कठिन vector integral को एक variable के scalar integral में बदल देता है। वो एक सवाल उसके बाद आने वाली पूरी calculus से ज्यादा marks बचाता है।

और इसके साथ पिछले subtopics की habit जोड़ो: हर result को उसकी limits पर sanity-check करो। बहुत पास खड़े होने पर disc को infinite sheet बनना चाहिए, और दूर जाने पर point charge। अगर तुम्हारा formula दोनों नहीं करता, तो वो गलत है, और तुमने खुद पकड़ लिया।

अब, आगे बढ़ने से पहले, उस tension को notice करो जो पूरे subtopic में बन रही थी। हमारा method तब खूबसूरती से काम करता है जब object में symmetry हो -- rings, discs, arcs सब साफ-साफ निकल आए। लेकिन हमने शुरू में ही माना था कि पर्याप्त symmetry के बिना, vector integral genuinely brutal हो जाता है।

तो यह सवाल आगे ले जाओ। हम बार-बार symmetry का इस्तेमाल एक कठिन integral को बचाने के लिए कर रहे हैं। अगर इसके बजाय कोई ऐसा law हो जो symmetry का इस्तेमाल integral से पूरी तरह बचने के लिए करे तो? वो law मौजूद है, वो चार Maxwell equations में से एक है, और वहीं हम अगली बार जाएँगे। Gauss's law।

sections.title: Electric Flux: Counting What Passes Through

board_events.text: Electric Flux: Counting What Passes Through
Picture holding a rectangular net in a flowing river. How much water passes through it each second?
It depends on three things: how fast the water flows, how big the net is, and -- crucially -- the angle you hold it.

segments.text: We arrive at the last subtopic of the chapter, and it opens with a quantity we have not met yet -- electric flux.
Start with a picture that has nothing to do with electricity. Imagine holding a rectangular net in a flowing river. How much water passes through that net each second?

Three things control the answer. How fast the water is flowing. How big the net is. And -- this is the one people forget -- the angle at which you hold it. Hold the net face-on to the current and you catch the maximum flow. Turn it edge-on and almost nothing passes through, even though the net has not shrunk at all.
Electric flux is exactly this idea, with the electric field playing the role of the river's flow. Look at the same surface in the same field at three different angles -- face-on, tilted, and edge-on.
Quantitatively, for a flat surface of area A in a uniform field: flux equals E A cos theta, which is neatly written as the dot product of E with the area vector A.

Now, what is this area vector? It is a vector of magnitude A that points perpendicular -- normal -- to the surface. And theta is measured between the field and that normal, not between the field and the surface itself. Getting that reference direction wrong is a classic way to end up with sine where you needed cosine.

Here is the mental model that makes flux intuitive. Think of field lines as threads piercing the surface. Flux is simply the number of threads passing through. Tilt the surface, and fewer threads make it through, because the surface now presents a smaller effective area to the flow -- exactly A cos theta.

<curious> But real surfaces are rarely flat, and real fields are rarely uniform. So what then? We do what we always do in this chapter: we chop. Break the surface into patches small enough that each is effectively flat, with its own normal and its own local field.
Compute E dotted with d A on every patch, and add them all up. That sum is the surface integral, and it is the general definition of flux. Same idea as before, just handled piece by piece.
हम chapter के आखिरी subtopic पर पहुँचते हैं, और यह एक ऐसी quantity से खुलता है जो अभी तक नहीं मिली -- electric flux।
एक ऐसी picture से शुरू करो जिसका बिजली से कोई लेना-देना नहीं। सोचो एक बहती नदी में एक rectangular जाल पकड़े हुए हो। हर second उस जाल से कितना पानी गुज़रता है?

तीन चीज़ें जवाब तय करती हैं। पानी कितनी तेज़ बह रहा है। जाल कितना बड़ा है। और -- यही वो है जो लोग भूल जाते हैं -- तुम उसे किस कोण पर पकड़ते हो। जाल को धारा के सामने face-on पकड़ो और तुम maximum flow पकड़ते हो। उसे edge-on घुमाओ और लगभग कुछ भी नहीं गुज़रता, जबकि जाल बिलकुल छोटा नहीं हुआ।
Electric flux exactly यही idea है, जहाँ electric field नदी के बहाव का role निभाता है। एक ही surface को एक ही field में तीन अलग कोणों पर देखो -- face-on, tilted, और edge-on।
Quantitatively, uniform field में area A के flat surface के लिए: flux equals E A cos theta, जिसे साफ-सुथरे तरीके से E और area vector A के dot product की तरह लिखा जाता है।

अब, यह area vector क्या है? यह magnitude A वाला एक vector है जो surface के perpendicular -- normal -- point करता है। और theta field और उस normal के बीच मापा जाता है, field और surface के बीच नहीं। उस reference direction को गलत करना एक classic तरीका है sine वहाँ लगा देने का जहाँ cosine चाहिए था।

यह रहा वो mental model जो flux को intuitive बना देता है। Field lines को surface को छेदते धागों की तरह सोचो। Flux बस उन धागों की गिनती है जो पार होते हैं। Surface को tilt करो, और कम धागे पार होते हैं, क्योंकि surface अब बहाव को छोटा effective area दिखाता है -- exactly A cos theta।

<curious> लेकिन असली surfaces शायद ही flat होते हैं, और असली fields शायद ही uniform। तो फिर? हम वही करते हैं जो इस chapter में हमेशा करते हैं: हम काटते हैं। Surface को इतने छोटे patches में तोड़ो कि हर एक effectively flat हो, अपने normal और अपने local field के साथ।
हर patch पर E dotted with d A निकालो, और सबको जोड़ दो। वो sum ही surface integral है, और यही flux की general definition है। वही idea, बस टुकड़े-टुकड़े में संभाला गया।

sections.title: Gauss's Law: Charge Controls the Net Flux

board_events.text: Gauss's Law: Charge Controls the Net Flux
Now here is the magic. Take any closed surface -- a balloon of any lumpy shape -- and add up the flux poking outward through all of it.
