<text x="350" y="362" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" font-style="italic" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Total outward flux ignores the shape, the size, and everything outside</text>
</svg>
board_events.caption: A lumpy closed surface with charge inside, and an outside charge whose lines enter and leave again

board_events.text: Gauss discovered something astonishing: this total outward flux does not care about the shape or size of the surface, or how the charges are arranged inside, or even what charges sit outside.
It depends on one thing only -- the net charge trapped inside.
Imagine a gulab jamun in a sealed box. All its syrup must eventually escape through the walls, so the total leaking out equals the total inside -- no matter how oddly the box is shaped.
A second sweet placed outside contributes nothing: whatever syrup of its enters one wall leaves through another.
This is more than a calculation trick. It is one of the four Maxwell equations -- a foundational law of nature.

segments.text: Flux on its own is just a bookkeeping quantity. What makes it powerful is a discovery about closed surfaces, and it is genuinely astonishing the first time you meet it.
Take any closed surface at all -- a balloon of any lumpy, irregular shape you like -- and add up all the flux poking outward through every part of it.
Look at the picture. A completely arbitrary blob of a surface, a charge sitting somewhere inside it, and another charge outside.

<excited> Gauss discovered that the total outward flux does not care about the shape of the surface. It does not care about the size. It does not care about where inside the charges sit or how they are arranged. And remarkably, it does not care about what charges are sitting outside either.

All of that collapses into one equation. The closed surface integral of E dotted with d A equals the enclosed charge divided by epsilon nought. That circle on the integral sign simply means the surface is closed.
It depends on one thing and one thing only: the net charge trapped inside.

Here is the picture that makes it feel inevitable. Imagine a gulab jamun sitting inside a sealed box. All the syrup it releases has to escape through the walls eventually -- so the total amount leaking out equals the total amount of syrup inside. It makes no difference how oddly shaped the box is.

And now the part about outside charges. Put a second sweet outside the box. Does it change what leaks out of this box? No -- whatever syrup of its enters through one wall simply leaves through another. Net contribution: exactly zero. In the field picture, an outside charge's lines pierce the surface going in and pierce it again coming out, and the two cancel.

One thing to be clear about: this is far more than a calculation trick. Gauss's law is one of the four Maxwell equations -- a foundational law of nature, on the same footing as Coulomb's law itself. But it does have a hugely practical payoff, and that is what we will spend the rest of this part on.
Flux अपने आप में बस एक bookkeeping quantity है। इसे powerful बनाती है closed surfaces के बारे में की गई एक खोज, और पहली बार मिलने पर वो genuinely हैरान करती है।
कोई भी closed surface लो -- किसी भी lumpy, irregular shape का गुब्बारा -- और उसके हर हिस्से से बाहर निकलता सारा flux जोड़ लो।
Picture देखो। एक बिलकुल arbitrary blob जैसी surface, उसके अंदर कहीं बैठा एक charge, और बाहर एक और charge।

<excited> Gauss ने पाया कि total outward flux को surface के shape की परवाह नहीं। Size की परवाह नहीं। इसकी परवाह नहीं कि charges अंदर कहाँ बैठे हैं या कैसे arranged हैं। और remarkably, इसकी भी परवाह नहीं कि बाहर कौन से charges बैठे हैं।
यह सब एक equation में सिमट जाता है। E dotted with d A का closed surface integral बराबर है enclosed charge divided by epsilon nought। Integral sign पर वो circle बस यह बताता है कि surface closed है।
यह सिर्फ एक चीज़ पर depend करता है: अंदर फँसा net charge।

यह रही वो picture जो इसे inevitable महसूस कराती है। सोचो एक sealed डिब्बे में रखा गुलाब जामुन। उसका छोड़ा हुआ सारा चाशनी आखिरकार दीवारों से बाहर निकलेगा ही -- तो जितना बाहर रिसता है वो अंदर की कुल चाशनी के बराबर है। डिब्बा कितने भी अजीब shape का हो, फर्क नहीं पड़ता।

और अब बाहर वाले charges की बात। डिब्बे के बाहर एक और मिठाई रख दो। क्या इससे इस डिब्बे से रिसने वाली मात्रा बदलती है? नहीं -- उसकी जो चाशनी एक दीवार से अंदर आती है वो दूसरी दीवार से बाहर निकल जाती है। Net contribution: exactly zero। Field की भाषा में, बाहरी charge की lines surface को अंदर जाते हुए छेदती हैं और बाहर आते हुए फिर छेदती हैं, और दोनों cancel हो जाती हैं।

एक बात साफ रखो: यह सिर्फ calculation trick से कहीं ज्यादा है। Gauss's law चार Maxwell equations में से एक है -- प्रकृति का एक foundational law, खुद Coulomb's law के बराबर दर्जे का। लेकिन इसका एक बहुत practical फायदा भी है, और इस part का बाकी हिस्सा हम उसी पर खर्च करेंगे।

sections.title: Foundation: Why the Flux Is q over Epsilon Nought

board_events.text: Foundation: Why the Flux Is q over Epsilon Nought
Before applying Gauss's law, let's see where the $Q/\varepsilon_0$ comes from. Place a point charge $q$ at the centre of an imaginary sphere of radius $r$.

board_events.caption: A point charge at the centre of a sphere, with the field radial and parallel to the normal everywhere

board_events.text: By symmetry, $\vec{E}$ points radially outward and has the same magnitude everywhere on the surface -- and it is parallel to $d\vec{A}$ at every single point.
That is what lets us pull $E$ straight out of the integral. The dot product becomes a plain product, and $E$ is constant, so it comes out as a factor.
Watch what happened: the $r^2$ from the field cancelled the $r^2$ from the sphere's area. The flux is independent of the sphere's size -- foreshadowing the full law.
That cancellation is not a coincidence. It happens because the field falls as $1/r^2$ while area grows as $r^2$ -- the inverse-square law and Gauss's law are two faces of the same fact.

segments.text: Before we start applying Gauss's law, it is worth seeing where that q over epsilon nought actually comes from. It is not arbitrary.
Take the simplest possible case. Place a point charge q at the exact centre of an imaginary sphere of radius r, and work out the flux through that sphere directly.
Look at the geometry, because it is doing all the work. The field radiates outward from the centre, and the sphere's outward normal also points radially outward, everywhere.

So by symmetry, two things are true at once. The field points radially outward and has exactly the same magnitude at every point on the surface. And it is parallel to the area vector d A at every single point, so the angle theta is zero and cos theta is one.

<curious> That is precisely what lets us pull E straight out of the integral. The dot product collapses to an ordinary product because the vectors are parallel. And since E has the same value everywhere on the sphere, it is a constant and comes out as a simple factor. Hold on to that reasoning, because it is the reasoning behind every Gauss application we are about to do.

So the flux is E times the integral of d A, which is just E times the total surface area. Substitute the point-charge field, one over four pi epsilon nought times q over r squared, and multiply by the sphere's area, four pi r squared.
Everything cancels beautifully and you are left with simply q over epsilon nought.

<excited> Now look carefully at what just happened in that cancellation. The r squared sitting in the denominator of the field was exactly cancelled by the r squared in the sphere's area. So the radius disappeared completely. Draw a sphere twice as big and the flux is identical. That is already the full Gauss's law in miniature -- flux independent of surface size.

And that cancellation is not a lucky coincidence. It happens precisely because the field falls off as one over r squared while surface area grows as r squared. Those two powers are the same power, so they annihilate. In a real sense, the inverse-square law and Gauss's law are two faces of the very same fact about our universe.
Gauss's law apply करना शुरू करने से पहले, यह देखना ज़रूरी है कि वो q over epsilon nought आता कहाँ से है। यह arbitrary नहीं है।
सबसे simple case लो। एक point charge q को r radius के imaginary sphere के exact centre पर रखो, और उस sphere से flux सीधा निकालो।
Geometry देखो, क्योंकि वही सारा काम कर रही है। Field centre से बाहर की तरफ फैलता है, और sphere का outward normal भी हर जगह radially बाहर की तरफ point करता है।

तो symmetry से, दो बातें एक साथ सच हैं। Field radially बाहर point करता है और surface के हर point पर उसकी exactly same magnitude है। और वो हर एक point पर area vector d A के parallel है, तो कोण theta zero है और cos theta one है।

<curious> यही ठीक वो चीज़ है जो हमें E को integral से सीधा बाहर खींचने देती है। Dot product एक साधारण product में सिमट जाता है क्योंकि vectors parallel हैं। और चूँकि sphere पर हर जगह E की same value है, वो constant है और एक simple factor की तरह बाहर आ जाता है। इस reasoning को पकड़े रखो, क्योंकि यही reasoning हर उस Gauss application के पीछे है जो हम अभी करने वाले हैं।

तो flux है E times d A का integral, यानी E times total surface area। Point-charge field substitute करो, one over four pi epsilon nought times q over r squared, और sphere के area four pi r squared से multiply करो।
सब कुछ खूबसूरती से cancel हो जाता है और बचता है simply q over epsilon nought।

<excited> अब ध्यान से देखो उस cancellation में क्या हुआ। Field के denominator में बैठा r squared, sphere के area के r squared से exactly cancel हो गया। तो radius पूरी तरह गायब हो गई। दोगुना बड़ा sphere बनाओ और flux वही रहेगा। यह पहले से ही पूरा Gauss's law है, छोटे रूप में -- flux, surface के size से independent।

और वो cancellation कोई किस्मत का coincidence नहीं है। यह ठीक इसलिए होता है क्योंकि field one over r squared के हिसाब से गिरता है जबकि surface area r squared के हिसाब से बढ़ता है। वो दोनों powers एक ही power हैं, तो वो एक दूसरे को मिटा देते हैं। एक असली अर्थ में, inverse-square law और Gauss's law हमारे universe के एक ही तथ्य के दो चेहरे हैं।

sections.title: Derivation: Field of an Infinite Line Charge

board_events.text: Derivation: Field of an Infinite Line Charge
Consider an infinite straight wire with uniform linear density $\lambda$. First, the symmetry argument -- it decides everything.
The field must point radially outward, perpendicular to the wire, and depend only on the perpendicular distance $r$. There is no reason for it to favour any direction along or around the wire.

board_events.text: So choose a coaxial cylinder of radius $r$ and length $L$. The flux splits into three parts, and two of them vanish.
The two flat end caps contribute nothing -- there $\vec{E}$ lies along the surface, so $\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$. On the curved surface $\vec{E}$ is everywhere perpendicular and constant.

board_events.latex: E\,(2\pi r L) = \frac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0} \;\Rightarrow\; E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

board_events.text: Note the $1/r$ dependence -- slower than a point charge's $1/r^2$, because the line keeps feeding the field as you move along it.

segments.text: Now for the payoff. Three standard derivations, and the board asks for one of them almost every year. This is the first.
Consider an infinite straight wire carrying uniform linear charge density lambda. And before we choose any surface, we do the symmetry argument -- because that decides everything that follows.

Ask what the field could possibly look like. It must point radially outward, perpendicular to the wire, and depend only on the perpendicular distance r. Why? Because the wire is infinite and uniform, so there is no reason for the field to favour any particular direction along the wire, or any particular direction around it. Symmetry forbids anything else.
That tells us which Gaussian surface to pick. We want a surface where the field is either perpendicular to it with constant magnitude, or lies flat along it. A coaxial cylinder does exactly that.

So choose a cylinder of radius r and length L, sharing its axis with the wire. The flux now splits into three pieces: the two flat end caps, and the curved side. And two of those three vanish immediately.

<excited> Look at the end caps. There the field points radially outward, which means it lies flat along the cap, parallel to the surface rather than through it. So E dotted with d A is zero, and the caps contribute nothing at all. On the curved surface, by contrast, the field is perpendicular at every point and has the same constant magnitude everywhere. This split is where the marks are.
So the flux is simply E times the curved area, which is two pi r L. And the charge enclosed by our cylinder is lambda times L -- just the density times the length of wire we have captured.
Set them equal through Gauss's law. The L cancels on both sides, which it must, since our choice of cylinder length was arbitrary. Rearranging gives E equals lambda over two pi epsilon nought r.

Now read the result. The field falls as one over r -- not one over r squared. That is slower than a point charge, and there is a physical reason. As you move away from a point charge, you leave it behind. But as you move away from an infinite line, more and more of the line comes into view at a favourable angle, so the line keeps feeding the field. That extra contribution is exactly what softens the falloff from one over r squared to one over r.
अब असली फायदा। तीन standard derivations, और board इनमें से एक लगभग हर साल पूछता है। यह पहली है।
एक infinite straight wire लो जो uniform linear charge density lambda रखता है। और कोई surface चुनने से पहले, हम symmetry argument करते हैं -- क्योंकि आगे जो कुछ होगा वो यही तय करता है।

पूछो field आखिर दिख कैसा सकता है। उसे radially बाहर point करना ही होगा, wire के perpendicular, और सिर्फ perpendicular distance r पर depend करना होगा। क्यों? क्योंकि wire infinite और uniform है, तो field के पास wire के along किसी खास direction को, या उसके चारों तरफ किसी खास direction को, तरजीह देने की कोई वजह नहीं। Symmetry बाकी सब मना कर देती है।

यही बताता है कि कौन सा Gaussian surface चुनना है। हमें ऐसा surface चाहिए जहाँ field या तो उसके perpendicular हो constant magnitude के साथ, या उसके along सपाट पड़ा हो। एक coaxial cylinder exactly यही करता है।
तो r radius और L लंबाई का एक cylinder चुनो, जो अपना axis wire के साथ share करता हो। अब flux तीन टुकड़ों में बँटता है: दो flat end caps, और curved side। और उन तीन में से दो तुरंत गायब हो जाते हैं।

<excited> End caps देखो। वहाँ field radially बाहर point करता है, मतलब वो cap के along सपाट पड़ा है, surface के आर-पार जाने के बजाय उसके parallel। तो E dotted with d A zero है, और caps कुछ भी contribute नहीं करते। इसके उलट curved surface पर, field हर point पर perpendicular है और हर जगह उसकी same constant magnitude है। यही split वो जगह है जहाँ marks हैं।
तो flux है simply E times curved area, यानी two pi r L। और हमारे cylinder द्वारा enclosed charge है lambda times L -- बस density times wire की वो लंबाई जो हमने पकड़ी।

Gauss's law से दोनों बराबर रखो। L दोनों तरफ cancel हो जाता है, और होना ही चाहिए, क्योंकि cylinder की लंबाई हमने arbitrary चुनी थी। Rearrange करने पर मिलता है E equals lambda over two pi epsilon nought r।

अब result पढ़ो। Field one over r के हिसाब से गिरता है -- one over r squared नहीं। यह point charge से धीमा है, और इसकी एक physical वजह है। Point charge से दूर जाओ तो तुम उसे पीछे छोड़ आते हो। लेकिन infinite line से दूर जाओ तो line का ज्यादा से ज्यादा हिस्सा favourable कोण पर नज़र में आता जाता है, तो line field को खिलाती रहती है। वही extra contribution one over r squared के falloff को नरम करके one over r बना देता है।

sections.title: Derivation: Field of an Infinite Plane Sheet

board_events.text: Derivation: Field of an Infinite Plane Sheet
For an infinite sheet of uniform surface density $\sigma$, symmetry demands the field point straight away from the sheet, with equal magnitude on both sides and independent of distance.

segments.text: Second derivation, and the same method applies -- symmetry first, then choose the surface that matches it.

For an infinite sheet of uniform surface density sigma, ask what symmetry allows. The field must point straight away from the sheet, perpendicular to it. It must have equal magnitude on both sides. And it cannot depend on distance, because the sheet is infinite in every direction.

That last point deserves a moment. It sounds wrong -- surely the field should weaken as you back away? But the sheet has no size to compare your distance against. Step back and you see more of it, exactly compensating. So the field is genuinely constant.
Now match the surface to that symmetry. Choose a pillbox -- a short, squat cylinder -- piercing straight through the sheet, with one flat cap of area A poking out on either side.

Do the flux split as before. The curved side of the pillbox contributes nothing, because the field lies flat along it. Each flat cap has the field passing straight through it, perpendicular, so each contributes E times A. And crucially, there are two caps -- one on each side.
So the total flux is E A plus E A, which is two E A. And the charge enclosed is sigma times A, the charge on the patch of sheet the pillbox has captured.
Apply Gauss's law and set them equal. The area A cancels on both sides, as it must, and we are left with E equals sigma over two epsilon nought.

So the field really is uniform. Notice it contains no distance variable at all -- stand one centimetre from the sheet or one kilometre, and the field is identical. That is only true because the sheet is infinite, and any real sheet behaves this way only when you are close compared with its size.
<whisper> And now the trap that this chapter punishes more than any other. Compare a thin charged sheet with the surface of a charged conductor.

A thin non-conducting sheet radiates both ways, so the pillbox has two active caps and we get sigma over two epsilon nought. But at a conductor's surface, there is metal behind the charge and the field exists on one side only -- the pillbox has just one active cap. That gives sigma over epsilon nought, twice as big. Tag which situation the problem describes before you write down a single line.
दूसरी derivation, और वही method लागू होता है -- पहले symmetry, फिर उससे match करता surface चुनो।

Uniform surface density sigma वाली infinite sheet के लिए, पूछो symmetry क्या इजाज़त देती है। Field को sheet से सीधा दूर point करना होगा, उसके perpendicular। दोनों तरफ उसकी magnitude बराबर होनी चाहिए। और वो distance पर depend नहीं कर सकता, क्योंकि sheet हर direction में infinite है।

वो आखिरी बात एक पल की हकदार है। यह गलत लगता है -- पीछे हटने पर field कमज़ोर होना चाहिए न? लेकिन sheet के पास कोई size ही नहीं है जिससे तुम्हारी दूरी की तुलना हो। पीछे हटो और तुम उसका ज्यादा हिस्सा देखते हो, जो exactly भरपाई कर देता है। तो field genuinely constant है।
अब surface को उस symmetry से match करो। एक pillbox चुनो -- एक छोटा, चपटा cylinder -- जो sheet के आर-पार सीधा निकलता हो, दोनों तरफ area A का एक-एक flat cap बाहर निकाले हुए।

पहले की तरह flux split करो। Pillbox का curved side कुछ contribute नहीं करता, क्योंकि field उसके along सपाट पड़ा है। हर flat cap से field सीधा perpendicular गुज़रता है, तो हर एक contribute करता है E times A। और crucially, दो caps हैं -- हर तरफ एक।
तो total flux है E A plus E A, यानी two E A। और enclosed charge है sigma times A, यानी sheet के उस टुकड़े का charge जो pillbox ने पकड़ा।
Gauss's law लगाकर दोनों बराबर रखो। Area A दोनों तरफ cancel हो जाता है, और होना ही चाहिए, और बचता है E equals sigma over two epsilon nought।

तो field सच में uniform है। Notice करो इसमें कोई distance variable है ही नहीं -- sheet से एक centimetre खड़े हो या एक kilometre, field वही है। यह सिर्फ इसलिए सच है क्योंकि sheet infinite है, और कोई भी असली sheet ऐसा तभी behave करती है जब तुम उसके size के मुकाबले पास हो।
<whisper> और अब वो trap जिसे यह chapter बाकी सबसे ज्यादा सज़ा देता है। एक thin charged sheet की तुलना एक charged conductor की surface से करो।

Thin non-conducting sheet दोनों तरफ field फेंकती है, तो pillbox के दो active caps हैं और मिलता है sigma over two epsilon nought। लेकिन conductor की surface पर, charge के पीछे धातु है और field सिर्फ एक तरफ मौजूद है -- pillbox का सिर्फ एक active cap है। इससे मिलता है sigma over epsilon nought, दोगुना बड़ा। एक भी line लिखने से पहले tag करो कि problem किस situation की बात कर रही है।

sections.title: Derivation: Field of a Thin Spherical Shell

board_events.text: Derivation: Field of a Thin Spherical Shell
A thin shell of radius $R$ carries total charge $Q$ spread uniformly over its surface. By spherical symmetry, $\vec{E}$ is radial and constant in magnitude over any concentric sphere.

board_events.text: Outside, take a Gaussian sphere of radius $r$ greater than $R$. It encloses the full charge $Q$.
So from outside, the shell behaves exactly like a point charge $Q$ sitting at its centre. At the surface itself, $E = kQ/R^2$.
Inside, take a Gaussian sphere of radius $r$ less than $R$. It lies entirely within the shell, so it encloses no charge at all.
The field is exactly zero everywhere inside a charged shell -- a deep result, and one of the most frequently tested in the chapter. It jumps abruptly to $kQ/R^2$ as you cross the surface.

segments.text: Third and final derivation, and this one produces a result that surprises most students the first time they meet it.

A thin shell of radius R carries total charge Q spread uniformly over its surface -- nothing in the interior, all of it on the skin. By spherical symmetry, the field must be radial and must have constant magnitude over any sphere concentric with the shell.
That symmetry tells us to use spherical Gaussian surfaces. And this time we need two of them, because there are two genuinely different regions: outside the shell and inside it.
Start outside. Take a Gaussian sphere of radius r larger than R, shown dashed in the figure. It sits entirely outside the shell, so it encloses the full charge Q.

The flux is E times four pi r squared, since the field is perpendicular to the sphere and constant over it. Set that equal to Q over epsilon nought, and rearranging gives E equals one over four pi epsilon nought times Q over r squared.

<excited> Look at what that is. It is exactly the field of a point charge Q sitting at the centre. From outside, a uniformly charged shell is completely indistinguishable from a point charge at its middle. All that spread-out charge behaves as though it were concentrated at one spot. And right at the surface, putting r equals R gives k Q over R squared.

Now go inside. Take a Gaussian sphere of radius r smaller than R. This sphere lies entirely within the hollow interior of the shell. And here is the key observation: all the charge sits on the shell at radius R, which is outside our Gaussian surface. So this surface encloses no charge whatsoever.
Gauss's law then gives E times four pi r squared equals zero over epsilon nought. Since the area is certainly not zero, the field itself must be zero.

<whisper> And that is a genuinely deep result, tested more often than almost anything else in this chapter. The field is exactly zero everywhere inside a charged shell -- not small, not approximately zero, but precisely zero at every interior point. Then as you cross the surface it jumps abruptly to k Q over R squared. Nothing gradual about it.
तीसरी और आखिरी derivation, और यह वो result देती है जो ज़्यादातर students को पहली बार हैरान कर देता है।

R radius का एक thin shell total charge Q रखता है जो उसकी surface पर uniformly फैला है -- अंदर कुछ नहीं, सब कुछ खाल पर। Spherical symmetry से, field radial होना चाहिए और shell के साथ concentric किसी भी sphere पर constant magnitude रखनी चाहिए।
वो symmetry हमें spherical Gaussian surfaces इस्तेमाल करने को कहती है। और इस बार हमें दो चाहिए, क्योंकि दो genuinely अलग regions हैं: shell के बाहर और अंदर।
बाहर से शुरू करो। R से बड़ी radius r का एक Gaussian sphere लो, figure में dashed दिखाया गया। वो पूरी तरह shell के बाहर बैठा है, तो वो पूरा charge Q enclose करता है।

Flux है E times four pi r squared, क्योंकि field sphere के perpendicular है और उस पर constant है। उसे Q over epsilon nought के बराबर रखो, और rearrange करने पर मिलता है E equals one over four pi epsilon nought times Q over r squared।

<excited> देखो यह क्या है। यह exactly centre पर बैठे point charge Q का field है। बाहर से, uniformly charged shell एक point charge से पूरी तरह अलग नहीं किया जा सकता। वो सारा फैला हुआ charge ऐसे behave करता है जैसे एक ही जगह इकट्ठा हो। और ठीक surface पर, r equals R रखने से मिलता है k Q over R squared।

अब अंदर जाओ। R से छोटी radius r का Gaussian sphere लो। यह sphere पूरी तरह shell के खोखले अंदरूनी हिस्से में है। और यह रही key observation: सारा charge R radius पर shell पर बैठा है, जो हमारी Gaussian surface के बाहर है। तो यह surface कोई charge enclose करता ही नहीं।
Gauss's law तब देता है E times four pi r squared equals zero over epsilon nought। चूँकि area निश्चित रूप से zero नहीं है, field खुद zero होना ही चाहिए।

<whisper> और यह एक genuinely deep result है, जो इस chapter की लगभग बाकी हर चीज़ से ज्यादा test होता है। Charged shell के अंदर हर जगह field exactly zero है -- छोटा नहीं, लगभग zero नहीं, बल्कि हर अंदरूनी point पर बिलकुल zero। फिर surface पार करते ही वो अचानक उछलकर k Q over R squared हो जाता है। इसमें कुछ भी gradual नहीं है।

sections.title: When Gauss's Law Actually Helps

board_events.text: When Gauss's Law Actually Helps
Gauss's law is always true, for any closed surface whatsoever. But it is only useful for finding $\vec{E}$ under one condition.
You need enough symmetry -- spherical, cylindrical, or planar -- to pull $E$ outside the integral. Without that, you cannot solve for it.
Match the surface to the symmetry: a sphere for spherical, a cylinder for linear, a pillbox for planar. On a random surface $E$ varies across it and refuses to come out.
Second subtlety: the $\vec{E}$ inside the flux integral is the TOTAL field from all charges, inside and outside. Only the net flux depends solely on the enclosed charge.
So an outside charge genuinely does change the field at points on your surface. It just contributes zero to the net flux, because its lines enter and leave again.
Third: the Gaussian surface is imaginary. Choose it freely, wherever you like -- it is a bookkeeping device, not a physical object.
But never let it pass through a point charge, where the field is undefined. It may pass through a continuous distribution without trouble.
This is precisely the gap we flagged at the end of the last subtopic. Where symmetry exists, Gauss replaces a brutal integral with two or three lines.

segments.text: Before we start solving problems, we need to be precise about when this law actually earns its keep -- because there is a gap between being true and being useful.

Gauss's law is always true. For any closed surface whatsoever, however absurd its shape, the net flux equals the enclosed charge over epsilon nought. No exceptions. But being always true does not make it always useful for finding the field.

To actually solve for E, you need enough symmetry -- spherical, cylindrical, or planar -- to pull E outside the integral. That is the step we used in all three derivations. Without that symmetry, E stays trapped inside the integral and you cannot isolate it. The law still holds; it just will not tell you the field.

Which is why the choice of surface is not free in practice. Match the surface to the symmetry: a sphere for spherical symmetry, a cylinder for a line, a pillbox for a plane. Pick some random surface instead, and E varies from point to point across it, refuses to come out as a constant, and the whole method stalls.

<curious> Second subtlety, and this one causes real confusion. The E sitting inside that flux integral is the total field from all charges -- the ones inside your surface and the ones outside it too. It is not somehow only the field of the enclosed charge.

So think carefully about what that means. An outside charge genuinely does change the field at points on your surface. Move a charge nearby and the field at every point on your balloon really is different. What stays unchanged is the net flux, because that outside charge's lines enter through one part of the surface and leave through another, cancelling exactly. Field changes; net flux does not.

Third point: the Gaussian surface is imaginary. It is a bookkeeping device we draw in space, not a physical object. Nothing is really there. So you may place it wherever it is convenient, and you should choose it purely to make the mathematics easy.

With one restriction: never let it pass through a point charge, because the field is undefined at that location and the integral becomes meaningless. It may pass through a continuous charge distribution without any trouble at all, since there is no singularity there.

And notice that this is exactly the gap we flagged at the end of the last subtopic. We said that without symmetry, the Coulomb integral becomes brutal. Gauss's law does not remove that limitation -- it also needs symmetry. But where the symmetry does exist, it replaces a brutal integral with two or three lines of work. That is the trade, and it is a very good one.
Problems हल करना शुरू करने से पहले, हमें साफ होना पड़ेगा कि यह law actually कब अपनी कीमत वसूल करता है -- क्योंकि सच होने और काम का होने के बीच फर्क है।

Gauss's law हमेशा सच है। किसी भी closed surface के लिए, चाहे उसका shape कितना भी बेतुका हो, net flux बराबर है enclosed charge over epsilon nought। कोई अपवाद नहीं। लेकिन हमेशा सच होना उसे field निकालने के लिए हमेशा useful नहीं बना देता।

E के लिए actually हल करने को, तुम्हें पर्याप्त symmetry चाहिए -- spherical, cylindrical, या planar -- ताकि E को integral से बाहर खींचा जा सके। यही वो step है जो हमने तीनों derivations में इस्तेमाल किया। उस symmetry के बिना, E integral के अंदर फँसा रहता है और तुम उसे अलग नहीं कर सकते। Law फिर भी चलता है; वो बस तुम्हें field नहीं बताएगा।

इसीलिए practice में surface का choice आज़ाद नहीं है। Surface को symmetry से match करो: spherical symmetry के लिए sphere, line के लिए cylinder, plane के लिए pillbox। इसके बजाय कोई random surface चुनो, और E उस पर point-to-point बदलता रहता है, constant बनकर बाहर आने से मना कर देता है, और पूरा method अटक जाता है।

<curious> दूसरी subtlety, और यह असली confusion पैदा करती है। उस flux integral के अंदर बैठा E सारे charges का total field है -- वो भी जो तुम्हारी surface के अंदर हैं और वो भी जो बाहर। यह किसी तरह सिर्फ enclosed charge का field नहीं है।

तो ध्यान से सोचो इसका मतलब क्या है। बाहर का charge genuinely तुम्हारी surface के points पर field बदल देता है। पास में कोई charge हिलाओ और तुम्हारे गुब्बारे के हर point पर field सच में अलग हो जाता है। जो नहीं बदलता वो है net flux, क्योंकि उस बाहरी charge की lines surface के एक हिस्से से अंदर आती हैं और दूसरे से बाहर निकल जाती हैं, exactly cancel होती हुई। Field बदलता है; net flux नहीं।

तीसरी बात: Gaussian surface काल्पनिक है। यह एक bookkeeping device है जिसे हम space में खींचते हैं, कोई physical object नहीं। वहाँ सच में कुछ है ही नहीं। तो तुम उसे जहाँ सुविधाजनक हो वहाँ रख सकते हो, और उसे purely इसलिए चुनना चाहिए ताकि गणित आसान हो जाए।

एक पाबंदी के साथ: उसे कभी किसी point charge के आर-पार मत जाने दो, क्योंकि वहाँ field undefined है और integral बेमानी हो जाता है। वो continuous charge distribution के आर-पार बिना किसी परेशानी के गुज़र सकती है, क्योंकि वहाँ कोई singularity नहीं है।

और notice करो कि यह exactly वही gap है जो हमने पिछले subtopic के अंत में flag किया था। हमने कहा था कि symmetry के बिना Coulomb integral brutal हो जाता है। Gauss's law उस limitation को हटाता नहीं -- उसे भी symmetry चाहिए। लेकिन जहाँ symmetry मौजूद है, वो एक brutal integral की जगह दो-तीन line का काम रख देता है। यही सौदा है, और यह बहुत अच्छा सौदा है।

sections.title: Flux and Gauss's Law: Formulas and Standard Results

board_events.text: Flux and Gauss's Law -- Formulas and Standard Results
SI unit of flux: newton metre squared per coulomb, equivalently volt metre. Dimensional formula $[ML^{3}T^{-3}A^{-1}]$.
Here $Q_{\text{enc}}$ is the net charge enclosed -- an algebraic sum, so signs matter.
Point charge in a cube: total flux $q/\varepsilon_0$; through one face $q/6\varepsilon_0$; at a corner $q/8\varepsilon_0$.

segments.text: Let's collect the formulas for this subtopic, including the standard results that come up again and again.
First, flux itself. For a flat surface in a uniform field, it is E dot A, which is E A cos theta. In general, it is the surface integral of E dotted with d A.

Its SI unit is newton metre squared per coulomb, which you will also see written as volt metre. The dimensional formula is M L cubed T to the minus three, A to the minus one. Derive it if you forget: field times area.
Then Gauss's law itself, with the circle on the integral marking a closed surface: the net flux equals the enclosed charge over epsilon nought.
And note carefully that Q enclosed is a net, algebraic sum. If a surface contains plus five and minus three microcoulomb, the enclosed charge is plus two, not eight.
Now the three standard applications. An infinite line charge gives lambda over two pi epsilon nought r, directed radially, falling as one over r.

An infinite sheet gives sigma over two epsilon nought, uniform and independent of distance. And beside it, the one that gets confused with it: a conductor's surface gives sigma over epsilon nought, twice as large.
A thin spherical shell gives the point-charge field k Q over r squared outside, and exactly zero inside.

And worth adding alongside it, because they are constantly confused: inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, the field is rho r over three epsilon nought, which is k Q r over R cubed. That grows linearly with r, rather than being zero. Shell is zero inside; solid sphere is linear inside.

<whisper> One last set worth memorising outright, because it turns a whole question into one line. A point charge at the centre of a cube gives total flux q over epsilon nought, and by symmetry q over six epsilon nought through each face. And if the charge sits at a corner of the cube instead, it is shared by eight cubes, so the flux through this one is q over eight epsilon nought.
चलिए इस subtopic के formulas इकट्ठा करते हैं, उन standard results समेत जो बार-बार आते हैं।
पहले flux खुद। Uniform field में flat surface के लिए, यह है E dot A, यानी E A cos theta। General रूप में, यह E dotted with d A का surface integral है।
इसकी SI unit है newton metre squared per coulomb, जिसे volt metre भी लिखा देखोगे। Dimensional formula है M L cubed T to the minus three, A to the minus one। भूल जाओ तो derive कर लो: field times area।
फिर Gauss's law खुद, integral पर बना circle closed surface दिखाता हुआ: net flux बराबर है enclosed charge over epsilon nought।
और ध्यान से notice करो कि Q enclosed एक net, algebraic sum है। अगर surface में plus five और minus three microcoulomb हैं, तो enclosed charge plus two है, आठ नहीं।
अब तीन standard applications। Infinite line charge देता है lambda over two pi epsilon nought r, radially directed, one over r के हिसाब से गिरता हुआ।

Infinite sheet देता है sigma over two epsilon nought, uniform और distance से independent। और उसके बगल में, वो जिससे यह confuse होता है: conductor की surface देती है sigma over epsilon nought, दोगुना बड़ा।
Thin spherical shell बाहर point-charge field k Q over r squared देता है, और अंदर exactly zero।

और साथ में जोड़ने लायक, क्योंकि ये लगातार confuse होते हैं: uniformly charged solid sphere के अंदर, field है rho r over three epsilon nought, यानी k Q r over R cubed। वो r के साथ linearly बढ़ता है, zero होने के बजाय। Shell अंदर zero; solid sphere अंदर linear।

<whisper> एक आखिरी set सीधा रट लेने लायक है, क्योंकि यह पूरे question को एक line बना देता है। Cube के centre पर point charge total flux q over epsilon nought देता है, और symmetry से हर face से q over six epsilon nought। और अगर charge cube के corner पर हो, तो वो आठ cubes में बँटता है, तो इस एक से flux है q over eight epsilon nought।

A point charge $q = +6\ \mu\text{C}$ sits at the centre of a cube of side ten centimetres. Find the total flux through the cube, and the flux through one face.

board_events.text: Notice the side length never entered the calculation. Flux is size-independent -- the ten centimetres was a distractor.
Example 2 -- NEET Speed Trap
A charge $+Q$ sits inside a closed surface; the flux is $\Phi_0$. Then the surface is enlarged to twice its size, and separately a charge $+3Q$ is brought just outside. What is the flux in each case?
The trap: students instinctively think a bigger surface or a nearby external charge must change the flux. Neither does.
Enlarging the surface does not change what is enclosed -- still $+Q$. And the $+3Q$ is outside, so $Q_{\text{enc}}$ is still $+Q$. The flux is $\Phi_0$ in both cases.

segments.text: Two examples now, and both are really testing the same insight: that flux only ever asks one question.

First, a board favourite. A point charge of plus six microcoulomb sits at the centre of a cube of side ten centimetres. Part a: find the total flux through the cube. Part b: find the flux through one face.
Picture the setup -- the charge at the dead centre, and six identical faces surrounding it.

Part a needs no field calculation at all. By Gauss's law the total flux depends only on the enclosed charge, whatever the shape. So it is q over epsilon nought: six times ten to the minus six, divided by eight point eight five four times ten to the minus twelve. That gives six point seven eight times ten to the power five newton metre squared per coulomb.

Part b uses symmetry. Because the charge sits at the exact centre, the six faces are completely equivalent -- there is no reason for any face to receive more than another. So each gets one sixth of the total, which is one point one three times ten to the power five.

<curious> Now notice something about that solution. The side length, ten centimetres, never entered the calculation anywhere. It was a distractor. Flux through a closed surface is size-independent, and a cube of side one metre with the same charge inside would give exactly the same answer.
That point is exactly what the next example attacks head-on.

A charge plus Q sits inside a closed surface, and the flux through it is Phi nought. Now two separate changes. First, the surface is enlarged to twice its size. Second, and independently, a charge of plus three Q is brought to a point just outside the surface. What is the flux in each case?

<whisper> Here is the trap, and it works because both changes feel like they should matter. A bigger surface -- surely more flux? A big charge sitting right there -- surely that does something? Neither does. Flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge over epsilon nought, full stop.

Take them in turn. Enlarging the surface does not change what is enclosed -- the charge plus Q is still the only thing inside, so the flux is unchanged at Phi nought. And the plus three Q is outside the surface, so Q enclosed is still just plus Q. Its field lines enter one part of the surface and leave through another, contributing exactly zero net flux. So again the answer is Phi nought. The shortcut for every question of this type is a single question: what is inside?
अब दो examples, और दोनों असल में एक ही insight test कर रहे हैं: कि flux हमेशा सिर्फ एक सवाल पूछता है।
पहला, एक board favourite। Plus six microcoulomb का point charge दस centimetre भुजा वाले cube के centre पर बैठा है। Part a: cube से total flux निकालो। Part b: एक face से flux निकालो।
Setup की कल्पना करो -- charge बिलकुल बीच में, और उसके चारों तरफ छह एक जैसे faces।

Part a को किसी field calculation की ज़रूरत ही नहीं। Gauss's law से total flux सिर्फ enclosed charge पर depend करता है, shape चाहे जो हो। तो यह है q over epsilon nought: six times ten to the minus six, divided by eight point eight five four times ten to the minus twelve। इससे मिलता है six point seven eight times ten to the power five newton metre squared per coulomb।

Part b symmetry इस्तेमाल करता है। क्योंकि charge exact centre पर बैठा है, छहों faces पूरी तरह बराबर हैं -- किसी एक face को दूसरे से ज्यादा मिलने की कोई वजह नहीं। तो हर एक को total का छठा हिस्सा मिलता है, यानी one point one three times ten to the power five।

<curious> अब उस solution के बारे में एक बात notice करो। भुजा की लंबाई, दस centimetre, कहीं भी calculation में आई ही नहीं। वो एक distractor था। Closed surface से flux size-independent है, और एक metre भुजा वाला cube उसी charge के साथ exactly वही जवाब देता।
और अगला example ठीक उसी बात पर सीधा हमला करता है।

Plus Q charge एक closed surface के अंदर बैठा है, और उससे flux है Phi nought। अब दो अलग बदलाव। पहला, surface को दोगुना बड़ा कर दिया जाता है। दूसरा, और अलग से, plus three Q का charge surface के ठीक बाहर एक point पर लाया जाता है। हर case में flux क्या है?

<whisper> यह रहा trap, और यह इसलिए काम करता है क्योंकि दोनों बदलाव ऐसे लगते हैं जैसे उन्हें matter करना चाहिए। बड़ी surface -- तो ज्यादा flux होगा न? इतना बड़ा charge ठीक बगल में -- वो कुछ तो करेगा? दोनों कुछ नहीं करते। Closed surface से flux बराबर है enclosed charge over epsilon nought, बस।

एक-एक करके लो। Surface बड़ी करने से अंदर क्या है वो नहीं बदलता -- charge plus Q अभी भी अंदर की इकलौती चीज़ है, तो flux unchanged है, Phi nought। और plus three Q surface के बाहर है, तो Q enclosed अभी भी सिर्फ plus Q है। उसकी field lines surface के एक हिस्से से अंदर आती हैं और दूसरे से बाहर निकल जाती हैं, exactly zero net flux देती हुईं। तो जवाब फिर Phi nought है। इस तरह के हर question का shortcut एक ही सवाल है: अंदर क्या है?

board_events.text: Each sheet alone produces a uniform field $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, pointing away from the positive sheet and towards the negative one. Then use superposition.
Between the sheets, the positive sheet pushes the field to the right, and the negative sheet pulls it to the right as well -- so they add.
Outside, in either region, the two contributions point in opposite directions and cancel exactly.
This is the ideal parallel-plate capacitor field -- uniform and confined between the plates, zero outside. It drops straight out of Gauss plus superposition.

segments.text: Now a JEE Main problem that combines a Gauss result with superposition -- and produces one of the most important field configurations in all of physics.
Two large parallel sheets carry uniform surface densities plus sigma and minus sigma. Find the field in the region between the sheets, and in the regions outside them.
Look at the arrangement. The positive sheet on the left, the negative sheet on the right, and three distinct regions to consider: left of both, between them, and right of both.

The key move is to treat each sheet separately and then superpose. We derived the single-sheet result a moment ago: each sheet alone produces a uniform field of sigma over two epsilon nought. And the directions: away from the positive sheet, and towards the negative one, since that is where field lines start and end.

Now work region by region. Between the sheets, think about which way each contribution points. The positive sheet on the left pushes its field away from itself, so to the right. The negative sheet on the right pulls its field towards itself, which is also to the right. Both point the same way.

<excited> So between the plates they reinforce. Sigma over two epsilon nought plus sigma over two epsilon nought gives sigma over epsilon nought, directed from the positive sheet towards the negative one. The factor of two doubles the field.

Now outside, and take the region to the right of both sheets. The positive sheet, being to your left, pushes its field further right. The negative sheet, also to your left now, pulls its field back towards itself, so to the left. The two point in opposite directions.

And since both have exactly the same magnitude, sigma over two epsilon nought, they cancel completely. The field outside is exactly zero. The same argument works in the region to the left of both sheets.

Now step back and appreciate what we have just built. A uniform field, confined entirely between the plates, and exactly zero everywhere outside. That is the ideal parallel-plate capacitor, the device at the heart of the next chapter. And it dropped straight out of Gauss's law plus superposition, with no integration at all.
अब एक JEE Main problem जो Gauss के एक result को superposition से जोड़ती है -- और पूरी physics के सबसे important field configurations में से एक बनाती है।
दो बड़ी parallel sheets uniform surface densities plus sigma और minus sigma रखती हैं। Sheets के बीच के region में, और उनके बाहर के regions में field निकालो।
Arrangement देखो। बाईं तरफ positive sheet, दाईं तरफ negative sheet, और सोचने के लिए तीन अलग regions: दोनों के बाईं तरफ, उनके बीच, और दोनों के दाईं तरफ।

Key move है हर sheet को अलग मानकर फिर superpose करना। Single-sheet का result हमने अभी थोड़ी देर पहले derive किया: हर sheet अकेले sigma over two epsilon nought का uniform field बनाती है। और directions: positive sheet से दूर, और negative sheet की तरफ, क्योंकि field lines वहीं शुरू और खत्म होती हैं।

अब region दर region काम करो। Sheets के बीच, सोचो हर contribution किस तरफ point करता है। बाईं तरफ की positive sheet अपना field खुद से दूर धकेलती है, यानी दाईं तरफ। दाईं तरफ की negative sheet अपना field अपनी तरफ खींचती है, जो भी दाईं तरफ ही है। दोनों एक ही तरफ point करते हैं।

<excited> तो plates के बीच वो एक दूसरे को मज़बूत करते हैं। Sigma over two epsilon nought plus sigma over two epsilon nought देता है sigma over epsilon nought, positive sheet से negative sheet की तरफ। दो का factor field को दोगुना कर देता है।

अब बाहर, और दोनों sheets के दाईं तरफ वाला region लो। Positive sheet, जो अब तुम्हारी बाईं तरफ है, अपना field और दाईं तरफ धकेलती है। Negative sheet, जो अब भी तुम्हारी बाईं तरफ है, अपना field अपनी तरफ वापस खींचती है, यानी बाईं तरफ। दोनों opposite directions में point करते हैं।

और चूँकि दोनों की exactly same magnitude है, sigma over two epsilon nought, वो पूरी तरह cancel हो जाते हैं। बाहर field exactly zero है। वही argument दोनों sheets के बाईं तरफ वाले region में भी चलता है।

अब पीछे हटकर देखो कि हमने अभी क्या बनाया। एक uniform field, पूरी तरह plates के बीच सीमित, और बाहर हर जगह exactly zero। यही है ideal parallel-plate capacitor, अगले chapter के दिल में बैठा device। और यह सीधा Gauss's law plus superposition से निकल आया, बिना किसी integration के।

sections.title: Worked Example: Sphere With Non-Uniform Volume Density

board_events.text: Example 4 -- JEE Advanced Level
A solid sphere of radius $R$ carries a volume charge density that varies as $\rho(r) = \rho_0(1 - r/R)$ for $r \leq R$. Find the field inside and outside, then verify the two agree at $r = R$.
The density is non-uniform, so we cannot just write charge equals density times volume. We must integrate over spherical shells of thickness $dr'$, each of volume $4\pi r'^2 dr'$.
For an exterior point, the same integral now runs over the whole sphere, giving the total charge.

board_events.latex: Q = 4\pi\rho_0\left(\frac{R^3}{3} - \frac{R^3}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi\rho_0 R^3}{3} \;\Rightarrow\; E = \frac{\rho_0 R^3}{12\,\varepsilon_0 r^2} \quad (r \gt R)

board_events.text: Now verify at the boundary. Interior at $r = R$ gives $\rho_0 R/12\varepsilon_0$. Exterior at $r = R$ gives the same.
They match -- the field is continuous across the surface, which confirms both results. A boundary check like this catches almost any algebra slip.

segments.text: This is the JEE Advanced version, and it removes the one crutch every previous Gauss problem gave us: uniform density.

A solid sphere of radius R carries a volume charge density that varies with position, as rho nought times one minus r over R, for r less than or equal to R. So the density is highest at the centre and falls linearly to zero at the surface. Find the field at an interior point and at an exterior point, then verify the two expressions agree at r equals R.

<curious> Here is what changes. In every previous problem, the enclosed charge was just density times volume, because the density was constant. Now it is not. So we have to integrate, and the natural way is to build the sphere out of thin spherical shells of radius r dash and thickness d r dash, each with volume four pi r dash squared d r dash.

So the enclosed charge within radius r is the integral of rho times that shell volume, from zero out to r. Expanding the bracket gives two simple power terms, and integrating each gives four pi rho nought times r cubed over three, minus r to the fourth over four R.

Now apply Gauss's law over a sphere of radius r. Spherical symmetry still holds -- the density varies with radius, but not with direction -- so E times four pi r squared equals Q enclosed over epsilon nought. Divide through, and the r squared cancels neatly against the powers in Q, leaving E equals rho nought over epsilon nought, times r over three minus r squared over four R.
For an exterior point, the logic is the same but the integral now runs over the entire sphere, from zero all the way to R, because everything is enclosed.

That gives total charge four pi rho nought times R cubed over three minus R cubed over four. The bracket is R cubed times one twelfth, so the total is pi rho nought R cubed over three. Feed that into Gauss's law and the exterior field is rho nought R cubed over twelve epsilon nought r squared -- which falls as one over r squared, exactly as any point charge would.

Now the verification, and this is the part that earns the last marks. Put r equals R into the interior expression: rho nought over epsilon nought, times R over three minus R over four. That bracket is R over twelve, so we get rho nought R over twelve epsilon nought. Now put r equals R into the exterior expression: rho nought R cubed over twelve epsilon nought R squared, which is also rho nought R over twelve epsilon nought.

<excited> They match exactly. The field is continuous as you cross the surface, which is precisely what physics demands for a volume distribution -- there is no surface layer of charge to make it jump. That agreement confirms both results at once, and a boundary check like this will catch almost any algebra slip you might have made along the way.
यह JEE Advanced वाला version है, और यह वो एक सहारा छीन लेता है जो हर पिछली Gauss problem ने दिया था: uniform density।

R radius का एक solid sphere ऐसी volume charge density रखता है जो position के साथ बदलती है, rho nought times one minus r over R, r के R से कम या बराबर होने पर। तो density centre पर सबसे ज्यादा है और surface पर linearly घटकर zero हो जाती है। एक interior point और एक exterior point पर field निकालो, फिर verify करो कि दोनों expressions r equals R पर agree करते हैं।

<curious> यह रहा जो बदलता है। हर पिछली problem में, enclosed charge बस density times volume था, क्योंकि density constant थी। अब नहीं है। तो हमें integrate करना पड़ेगा, और natural तरीका है sphere को r dash radius और d r dash मोटाई वाले thin spherical shells से बनाना, हर एक का volume four pi r dash squared d r dash।

तो radius r के अंदर enclosed charge है rho times उस shell volume का integral, zero से r तक। Bracket expand करने पर दो simple power terms मिलते हैं, और हर एक को integrate करने पर मिलता है four pi rho nought times r cubed over three, minus r to the fourth over four R।

अब r radius के sphere पर Gauss's law लगाओ। Spherical symmetry अभी भी चलती है -- density radius के साथ बदलती है, direction के साथ नहीं -- तो E times four pi r squared बराबर है Q enclosed over epsilon nought। Divide करो, और r squared, Q की powers से साफ-सुथरा cancel हो जाता है, बचता है E equals rho nought over epsilon nought, times r over three minus r squared over four R।
Exterior point के लिए, logic वही है लेकिन integral अब पूरे sphere पर चलता है, zero से लेकर R तक, क्योंकि सब कुछ enclosed है।

इससे मिलता है total charge four pi rho nought times R cubed over three minus R cubed over four। Bracket है R cubed times एक बटा बारह, तो total है pi rho nought R cubed over three। इसे Gauss's law में डालो और exterior field है rho nought R cubed over twelve epsilon nought r squared -- जो one over r squared के हिसाब से गिरता है, exactly जैसे कोई point charge करता।

अब verification, और यही वो हिस्सा है जो आखिरी marks कमाता है। Interior expression में r equals R रखो: rho nought over epsilon nought, times R over three minus R over four। वो bracket है R over twelve, तो मिलता है rho nought R over twelve epsilon nought। अब exterior expression में r equals R रखो: rho nought R cubed over twelve epsilon nought R squared, जो भी है rho nought R over twelve epsilon nought।

<excited> दोनों exactly match करते हैं। Surface पार करते वक्त field continuous है, जो volume distribution के लिए physics की माँग है -- वहाँ charge की कोई surface layer नहीं है जो उसे उछाल दे। वो agreement एक साथ दोनों results confirm कर देता है, और ऐसा boundary check तुम्हारी लगभग हर algebra की चूक पकड़ लेगा।

sections.title: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Flux and Gauss's Law

board_events.text: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips for Flux and Gauss's Law
Pitfall: confusing field on the surface with flux through it. The $\vec{E}$ in the integral is the total field from all charges. But the NET flux depends only on the enclosed charge.
So external charges do affect the field at points on your surface -- they just contribute zero net flux. Students routinely collapse those two statements into one wrong one.

Pitfall: the $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ versus $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ trap. A thin charged sheet gives $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, with field on both sides. A conductor's surface gives $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, with field on one side only.
Pitfall: choosing a poor Gaussian surface. Gauss only helps when the surface matches the symmetry -- sphere for spherical, cylinder for linear, pillbox for planar.
Pitfall: merging shell with solid sphere. Inside a shell, $E = 0$. Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, $E = \rho r/3\varepsilon_0$, growing with $r$. Keep them apart.
Pro-tip: identify the symmetry first, then draw the matching surface, then split the flux into faces where $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular and faces where it lies flat. Half the marks are in that split.
And for any 'flux through a closed surface' question, never compute the field at all. Just read off the enclosed charge over epsilon nought.

segments.text: Let's close this subtopic with the four errors that cost the most marks, and the routine that prevents nearly all of them.

First pitfall, and the most conceptual: confusing the field on a surface with the flux through it. The E sitting inside that integral is the total field from every charge in the universe, inside and outside. But the net flux depends only on the charge enclosed.

Both statements are true simultaneously, and students routinely collapse them into a single wrong one. External charges genuinely do change the field at points on your surface. They simply contribute zero to the net flux, because their lines enter and leave again. Hold both ideas at once and this whole family of questions becomes easy.

Second pitfall, and the most punished in the whole chapter: the sigma over two epsilon nought versus sigma over epsilon nought trap. A thin charged sheet gives sigma over two epsilon nought, because the field exists on both sides and the pillbox has two active caps. A conductor's surface gives sigma over epsilon nought, because the field exists on one side only. Tag which one the problem describes before writing anything down.

Third pitfall: choosing a poor Gaussian surface. The law is always true, but it only helps you find the field when the surface matches the symmetry. Sphere for spherical, cylinder for linear, pillbox for planar. On a randomly chosen surface, E varies from point to point and simply will not come out of the integral.

Fourth pitfall: merging the shell with the solid sphere. Inside a shell, the field is exactly zero. Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, the field is rho r over three epsilon nought, which grows linearly with r. These two results live very close together in memory and one tends to overwrite the other under pressure.

<curious> Now the routine, and I want you to follow it in this exact order for every Gauss problem. First, identify the symmetry -- spherical, cylindrical, or planar. Second, draw the Gaussian surface that matches it. Third, split the flux into faces where the field is perpendicular to the surface, which contribute E times area, and faces where it lies flat along the surface, which contribute nothing. Half the marks in a board derivation are in that split, so write it out explicitly rather than doing it in your head.

And one final shortcut worth internalising. For any question asking for the flux through a closed surface, do not compute the field at all. Do not even start. Just ask what charge is inside, and divide by epsilon nought. We saw that turn a full problem into one line twice in this part alone.
इस subtopic को बंद करते हैं उन चार errors के साथ जो सबसे ज्यादा marks काटती हैं, और उस routine के साथ जो इनमें से लगभग सब रोक देती है।

पहला pitfall, और सबसे conceptual: surface पर field को उससे गुज़रने वाले flux से confuse करना। उस integral के अंदर बैठा E ब्रह्मांड के हर charge का total field है, अंदर वाले भी और बाहर वाले भी। लेकिन net flux सिर्फ enclosed charge पर depend करता है।

दोनों statements एक साथ सच हैं, और students अक्सर उन्हें एक गलत statement में मिला देते हैं। बाहरी charges genuinely तुम्हारी surface के points पर field बदल देते हैं। वो बस net flux में zero contribute करते हैं, क्योंकि उनकी lines अंदर आकर फिर बाहर निकल जाती हैं। दोनों ideas एक साथ पकड़ो और questions का यह पूरा परिवार आसान हो जाता है।

दूसरा pitfall, और पूरे chapter में सबसे ज्यादा सज़ा देने वाला: sigma over two epsilon nought बनाम sigma over epsilon nought का trap। Thin charged sheet देती है sigma over two epsilon nought, क्योंकि field दोनों तरफ मौजूद है और pillbox के दो active caps हैं। Conductor की surface देती है sigma over epsilon nought, क्योंकि field सिर्फ एक तरफ मौजूद है। कुछ भी लिखने से पहले tag करो कि problem किसकी बात कर रही है।

तीसरा pitfall: खराब Gaussian surface चुनना। Law हमेशा सच है, लेकिन वो field निकालने में तभी मदद करता है जब surface symmetry से match करे। Spherical के लिए sphere, linear के लिए cylinder, planar के लिए pillbox। किसी भी randomly चुनी surface पर, E point-to-point बदलता है और integral से बाहर आएगा ही नहीं।

चौथा pitfall: shell को solid sphere से मिला देना। Shell के अंदर, field exactly zero है। Uniformly charged solid sphere के अंदर, field है rho r over three epsilon nought, जो r के साथ linearly बढ़ता है। ये दोनों results memory में बहुत पास-पास रहते हैं और दबाव में एक दूसरे को overwrite कर देता है।

<curious> अब routine, और मैं चाहता हूँ तुम हर Gauss problem में इसे इसी क्रम में follow करो। पहला, symmetry पहचानो -- spherical, cylindrical, या planar। दूसरा, उससे match करती Gaussian surface बनाओ। तीसरा, flux को उन faces में बाँटो जहाँ field surface के perpendicular है, जो E times area देते हैं, और उन faces में जहाँ वो surface के along सपाट पड़ा है, जो कुछ नहीं देते। Board derivation के आधे marks उसी split में हैं, तो उसे दिमाग में करने के बजाय explicitly लिखो।

और एक आखिरी shortcut आत्मसात करने लायक। किसी भी ऐसे question में जो closed surface से flux पूछे, field बिलकुल मत निकालो। शुरू भी मत करो। बस पूछो अंदर क्या charge है, और epsilon nought से divide कर दो। हमने इसी part में दो बार इसे एक पूरी problem को एक line में बदलते देखा।

sections.title: Complete Formula Toolkit for the Chapter

board_events.text: Complete Formula Toolkit for the Chapter

board_events.latex: \begin{aligned} q &= ne, \quad e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C} \\[2pt] q_1' = q_2' &= \frac{q_1+q_2}{2} \quad \text{(identical conductors touching)} \end{aligned}

\begin{aligned} p &= q\cdot 2a \quad \text{(from } -q \text{ to } +q) \\[2pt] E_{\text{axial}} &= \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2p}{r^3}, \qquad E_{\text{eq}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{r^3}, \qquad E_{\text{axial}} = 2E_{\text{eq}} \end{aligned}
\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau} &= \vec{p}\times\vec{E}, \qquad \tau = pE\sin\theta \\[2pt] U &= -pE\cos\theta, \qquad W = pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2), \qquad F = p\frac{dE}{dr} \end{aligned}

\begin{aligned} E_{\text{ring, axis}} &= \frac{kQx}{(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}} \quad \text{(max at } x = R/\sqrt{2}) \\[2pt] E_{\text{disc, axis}} &= \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+R^2}}\right), \qquad E_{\text{arc, centre}} = \frac{2k\lambda}{R} \end{aligned}

\begin{aligned} E_{\text{line}} &= \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}, \qquad E_{\text{sheet}} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}, \qquad E_{\text{conductor}} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \\[2pt] E_{\text{shell}} &= \frac{kQ}{r^2}\;(r \gt R),\; 0\;(r \lt R), \qquad E_{\text{solid, in}} = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0} \end{aligned}

segments.text: Here is your complete toolkit for the chapter, all in one place. We are not re-teaching any of this -- just laying it out so you can see the whole structure at once.

Charge fundamentals. Quantisation: charge is n times e, with e about one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb. And charge sharing: identical conductors touching each end with the algebraic average of the two charges.

Coulomb's law, in all three forms you need. The magnitude with absolute values. The vector form with signs included, which handles attraction and repulsion in one shot. And the medium correction, force in a medium equals vacuum force divided by K.
The electric field. Its definition as force per unit positive charge, and the same relation run backwards to give force equals q E. The field of a point charge, and superposition for several sources.

The dipole. Moment p equals q times two a, directed from minus to plus. The axial field, twice p over r cubed. The equatorial field, p over r cubed, pointing the opposite way. And the golden ratio between them: axial is twice equatorial.

The dipole in a field. Torque is p cross E, with magnitude p E sine theta. Energy is minus p E cos theta -- mind that minus sign. Work to rotate is p E times the difference of the cosines. And in a non-uniform field only, a net force p times d E by d r.
Continuous distributions. The three densities: lambda per length, sigma per area, rho per volume. And the master integral that chops any object into point-charge elements.

The standard continuous results. The ring on its axis, peaking at R over root two. The disc on its axis, which becomes a sheet up close and a point charge far away. And the semicircular arc at its centre, two k lambda over R -- remembering that a full ring gives zero there.
Flux and Gauss's law. Flux as E dot A, and Gauss's law itself: the closed surface integral equals the enclosed charge over epsilon nought.

And finally the four Gauss applications. Infinite line, falling as one over r. Infinite sheet, uniform. A conductor's surface, twice the sheet value. And the spherical shell, a point charge outside and exactly zero inside -- alongside the solid sphere, which instead grows linearly inside. That is the entire chapter in ten lines.
यह रहा इस chapter का तुम्हारा complete toolkit, सब एक जगह। हम इसमें से कुछ दोबारा नहीं पढ़ा रहे -- बस इसे इस तरह रख रहे हैं कि तुम पूरा ढाँचा एक साथ देख सको।

Charge के fundamentals। Quantisation: charge है n times e, जहाँ e लगभग one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb है। और charge sharing: identical conductors touch करने पर हर एक दोनों charges का algebraic average लेता है।

Coulomb's law, तीनों रूपों में जो तुम्हें चाहिए। Absolute values वाली magnitude। Signs समेत vector form, जो attraction और repulsion एक ही बार में संभाल लेता है। और medium correction, medium में force बराबर vacuum force divided by K।
Electric field। इसकी definition per unit positive charge force के रूप में, और वही relation उल्टा चलाकर force equals q E। Point charge का field, और कई sources के लिए superposition।

Dipole। Moment p equals q times two a, minus से plus की तरफ directed। Axial field, two p over r cubed। Equatorial field, p over r cubed, उल्टी तरफ point करता हुआ। और उनके बीच golden ratio: axial, equatorial का दोगुना।

Field में dipole। Torque है p cross E, magnitude p E sine theta। Energy है minus p E cos theta -- उस minus sign का ध्यान रखो। घुमाने का work है p E times cosines का अंतर। और सिर्फ non-uniform field में, एक net force p times d E by d r।
Continuous distributions। तीन densities: lambda per length, sigma per area, rho per volume। और वो master integral जो किसी भी object को point-charge elements में काट देता है।

Standard continuous results। Ring अपने axis पर, R over root two पर peak करता हुआ। Disc अपने axis पर, जो पास से sheet और दूर से point charge बन जाता है। और semicircular arc अपने centre पर, two k lambda over R -- यह याद रखते हुए कि पूरा ring वहाँ zero देता है।
Flux और Gauss's law। Flux के रूप में E dot A, और खुद Gauss's law: closed surface integral बराबर enclosed charge over epsilon nought।

और आखिर में चार Gauss applications। Infinite line, one over r के हिसाब से गिरती हुई। Infinite sheet, uniform। Conductor की surface, sheet से दोगुनी। और spherical shell, बाहर point charge और अंदर exactly zero -- साथ में solid sphere, जो अंदर उल्टा linearly बढ़ता है। यही पूरा chapter है, दस lines में।

sections.title: Chapter Cheat Sheet: Quick Recall

board_events.text: Chapter Cheat Sheet -- Quick Recall
CHARGE. Two kinds: like repel, unlike attract. Charging is transfer of electrons, never creation. Conductors let charge move freely; insulators do not; earthing drains charge to ground.
Friction gives equal and opposite charges. Conduction gives the same sign and the rod loses charge. Induction gives the opposite sign and the rod keeps its charge.
Memory aids: charge moves, never made. Repulsion is the only sure test of charge. Induction means no touch, opposite charge, rod unharmed. Divide by e and it must be a whole number.

COULOMB. Product up, distance squared down. A medium divides the force by K, but the distance that restores it divides by root K. Central force, inverse-square, obeys Newton's third law. Forces are vectors -- never just add the numbers.

FIELD AND DIPOLE. Field lines start on positive, end on negative, never cross; density shows strength. A dipole dies as $1/r^3$ because opposites cancel. Axial is twice equatorial, and they point opposite ways. Uniform field: only twist, no push. And $p$ points minus to plus.

CONTINUOUS. Chop, cancel, integrate. Full loop gives zero at the centre; half loop gives $2k\lambda/R$. A disc up close is just an infinite sheet, and far away just a point charge. Lambda for length, sigma for surface, rho for volume.
GAUSS. Flux counts what is inside -- shape and outsiders do not matter. Match the surface to the symmetry. The sheet halves it, the conductor does not. Inside a shell nothing; inside a solid, linear.
Point charge in a cube: total $q/\varepsilon_0$, per face $q/6\varepsilon_0$, at a corner $q/8\varepsilon_0$.
That is the whole chapter, compressed to what you can rehearse the night before an exam.

segments.text: And here is the whole chapter compressed into what you can rehearse the night before an exam. Read it as a checklist, not as a lesson.

Charge. There are two kinds: like charges repel, unlike attract. Charging is always the transfer of electrons, never creation. Conductors let charge move freely, insulators do not, and earthing drains charge away to ground.

The three charging methods, each with its own signature. Friction leaves two bodies equally and oppositely charged. Conduction leaves the same sign on both, and the charging rod loses some charge. Induction leaves the opposite sign, and the rod keeps everything it had.

Four memory aids for this section. Charge moves, never made. Repulsion is the only sure test of charge. Induction means no touch, opposite charge, rod unharmed. And divide by e -- it must come out a whole number.

Coulomb. Product up, distance squared down. A medium divides the force by K, but the distance that restores the force divides by root K -- two different factors for two different questions. The force is central, inverse-square, and obeys Newton's third law exactly. And the line to repeat to yourself in every multi-charge problem: forces are vectors, never just add the numbers.

Field and dipole. Field lines start on positive, end on negative, never cross, and their density shows the field strength. A dipole's field dies as one over r cubed, because the opposite charges nearly cancel. Axial is twice equatorial, and the two point opposite ways. In a uniform field a dipole gets only a twist, never a push. And p points minus to plus.

Continuous distributions. Chop, cancel, integrate. A full loop gives zero at its centre; a half loop gives two k lambda over R. A disc up close is just an infinite sheet, and far away just a point charge. And match the density to the geometry: lambda for length, sigma for surface, rho for volume.

Gauss. Flux counts what is inside -- the shape of the surface and any outside charges do not matter. Match the Gaussian surface to the symmetry. The sheet halves it, the conductor does not. And inside a shell there is nothing, while inside a solid sphere the field is linear.

One numerical set worth carrying in verbatim: a point charge at the centre of a cube gives total flux q over epsilon nought, q over six epsilon nought through each face, and q over eight epsilon nought if the charge sits at a corner instead.

<excited> That is Electric Charges and Fields, complete. You have gone from rubbing a comb on your hair to one of the four Maxwell equations, and every result in between was built, not asserted. Go and use it.
और यह रहा पूरा chapter, उसमें सिमटा हुआ जिसे तुम exam से एक रात पहले दोहरा सको। इसे checklist की तरह पढ़ो, lesson की तरह नहीं।

Charge। दो तरह के होते हैं: like charges repel करते हैं, unlike attract। Charging हमेशा electrons का transfer है, कभी creation नहीं। Conductors charge को freely चलने देते हैं, insulators नहीं, और earthing charge को ground में बहा देती है।

तीन charging methods, हर एक अपने signature के साथ। Friction दो bodies को equally और oppositely charged छोड़ती है। Conduction दोनों पर same sign छोड़ती है, और charging rod कुछ charge खो देता है। Induction opposite sign छोड़ती है, और rod अपना सब कुछ रखे रहता है।

इस हिस्से के लिए चार memory aids। Charge चलता है, बनता नहीं। Repulsion ही charge का इकलौता पक्का test है। Induction मतलब कोई touch नहीं, opposite charge, rod सही-सलामत। और e से divide करो -- जवाब whole number आना ही चाहिए।

Coulomb। Product ऊपर, distance squared नीचे। Medium force को K से divide करता है, लेकिन force वापस लाने वाली distance root K से divide होती है -- दो अलग सवालों के लिए दो अलग factors। Force central है, inverse-square है, और Newton's third law को exactly obey करता है। और हर multi-charge problem में खुद से दोहराने वाली line: forces vectors हैं, कभी सिर्फ numbers मत जोड़ो।

Field और dipole। Field lines positive पर शुरू होती हैं, negative पर खत्म, कभी cross नहीं करतीं, और उनकी density field की strength बताती है। Dipole का field one over r cubed के हिसाब से मरता है, क्योंकि opposite charges लगभग cancel हो जाते हैं। Axial, equatorial का दोगुना है, और दोनों उल्टी तरफ point करते हैं। Uniform field में dipole को सिर्फ twist मिलता है, push कभी नहीं। और p minus से plus की तरफ point करता है।

Continuous distributions। काटो, cancel करो, integrate करो। पूरा loop अपने centre पर zero देता है; आधा loop two k lambda over R। Disc पास से बस infinite sheet है, और दूर से बस point charge। और density को geometry से match करो: length के लिए lambda, surface के लिए sigma, volume के लिए rho।

Gauss। Flux गिनता है कि अंदर क्या है -- surface का shape और बाहर के charges matter नहीं करते। Gaussian surface को symmetry से match करो। Sheet उसे आधा करती है, conductor नहीं। और shell के अंदर कुछ नहीं है, जबकि solid sphere के अंदर field linear है।

एक numerical set हूबहू साथ रखने लायक: cube के centre पर point charge total flux q over epsilon nought देता है, हर face से q over six epsilon nought, और अगर charge corner पर हो तो q over eight epsilon nought।

<excited> यही है Electric Charges and Fields, पूरा। तुम बालों पर comb रगड़ने से चलकर चार Maxwell equations में से एक तक पहुँचे हो, और बीच का हर result बनाया गया है, थोपा नहीं गया। जाओ और इसका इस्तेमाल करो।
